title: Scalable Exact Non-Pauli Noise Simulation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum design relies on simulating noisy quantum error correction (QEC) circuits with hundreds to thousands of physical qubits and large circuit depths. High-throughput stabilizer simulators, such as Stim, are the de facto tools for this regime. However, these simulators typically support only Clifford gates and stochastic Pauli noise. As a result, more realistic device noise models-such as coherent control errors and thermal relaxation-are often approximated using Pauli Twirling. This replacement offers speed but can introduce inaccuracies. To address this, we propose QuasiStim for scalable exact QEC simulation of realistic noise, with QuasiFold as a compiler frontend and DeltaFrame as a sampling backend. QuasiFold lowers sampling overhead by merging equivalent non-Pauli sites in the quantum circuit. DeltaFrame samples the resulting stabilizer trajectories by reusing precomputed predicted references instead of resimulating the full tableau for each shot. QuasiFold can reduce the number of shots by over $100\times$ on bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes. Compared to a per-shot tableau simulator, DeltaFrame is $166\times$--$1331\times$ faster on rotated surface-code memory under coherent $R_Z$ noise as $d$ grows from 5 to 35. QuasiStim also makes the PTA bias measurable: the gap is non-negligible and varies with noise strength, decoder, and circuit schedule. QuasiStim will be open-sourced upon publication at https://github.com/isaachyw/QuasiStim
one_liner: QuasiStim enables scalable, exact fault-tolerant circuit simulation under coherent and other non-Pauli noise.
why_it_matters: It exposes noise-model biases hidden by Pauli twirling while making realistic large-scale QEC simulations substantially more tractable.
detailed_summary: QuasiStim combines the QuasiFold compiler frontend with the DeltaFrame trajectory-sampling backend to simulate realistic non-Pauli noise without replacing it by Pauli-twirled approximations. QuasiFold merges equivalent non-Pauli circuit sites, while DeltaFrame reuses predicted stabilizer references across shots. Reported benchmarks show over 100-fold shot reduction for bivariate-bicycle codes and 166–1331-fold speedups over per-shot tableau simulation for distance-5 to distance-35 surface-code memories under coherent RZ noise.
main_result: The framework scales exact non-Pauli QEC simulation while quantifying decoder-, schedule-, and noise-dependent bias from Pauli-twirled approximations.
application_angle: It supports more faithful hardware-aware evaluation of QEC codes, decoders, and control-error budgets before deployment on fault-tolerant processors.

title: QIAP: A Quantum-Inspired Authentication Protocol with BB84-Based Channel Monitoring
abstract: Authentication in quantum-aware communication settings requires mechanisms that verify user legitimacy while also assessing whether the communication channel exhibits excessive disturbance. This paper presents QIAP, a stateful hybrid framework that combines classical commitment-based challenge-response authentication with BB84-based quantum-channel monitoring. QIAP uses a dual-branch verification structure inspired by rectilinear and diagonal basis selection. In the rectilinear branch, the prover opens a hash-based commitment and the verifier checks consistency with the registered round token. In the diagonal branch, the prover returns an HMAC tag bound to the verifier nonce, round identifier, and submitted commitment without disclosing the round-specific sub-secret. Under the stated hash, HMAC, freshness, secure-registration, protected-storage, and high-entropy-secret assumptions, QIAP provides computational resistance to the modeled wrong-secret and replay attempts and protects the long-term master secret from direct recovery. After successful authentication, the BB84 module estimates the quantum bit error rate (QBER) and aborts the session when the measured value reaches or exceeds the configured threshold. In the reported simulation, no successful authentication was observed among 1,000 tested wrong-secret attempts per branch. The baseline and full intercept-resend conditions produced mean QBER values of approximately 0.02 and 0.25, respectively. The classical authentication stage required approximately 0.6 ms, and the implemented authentication messages required approximately 113 bytes per round. These results indicate that QIAP can provide a lightweight hybrid framework for combining secret-based identity verification with QBER-based channel-disturbance assessment under the stated threat model.
one_liner: QIAP couples commitment- and HMAC-based authentication to BB84 QBER monitoring in a stateful hybrid protocol.
why_it_matters: The design offers lightweight identity verification and quantum-channel disturbance screening, although its reported evidence is simulation-based.
detailed_summary: QIAP alternates between a commitment-opening branch and an HMAC branch that binds a verifier nonce, round identifier, and commitment without revealing the round sub-secret. After authentication, a BB84 module estimates QBER and aborts at a configured threshold. Simulations found no successful authentication among 1,000 wrong-secret trials per branch, with mean QBER near 0.02 at baseline and 0.25 under full intercept-resend; the classical stage took about 0.6 ms with roughly 113-byte messages.
main_result: Under the stated assumptions and simulated threat model, QIAP rejected tested wrong secrets and distinguished baseline from intercept-resend disturbance through QBER.
application_angle: The protocol targets low-overhead access control for quantum-aware links that need both user authentication and channel-integrity monitoring.

title: Device-to-protocol simulation of spectrally-resolved quantum photonic circuits
abstract: Predicting quantum-photonic circuit performance requires retaining source and device physics without making photon-counting calculations prohibitively expensive. Here we present PhoQuS, a framework that combines frequency-resolved source models, electromagnetic compact models and spatially correlated fabrication variation to simulate quantum photonic circuits. Covariance-Gram reduction after full-resolution Gaussian propagation lowers readout cost while retaining dominant spectral correlations. For continuous-variable state preparation, spectral reduction accelerates photon counting by 60.4-fold in an approximate Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill circuit. Frequency-resolved modeling guides the use of cascaded squeezing with temporal walk-off compensation, yielding 0.99 fidelity to the single-mode circuit reference and 0.98 conditional purity in lossless simulations. For discrete-variable state preparation, simulations of three-photon Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger circuits across a virtual wafer show that component robustness alone does not predict circuit fidelity, which depends jointly on source spectra, circuit architecture and control. PhoQuS connects device physics to protocol-level performance through a unified workflow that retains spectral detail while reducing readout cost.
one_liner: PhoQuS links spectral source physics, compact device models, fabrication variation, and protocol-level photonic performance.
why_it_matters: It makes frequency-resolved virtual prototyping practical and reveals circuit failures that component-only robustness metrics can miss.
detailed_summary: PhoQuS propagates frequency-resolved Gaussian source and device models together with spatially correlated fabrication variations, then applies covariance-Gram reduction before photon counting. The reduction accelerates readout by 60.4-fold for an approximate GKP preparation circuit while retaining dominant spectral correlations. Simulated cascaded squeezing with walk-off compensation reaches 0.99 fidelity and 0.98 conditional purity in the lossless case, while virtual-wafer GHZ studies show that source spectra, architecture, control, and component variation jointly determine fidelity.
main_result: PhoQuS provides a unified device-to-protocol workflow with a 60.4-fold photon-counting acceleration and high-fidelity spectrally compensated state preparation in simulation.
application_angle: The framework can guide fabrication-tolerant circuit design, source engineering, and wafer-scale yield assessment for photonic quantum processors.

title: Probe Signatures of Quantum Chaos with Quantum Sensing
abstract: The spectral form factor (SFF), which is the Fourier transform of the two-point spectral correlation, is a fundamental diagnostics of quantum chaos. Nevertheless, its experimental detection in quantum many-body systems was less unexplored until recently. Here, we establish a relationship between the SFF with the quantum Fisher information (QFI) by means of quantum sensing protocols. Furthermore, when the eigenvalues and eigenstates of the disordered Hamiltonian are statistically independent, we prove that QFI is typical both in short and long timescales while numerics suggest that it is also typical at intermediate timescales, which ensures self-averaging of QFI. The self-averaging property renders the experimental measurement of QFI with our protocol less noisy in contrast with the direct measurement of SFF which is known to be non-self-averaging. Our results reveal an intriguing connection between quantum noise and the signatures of quantum chaos.
one_liner: A quantum-sensing protocol connects quantum Fisher information to the spectral form factor used to diagnose many-body quantum chaos.
why_it_matters: Self-averaging QFI could provide a less noisy experimental route to chaos signatures than direct spectral-form-factor measurements.
detailed_summary: The work derives a relationship between quantum Fisher information and the spectral form factor through quantum-sensing protocols. When disordered-Hamiltonian eigenvalues and eigenstates are statistically independent, QFI is proven typical at short and long times, with numerics indicating typicality at intermediate times. This self-averaging behavior is proposed to reduce measurement noise relative to the non-self-averaging spectral form factor.
main_result: The study establishes QFI as a self-averaging proxy for spectral correlations and hence for signatures of quantum chaos under stated statistical conditions.
application_angle: The protocol may enable experimentally cleaner chaos diagnostics in controllable many-body platforms using established quantum-metrology observables.

title: Time-Frequency Continuous-Variable Quantum Teleportation with Single Photons
abstract: Quantum teleportation, a key building block for quantum technologies, enables distant parties, Alice and Bob, to transfer an unknown quantum state using entanglement, local operations, and classical communication. In this work, we propose a quantum teleportation protocol for single-photon time-frequency continuous variables, where time is the time of arrival at a detector. We detail the operational requirements of the protocol, notably the nonlinear interactions needed for the photon-photon time-frequency entangling gate. By explicitly treating the detector position as the reference frame for time of arrival, we show that, even with ideal classical and quantum channels, the input-output fidelity is not unity unless the receiving party can correct the detector-position mismatch. This results in a trade-off between teleportation fidelity and the temporal bandwidth of the input photon wavepacket. The protocol itself can be used for remote detector synchronization. In particular, we show that time-frequency cat and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states provide an internal temporal ruler through fidelity revivals. We further derive the classical and best-copy fidelity thresholds for single-photon Gaussian wavepackets, finding that the relevant vacuum-equivalent shot noise is input-dependent, in contrast with quadrature-based continuous-variable quantum teleportation. Our proposal derives from a quantum theory of space-time events, whereafter we establish space as a reference for the time degree of freedom, thereby grounding our work in ongoing research on reference frames and superselection rules in quantum optics and quantum information. Beyond protocols harnessing time-frequency continuous variables of single photons, this work points toward remote synchronization in quantum communication architectures.
one_liner: A protocol teleports single-photon time-frequency states while exposing detector position as a fidelity-limiting reference-frame mismatch.
why_it_matters: It connects photonic teleportation to remote clock synchronization and supplies operational fidelity benchmarks for time-frequency encodings.
detailed_summary: The proposed protocol teleports continuous time-frequency degrees of freedom of a single photon using entanglement, classical communication, and a nonlinear photon-photon entangling gate. Treating detector position as the reference frame for arrival time yields a bandwidth-dependent fidelity penalty unless Bob corrects the position mismatch. Time-frequency cat and GKP states produce fidelity revivals that act as an internal temporal ruler, and the work derives classical and best-copy thresholds for Gaussian wavepackets.
main_result: The theory identifies detector-reference mismatch as a fundamental teleportation error and shows how structured photonic states can support remote synchronization.
application_angle: The protocol could combine quantum-state transfer with detector or clock synchronization in time-frequency quantum networks.

title: Deterministic preparation of squeezed and non-Gaussian states in coupled qubit-boson systems
abstract: Deterministic preparation of bosonic resource states is a central task in continuous-variable quantum information processing and quantum metrology. Here we develop a measurement-based imaginary time evolution (MITE) protocol for preparing squeezed and non-Gaussian states. The protocol combines ancilla-mediated weak measurements of the Hamiltonian with a conditional phase rotation that suppresses excited state trapping and stabilizes convergence toward the ground state. The method is potentially applicable in hybrid discrete variable-continuous variable (DV-CV) platforms, where the qubit acts as the measurement readout. We demonstrate deterministic convergence over a broad range of parameters and show that the performance degradation near the stability boundary is governed by the shrinking Bogoliubov quasiparticle gap. The same framework also extends to non-Gaussian bosonic resource states, including Schrödinger cat states and excited states of the single-mode squeezing Hamiltonian, which display Wigner negativity. The squeezed states remain robust under bosonic loss over experimentally relevant regimes.
one_liner: Measurement-based imaginary-time evolution deterministically prepares squeezed, cat, and other non-Gaussian bosonic states.
why_it_matters: The method expands deterministic resource-state preparation for continuous-variable computation and sensing in hybrid qubit-boson hardware.
detailed_summary: The protocol uses ancilla-mediated weak Hamiltonian measurements plus conditional phase rotation to avoid excited-state trapping and drive convergence toward a target ground state. Numerical results show deterministic convergence across broad parameter ranges, with degradation near the stability boundary controlled by the closing Bogoliubov quasiparticle gap. Extensions prepare Schrödinger-cat states and excited squeezed-Hamiltonian states with Wigner negativity, while squeezed states remain robust under experimentally relevant bosonic loss.
main_result: The proposed MITE protocol deterministically converges to squeezed and non-Gaussian bosonic resource states across broad simulated operating regimes.
application_angle: It offers a hardware-compatible route to resource states for continuous-variable quantum processing, enhanced metrology, and bosonic encoding.

title: Collective Floquet engineering between two distant superconducting artificial atoms
abstract: A one-dimensional waveguide is a crucial medium for transferring propagating quantum information between remote qubits, yet the photon-mediated interaction is typically fixed by the static device geometry, qubit parameters, and their couplings to the transmission line. Such an interaction can be engineered to be coherent or dissipative via virtual- or real-photon exchange, respectively, yet its effective strength remains fixed in either case. Here we demonstrate dynamical control over this interaction by applying Floquet engineering to two superconducting qubits coupled to a waveguide terminated by a capacitive mirror. By positioning one qubit at an antinode and the other qubit at a node or an antinode of the resonant standing wave, we realize a Hermitian or non-Hermitian coupling between the two qubits. A periodic flux drive of the qubit frequencies then enables on-demand control of the coherent energy splitting and the collective decay. Our results establish Floquet engineering as a route to dynamically reshape both coherent and dissipative photon-mediated interactions between remote quantum emitters.
one_liner: Floquet driving dynamically tunes coherent and dissipative photon-mediated coupling between two remote superconducting qubits.
why_it_matters: On-demand control of remote-qubit interactions could enable reconfigurable waveguide-QED networks and engineered open-system dynamics.
detailed_summary: Two superconducting qubits are coupled through a one-dimensional waveguide terminated by a capacitive mirror. Placing the qubits at selected standing-wave nodes or antinodes realizes Hermitian or non-Hermitian coupling. Periodic flux modulation then controls the coherent energy splitting and collective decay on demand.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates dynamical Floquet control of both coherent and dissipative interactions between spatially separated artificial atoms.
application_angle: The technique supports programmable coupling in modular quantum processors, quantum networks, and dissipative state-engineering hardware.

title: Metasurface quantum graphs for polarization-independent certified randomness
abstract: Quantum random number generators are crucial for information security, yet existing implementations are hindered by bulky optics, device imperfections, and state alignment constraints. Here, using a compact metasurface platform, we achieve polarization-independent certified randomness by establishing a quantitative quantum graph framework. By mapping multi-channel nanophotonic responses onto graph vertices, we assign metasurface measurements an operational information-theoretic meaning, directly connecting weighted graph degrees to conditional min-entropy estimation. The resulting graph-certified measurements yield robust private randomness even under entanglement-based attacks without complex optics. Experimentally, we fabricate 4- and 6-channel dielectric metasurfaces to implement high-dimensional positive operator-valued measure graphs, successfully certifying randomness with heralded single photons and Poissonian light. By integrating complex quantum measurements into a single passive layer, our metasurface quantum graphs provide a scalable route for integrated quantum technologies.
one_liner: A passive dielectric metasurface implements high-dimensional measurements for polarization-independent certified quantum randomness.
why_it_matters: It replaces bulky alignment-sensitive optics with a compact layer while retaining security against entanglement-based attacks.
detailed_summary: The authors map multichannel nanophotonic responses onto quantum graphs whose weighted degrees determine conditional min-entropy. Fabricated four- and six-channel dielectric metasurfaces implement high-dimensional positive operator-valued measurements. Experiments certify private randomness using both heralded single photons and Poissonian light without requiring polarization alignment.
main_result: The metasurface experimentally certifies polarization-independent private randomness under an adversarial model that includes entanglement-based attacks.
application_angle: A single passive optical layer could enable compact, scalable quantum random-number generators for secure integrated photonic systems.

title: Pathfinder-BP: A Low-Latency Recursive Decoder for Topological Codes
abstract: We propose Pathfinder-BP, a recursive decoder for topological quantum codes that combines belief propagation with controlled bit-flipping. An initial BP pass identifies and permanently fixes high-confidence errors. Upon convergence failure, the decoder recursively explores alternative error patterns by tentatively flipping low-confidence variables. On surface codes, Pathfinder-BP achieves a noise threshold and logical error rate comparable to minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM). A crucial advantage of Pathfinder-BP is its highly parallelizable structure, which yields a worst-case decoding latency quasi-linear in the code distance, making it a suitable candidate for low-latency hardware implementation.
one_liner: Pathfinder-BP combines belief propagation and recursive bit flips to decode topological quantum codes with low latency.
why_it_matters: Its parallel structure offers MWPM-like surface-code performance with hardware-friendly, quasi-linear worst-case latency in code distance.
detailed_summary: Pathfinder-BP first uses belief propagation to identify and permanently fix high-confidence errors. If convergence fails, it recursively tests alternative patterns by flipping low-confidence variables. Surface-code simulations show thresholds and logical error rates comparable to minimum-weight perfect matching, while the architecture remains highly parallelizable.
main_result: The decoder achieves MWPM-comparable surface-code performance with worst-case latency that is quasi-linear in code distance.
application_angle: The approach is suited to real-time FPGA or ASIC decoding for fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: QBFF: Deep Quantum Bottleneck for Automatic Speaker Verification Anti-Spoofing
abstract: A central goal of quantum machine learning is to identify applications in which small quantum circuits can improve task performance while remaining executable on real hardware. We investigate deepfake (synthetic) speech detection, a largely unexplored application in this area, where reliable confidence scores are as important as discrimination performance because deployment decisions are made at fixed thresholds and overconfident errors can be costly. We introduce QBFF, which routes a compressed speech representation through a small 8-qubit variational circuit (VQC) used as a drop-in bottleneck, with a matched classical bottleneck as the control. The quantum circuit yields better-calibrated confidence in most matched comparisons, including out-of-distribution evaluation, though the downstream deployment-cost benefit is model-dependent. We then run the same circuit on a real IBM quantum processor. To our knowledge, this is the first anti-spoofing pipeline to run on a QPU; hardware execution demonstrates feasibility, with lower subset EER and $C_{llr}$ but higher mean actDCF than the matched classical reference. Together, these results show that hardware-executable quantum bottlenecks can improve score reliability, with gains that vary by evaluation setting.
one_liner: An eight-qubit variational bottleneck for speech anti-spoofing is evaluated in simulation and on an IBM quantum processor.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates an end-to-end anti-spoofing pipeline on real quantum hardware and probes calibration benefits beyond raw classification accuracy.
detailed_summary: QBFF compresses speech features and passes them through an eight-qubit variational quantum circuit used as a drop-in neural-network bottleneck. Against a matched classical bottleneck, it generally improves confidence calibration, including out-of-distribution tests, although deployment-cost gains vary by model. Execution on an IBM processor establishes hardware feasibility and produces mixed results across EER, calibration loss, and actDCF.
main_result: The study runs a quantum speech anti-spoofing pipeline on a QPU and finds setting-dependent improvements in score reliability and selected error metrics.
application_angle: Hardware-executable quantum bottlenecks may improve confidence estimation in security systems that detect synthetic or spoofed speech.

title: Magic-Free Certification of Logical Error Rates in Universal Fault-Tolerant Circuits
abstract: As quantum hardware enters the fault-tolerant regime, algorithms are beginning to be executed on encoded qubits, yet scalable certification of how well they run remains an open problem. Here we introduce magic-free certification, a certification protocol for universal fault-tolerant circuits that consumes no magic, the resource that generally places them beyond efficient classical simulation and is by far the most expensive element of a fault-tolerant computation. The protocol is code- and decoder-agnostic, runs interleaved with the target circuit on the same device, and has a sample complexity that grows linearly with the number of logical qubits and non-Clifford gates while remaining decoupled from the logical error rate itself. Given a predefined error tolerance $p_L^*$, the protocol determines at a chosen confidence level whether the device executes the target circuit at a logical error rate below $p_L^*$. The method relies on trap circuits, copies of the target with every magic state replaced by a stabilizer state, whose outcomes are deterministic and which, being indistinguishable from the target to stochastic Pauli noise, fail at the same rate. We illustrate the protocol in Steane-code simulations of a magic state injection gadget and a quantum Fourier transform.
one_liner: Magic-free trap circuits certify whether universal fault-tolerant computations meet a target logical-error threshold.
why_it_matters: The protocol avoids costly magic consumption and scales linearly with logical qubits and non-Clifford gates while remaining code-agnostic.
detailed_summary: The protocol interleaves a target fault-tolerant circuit with trap copies in which each magic state is replaced by a stabilizer state. These traps have deterministic outputs yet experience the same failure rate as the target under stochastic Pauli noise. Simulations using the Steane code cover a magic-state injection gadget and a quantum Fourier transform.
main_result: The method determines at chosen confidence whether a target circuit's logical error rate lies below a preset tolerance without consuming magic states.
application_angle: It provides a scalable acceptance test for encoded workloads as quantum processors transition into the fault-tolerant regime.

title: Fading Memory and Nonlinear Dynamics in a Microring Resonator Network and their Use in Computation
abstract: Silicon microring resonators are promising components for photonic reservoir computing because their nonlinear optical response can transform signals and retain information about recent inputs. Under constant optical excitation, their coupled free-carrier and thermal dynamics can generate self-pulsing: a periodic output response. However, constant-input behavior does not reveal how these dynamics respond to randomly modulated signals or whether their memory is useful for temporal processing. Here, we characterize a single silicon microring resonator and a passive network of microring resonators under random input modulation. The temporal component associated with self-pulsing remains observable under random modulation, but the largest fading memory occurs near the self-pulsing boundary, where no resolved self-pulsing-like oscillation is present. reservoir computing metrics, such as memory capacity, map this accessible memory, and its decay provides effective timescales associated mainly with free-carrier and thermal relaxation. Finally, we use NARMA reconstruction to test whether the measured memory profile supports nonlinear temporal processing. Responses with a resolved self-pulsing-like component perform worse on this task, and the intrinsic memory profile is not matched to the required input history. These results show that reservoir computing metrics can characterize nonlinear microring resonator dynamics even when the physical system is not an effective standalone reservoir for the selected task.
one_liner: Experiments map fading memory and nonlinear dynamics in silicon microrings under random modulation for reservoir computing.
why_it_matters: The work identifies where useful optical memory occurs and shows that visible self-pulsing does not necessarily improve temporal computation.
detailed_summary: A single silicon microring and a passive microring network are characterized under randomly modulated optical inputs. Memory capacity peaks near the self-pulsing boundary rather than where self-pulsing-like oscillations are resolved, with decay times linked mainly to carrier and thermal relaxation. NARMA reconstruction shows that the measured memory profile is poorly matched to the selected task and that resolved self-pulsing degrades performance.
main_result: The measurements locate maximum fading memory near the self-pulsing boundary and show that strong self-pulsing worsens NARMA reconstruction.
application_angle: The characterization method can guide operating-point and device selection for photonic reservoir computers and other nonlinear optical processors.

title: Deterministic positioning accuracy of B centers in hBN by electron irradiation
abstract: Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a promising material platform for quantum technologies, enabling both the realization of nanophotonic devices and the hosting of point defects that act as high-quality single-photon emitters (SPEs). Among these defects, B centers, which reproducibly emit at 436 nm, can be generated individually at predefined positions using electron beam irradiation, a crucial capability for top-down quantum photonics. Yet, the spatial accuracy of emitter creation strongly conditions the potential applications. Here, we generate arrays of individual B centers in a scanning electron microscope (SEM) with in-situ cathodoluminescence (CL) monitoring. We characterize the sources of random deviations from the target positions to identify the limitations to their deterministic positioning. In particular, we measure the distance between the electron beam and the emitter at the moment the emitter is created based on CL mapping. This approach provides a direct estimation of the spatial extent of the beam-emitter interaction. We find this contribution to be the main constraint to the emitter fabrication accuracy, yielding a standard deviation of 27 nm. Additional contributions, primarily from the finite density of UV-emitting carbon dimer precursors, increase the overall positional standard deviation to 40 nm. Our results highlight the possible improvements to the B center creation technique to reach sub-10 nm accuracy.
one_liner: In-situ cathodoluminescence maps quantify the nanoscale positioning accuracy of electron-beam-created B-center emitters in hBN.
why_it_matters: Identifying the dominant 27 nm beam–emitter interaction limit provides a concrete route toward sub-10 nm placement of single-photon sources in nanophotonic devices.
detailed_summary: Arrays of individual 436 nm B centers are written at predefined locations in hBN by SEM electron irradiation while their creation is monitored through in-situ cathodoluminescence. CL mapping directly measures the beam-to-emitter displacement at creation and attributes a 27 nm standard deviation to the spatial extent of the interaction. Precursor-density effects and other contributions raise the total positional standard deviation to 40 nm, while the analysis identifies pathways toward sub-10 nm accuracy.
main_result: The experiment measures 40 nm overall placement deviation and identifies the 27 nm beam–emitter interaction spread as the dominant fabrication limit.
application_angle: More accurate deterministic placement would enable efficient alignment of blue single-photon emitters with cavities, waveguides, and other top-down nanophotonic structures.

title: Bell's go theorem: regaining local causality with a new notion of realism
abstract: Bell's theorem is popularly stated as the inconsistency of quantum theory with local realism. Realism is here formalized by the ontological models framework, where elements of reality are points of a measurable space and probabilities obey the Kolmogorov axioms. In the Bell scenario, locally causal ontological models posit a common cause supporting a global valuation, a joint assignment of outcomes to all measurements at once, across incompatible contexts. Within this notion of realism, Bell's theorem makes any realist explanation of the quantum predictions conspiratorial: any mechanism, whether superluminal, superdeterministic, or retrocausal, must be finely tuned so as never to manifest operationally. We redefine realism through a new ontological framework that generalizes the standard one. The elements of reality, which we call records, are no longer points but relational parts of a point-free generalization of a topological space (sublocales of a locale). A record shared by two incompatible contexts establishes the sameness of a measurement across them, without such pairwise identities composing into a global valuation, and the common cause is then a web of such records. Within this framework, Bell's no-go theorem becomes a go theorem: local causality, restated for records, is no longer at odds with the quantum statistics. This is possible because modularity, the inclusion-exclusion law of classical probability, fails across incompatible contexts, so that the probability theory generalizes Kolmogorov's. We exhibit explicit models reproducing several quantum strategies, including the optimal CHSH violation. More broadly, locally causal models of this kind attain every Bell-CHSH value up to the algebraic maximum. A realist explanation of the quantum predictions need not be conspiratorial; every causal influence posited by these models is reflected in the operational predictions.
one_liner: A point-free ontological framework reproduces quantum Bell correlations while retaining a generalized form of local causality.
why_it_matters: The work proposes a mathematically unconventional foundation for locally causal explanations of Bell-test statistics, including optimal and algebraic CHSH values.
detailed_summary: The authors replace point-valued ontic states with relational records represented as sublocales of a locale. Pairwise records can identify measurements across incompatible contexts without composing into a global valuation, while probability need not obey classical modularity across those contexts. Explicit models reproduce several quantum strategies, including optimal CHSH violation, and the framework can attain Bell-CHSH values up to the algebraic maximum.
main_result: Generalized record-based ontological models reproduce quantum Bell statistics under a reformulated local-causality condition.
application_angle: Although foundational rather than device-oriented, the framework may affect how causal assumptions and security-relevant Bell correlations are interpreted in quantum networks.

title: Towards the Geometry of Quantum Optical Measurements: Kraus Trajectories in the Instrumental Weyl-Heisenberg Group Manifold
abstract: Since ancient Greek times, geometry has been a method by which humans can make inferences, by the use of similar triangles, about the world far beyond their immediate senses. Similarity plays an equally important role in quantum measurement, except that instead of triangles, the similarity is between the infinitesimal generators of rotation, canonical transformation, or some other virtual symmetry. For many quantum optical measurements of a single mode, these generators produce Kraus operators that are contained within a twelve-dimensional Lie group: the Instrumental Weyl-Heisenberg group manifold ($\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$). In particular, $\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$ is general enough to include all diffusively generated 'dyne measurements. In this paper, $\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$ will be used to develop two more general classes of 'dyne measurement: one that interpolates between diffusive homodyne and diffusive heterodyne (``slomodyne'') and one that adds to 'dyne measurements adaptive squeezing and displacement. Our analysis uses an approach known as the Instrument Manifold Program (IMP). In particular, a Harish-Chandra-like decomposition of $\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$ is used to calculate the vielbein transformation from a right-invariant basis to the corresponding coordinate basis, allowing us to universally and autonomously navigate $\mathrm{IWH}^{\textbf{12}}$ and locate the Kraus-operator of whatever selective process is being considered as it evolves in time according to the measurement record.
one_liner: A 12-dimensional Lie-group description unifies diffusive optical measurements and enables adaptive Kraus-trajectory tracking.
why_it_matters: The formalism supplies a systematic design and simulation toolkit for homodyne, heterodyne, interpolating, and adaptively squeezed optical measurements.
detailed_summary: Single-mode quantum-optical Kraus operators are embedded in a 12-dimensional Instrumental Weyl-Heisenberg group manifold that includes diffusively generated dyne measurements. The construction introduces “slomodyne” measurements interpolating between homodyne and heterodyne detection, plus dyne schemes with adaptive squeezing and displacement. A Harish-Chandra-like decomposition and vielbein transformation allow measurement-conditioned Kraus trajectories to be navigated in group coordinates.
main_result: The group-manifold formalism unifies standard diffusive dyne detection and constructs new interpolating and adaptive measurement classes.
application_angle: It could guide the design of adaptive receivers, continuous weak-measurement protocols, and feedback-enabled optical sensing systems.

title: Fisher-Information Certification from Bell Statistics: CHSH Bounds, Information Loss, and Finite-Data Guarantees
abstract: Bell-test data are typically used to certify nonlocal correlations, while quantum metrology is concerned with the sensitivity of measurement statistics to unknown parameters. Here we connect these tasks at the level of experimentally accessible Bell statistics. Using standard moment-based Fisher-information inequalities, we derive lower bounds on the classical Fisher information directly from Bell scores and their parameter dependence, without requiring full state tomography. For CHSH measurements we establish a hierarchy between the information contained in the full outcome record, the set of individual correlators, and the compressed Bell parameter, thereby quantifying the metrological cost of data compression. In polarization-phase sensing, this hierarchy reveals a Bell-metrology tradeoff: the point of maximal CHSH violation need not maximize, and can even suppress, the Fisher information carried by the Bell score itself. We further derive finite-sample lower-confidence bounds from coincidence counts and analyze the effects of biased marginals, accidental coincidences, visibility loss, and multipair emission. The framework provides a practical route for extracting metrological guarantees from Bell-type experiments using only standard correlation measurements.
one_liner: CHSH statistics are converted into tomography-free Fisher-information bounds with explicit finite-sample confidence guarantees.
why_it_matters: The method lets existing Bell-test measurements certify parameter sensitivity while exposing information lost when full coincidence records are compressed into one Bell score.
detailed_summary: Moment-based inequalities lower-bound classical Fisher information using measured Bell scores and their parameter derivatives, without full state tomography. For CHSH experiments, the authors compare information retained in complete outcomes, individual correlators, and the compressed Bell parameter. Polarization-phase analysis reveals that maximal Bell violation can suppress Bell-score sensitivity, while finite-count bounds incorporate biased marginals, accidentals, visibility loss, and multipair emission.
main_result: The framework derives experimentally accessible Fisher-information lower bounds and finite-sample confidence limits directly from Bell-test coincidence statistics.
application_angle: Bell experiments can reuse standard correlation data to certify sensing performance and quantify practical degradation without adding tomographic measurements.

title: Realistic simulation of universal multiport interferometers with losses within a Gaussian formalism
abstract: Photonic technologies are among the leading platform contenders for demonstrating quantum advantage. Nevertheless, photon losses represent the major hurdle for the realization of a fault-tolerant optical quantum computer, and the need for an accurate characterization of this phenomenon is crucial for classical simulations of quantum algorithms on noisy backends. The noisy regime would require the simulation of the algorithm on a Fock backend or rather assuming the a priori hypothesis on the uniformity of the optical losses, which may lead to wrong predictions about the outcome from the algorithm on a cerain hardware. We propose a Gaussian model that can reproduce a lossy dynamics through the experimental characterization of imperfect interferometers, yielding the corresponding mean vector and the covariance matrix. Such model can be adapted to any continuous-variable architecture (spatial or time-bin encoded) and for both the Gaussian boson sampling or general-dyne based algorithms. Eventually, we quantify the drift of optical losses from being uniform throughout the multiport interferometer by a numerical simulation. This work proposes a blueprint for future characterizations, tailor-suited for specific devices and architectures, as well as for potential error correction and mitigation techniques, and it paves the way for realistic simulations of quantum algorithms on NISQ optical platforms.
one_liner: A Gaussian model uses measured interferometer imperfections to simulate nonuniform loss in universal photonic multiports.
why_it_matters: Device-specific loss maps can make noisy optical-algorithm simulations more credible than models assuming uniform attenuation across an interferometer.
detailed_summary: The proposed model converts experimental characterization of an imperfect multiport into the mean vector and covariance matrix of its lossy Gaussian dynamics. It supports spatial- and time-bin continuous-variable architectures, including Gaussian boson sampling and general-dyne algorithms. Numerical analysis quantifies departures from uniform-loss assumptions and motivates device-tailored characterization, mitigation, and correction strategies.
main_result: The work provides a Gaussian blueprint for simulating experimentally characterized, spatially nonuniform losses in universal interferometers.
application_angle: The model supports hardware-faithful benchmarking, error mitigation, and algorithm assessment for near-term optical quantum processors.

title: Finite-event modulation transfer through forward-scattering media
abstract: How spatial structure is transferred through a forward-scattering medium depends jointly on pattern scale and propagation distance. Starting from photon exit displacements, we derive modulation transfer while retaining the number, depths, and projected angles of individual deflections, with event occurrences described by a homogeneous Poisson process along the propagation path. The second angular moment yields a leading low-frequency loss proportional to $k^2z^3$, where $k$ is angular spatial frequency and $z$ is thickness. At finite frequency, the model predicts two coupled departures: loss bends below its low-frequency quadratic extrapolation at fixed thickness, and transfer curves separate by thickness at fixed $k^2z^3$. The leading corrections to both effects arise from the same fourth angular moment. For symmetric, nondegenerate projected-angle distributions, the full response further establishes increasing loss with thickness in the same medium at fixed joint variable. Binary-pattern measurements through TiO$_2$ suspensions span five nominal loadings, seven thicknesses, and 20 spatial frequencies, supporting the approximate low-frequency scaling and showing both departures. A Gaussian effective-angle response calibrated only on lower-frequency data predicts the held-out higher-frequency band without refitting, with a logarithmic root-mean-square error of 0.0181 compared with 0.1021 for quadratic extrapolation. The results show that finite-event statistics provide a common physical origin for spectral bending and thickness-dependent departure from low-frequency scaling, linking coarse-pattern transport to finer spatial structure.
one_liner: Finite scattering-event statistics explain modulation-transfer bending and thickness dependence in forward-scattering media.
why_it_matters: The model predicts fine-pattern transmission substantially better than quadratic extrapolation, aiding imaging and optical transport through turbid materials.
detailed_summary: The theory derives spatial modulation transfer from discrete photon deflections whose occurrences follow a homogeneous Poisson process along the path. The second angular moment produces the low-frequency loss scaling as k²z³, while the fourth moment generates spectral bending and thickness-dependent separation at finite frequency. Measurements across five TiO2 loadings, seven thicknesses, and 20 spatial frequencies support these effects; a low-frequency-calibrated Gaussian effective-angle model predicts held-out high-frequency data with 0.0181 logarithmic RMSE versus 0.1021 for quadratic extrapolation.
main_result: A finite-event scattering model jointly explains observed low-frequency scaling, high-frequency bending, and thickness-dependent modulation transfer.
application_angle: Improved transfer prediction can inform imaging, optical diagnostics, and spatial-pattern design in forward-scattering biological or industrial media.

title: Cavity-modified static polarizabilities of atoms and small molecules within QED full configuration interaction
abstract: Static dipole polarizabilities of H$_2$, LiH, and helium confined in a single-mode optical cavity are computed using quantum-electrodynamical full configuration interaction (QED-FCI). Response properties are obtained as finite-field derivatives of the coupled electron-photon energy. The cavity-induced modification is found to arise from the competition of two contributions of opposite sign, the dipole self-energy and photon exchange, whose relative strength depends on both the cavity frequency and the number of photons involved in the exchange. The residual change suppresses the response of the molecular ground electronic states. For the metastable states of helium atom this balance changes qualitatively, and the differential response of the $2\,^3S_1 \to 2\,^1S_0$ clock transition, which governs its sensitivity to static electric fields and to thermal radiation, is strongly enhanced instead. Cavity confinement can therefore either reduce or increase the dc Stark and blackbody-radiation shifts of a frequency standard, depending on the electronic structure of the states involved. The reported data serve as a reference for cavity-modified response and underscore the need for an exact treatment of light-matter correlation in cavity-QED predictions.
one_liner: QED-FCI predicts that optical cavities suppress ground-state polarizability but strongly enhance a helium clock transition's differential response.
why_it_matters: The results show that cavity engineering could tune dc Stark and blackbody-radiation shifts in precision frequency standards.
detailed_summary: The authors calculate static dipole polarizabilities of H2, LiH, and helium in a single-mode optical cavity using finite-field derivatives of QED-FCI energies. Opposing dipole-self-energy and photon-exchange contributions generally suppress molecular ground-state response. For metastable helium, however, the cavity strongly enhances the differential polarizability of the 2^3S1 to 2^1S0 clock transition.
platform_or_system: Atoms and small molecules in a single-mode optical cavity
main_result: Exact correlated calculations reveal state-dependent cavity control of polarizability, including strong enhancement for a metastable-helium clock transition.
application_angle: Cavity-controlled polarizability may enable engineered Stark and blackbody-shift sensitivity in atomic clocks and precision sensors.

title: Geodesic steering for rapid dissipative entanglement distribution
abstract: We describe an optimal-control strategy designed to accelerate the dissipative preparation of complex, highly entangled quantum many-body states. Analogous to optimal steering of isolated quantum systems, our scheme identifies control pulses that guide the evolution of open quantum systems along trajectories of instantaneous steady states while minimizing leakage resulting from non-adiabatic transitions. In many cases of interest, these control parameters can be derived analytically and without the need for computationally expensive numerical simulations of the full many-body master equation. We apply this technique for the preparation of bi- and multipartite entangled states in qubit systems coupled to a common photonic waveguide or a distributed squeezed reservoir. In both scenarios, our optimal-control strategy significantly outperforms the bare relaxation dynamics after a quench, reducing preparation times of near-maximally entangled states by orders of magnitude. This drastic speedup makes dissipative entanglement distribution protocols compatible with high-fidelity quantum information processing applications and illustrates more broadly the potential of leakage minimization for accelerating reservoir-engineering schemes.
one_liner: Geodesic control accelerates dissipative preparation of entangled qubit states in photonic reservoirs by orders of magnitude.
why_it_matters: Faster reservoir-engineered entanglement could make dissipative state distribution practical within quantum processors' finite coherence budgets.
detailed_summary: The work constructs control pulses that steer open systems along instantaneous steady-state trajectories while minimizing nonadiabatic leakage. Applied to qubits coupled through a common photonic waveguide or a distributed squeezed reservoir, the method prepares bipartite and multipartite entangled states. In representative cases, near-maximal entanglement is reached orders of magnitude faster than after a simple quench, with controls often obtainable analytically.
platform_or_system: Qubit arrays coupled to photonic waveguides or squeezed reservoirs
main_result: Leakage-minimizing geodesic steering reduces dissipative entanglement-preparation times by orders of magnitude.
application_angle: The protocol supports rapid, high-fidelity entanglement distribution for networked processors and reservoir-engineered quantum hardware.

title: Foundations for a Lens of Quantum Governance
abstract: The second quantum revolution is a revolution of information. Advances in quantum computation, communication, and sensing offer new capabilities while raising questions about how quantum infrastructures will be organised, accessed, and governed. We argue that their significance for governance lies not in transforming political principles, but in how their technical and infrastructural requirements may affect existing relationships of authority, responsibility, legitimacy, and power. This paper develops a quantum governance lens that connects governance scholarship with quantum information science, examining interactions between technical design, institutional arrangements, and infrastructural dependencies. We apply this lens to five areas: quantum computation, quantum key distribution, Quantum Byzantine Agreement, blind quantum computation, and dual-use quantum sensing. These applications illustrate how technical capabilities may influence access, trust, privacy, oversight, and accountability, while demonstrating that technical guarantees cannot resolve institutional questions independently. We conclude that quantum technologies do not necessarily introduce unique governance challenges or require entirely new governance frameworks. Rather, they provide a context in which established questions of legitimacy, accountability, and equity must be reconsidered in relation to emerging technological capabilities and institutional choices.
one_liner: A governance framework links quantum-system design and infrastructure to access, trust, privacy, oversight, and accountability.
why_it_matters: It clarifies where technical guarantees in QKD, blind computing, consensus, and sensing end and institutional governance must begin.
detailed_summary: This conceptual study develops a governance lens connecting quantum-information architectures with institutional authority, responsibility, legitimacy, and power. It applies the framework to quantum computing, QKD, Quantum Byzantine Agreement, blind quantum computing, and dual-use sensing. The analysis argues that technical guarantees shape governance conditions but cannot independently settle questions of access, accountability, or equity.
platform_or_system: Quantum communication, computing, and sensing infrastructures
main_result: The paper provides a cross-domain framework for analyzing how quantum technical choices interact with established governance challenges.
application_angle: The framework can inform policy, procurement, access models, and oversight for deployed quantum networks and dual-use sensors.

title: Photon-stimulated decay of $χ$-matched ancillas causes unheralded bit flips in bosonic codes
abstract: Bosonic codes often read out their syndrome with a transmon ancilla whose computational levels $g$ and $f$ have equal parity and matched dispersive shifts: a decay $f\to e$ is then heralded and leaves the code intact, while the direct $f\to g$ is forbidden by parity. We show that the photons of the code open this decay at first order in the ancilla's decay rate. Dressing by the code mode lets the charge noise that limits the ancilla's $T_1$ drive a photon-stimulated Raman decay $|f,n\rangle\to|g,n+1\rangle$, at $(n+1)(χ_{ge}/2g_{01})^2$ times the $f\to e$ rate for a smooth noise spectrum. When the matching is set by the detuning, the decay costs $\approxΓ_{fe}/α$ per gate and photon, whatever the coupling strength; a deliberate mismatch or matching by a drive lowers this cost, and a qubit ancilla has no such channel. The opened decay is unheralded and flips a cat with probability $\approx 1/2$; being first order, it overtakes the second-order double decay $f\to e\to g$ as the ancilla improves. In a microscopic model of the Ocelot repetition cat code, it makes the bit-flip floor of the gates grow linearly with the cat size, by a factor 1.2-1.7 from four to ten photons, which would limit the noise bias to $\sim 10^3$. The published gate data end at four photons and do not yet test this growth.
one_liner: Code photons can trigger an unheralded ancilla Raman decay that adds photons and causes bit flips in bosonic cat codes.
why_it_matters: This first-order channel may impose a growing error floor and cap the noise bias of otherwise improving bosonic-code hardware.
detailed_summary: Dispersive dressing allows ancilla charge noise to drive the nominally forbidden transition |f,n> to |g,n+1>, with a rate proportional to n+1. Because the decay is unheralded, it flips a cat state with roughly one-half probability and can dominate second-order cascade decay as ancilla quality improves. A microscopic Ocelot-code model predicts a bit-flip floor growing linearly with cat size and a noise-bias limit near 10^3.
platform_or_system: Circuit-QED bosonic cat code with transmon ancilla
main_result: The analysis identifies a first-order photon-stimulated ancilla-decay channel that creates an unheralded, cat-size-dependent bit-flip floor.
application_angle: The derived scaling and mitigation options guide ancilla selection, dispersive matching, and gate design for fault-tolerant bosonic processors.

title: Enhanced Quantum Metrology via Saddle-Point Scrambling in Phase Space
abstract: Nonlinear effects are widely utilized in quantum metrology to enhance measurement precision by leveraging complex dynamical behaviors. Here, we propose a quantum scrambling-integrated scheme that optimizes the selection of initial states and parameter encoding by exploiting the nonlinear dynamical trajectories and their geometric properties in phase space. We consider a two-mode Bose-Einstein condensate as a typical example. Within a certain parameter range, using uncorrelated spin coherent states located at saddle points and separatrices enables the measurement precision to reach the Heisenberg scaling. An analytical expression for the quantum Fisher information under long-time evolution is provided, and our analysis further reveals that the enhancement mechanism is governed by the sensitivity of the energy spectrum to parameter variations. Compared to the criticality-enhanced protocol that requires parameters to approach the critical point, our scheme offers a distinct advantage in its applicability over a broader range of parameters. Moreover, this scheme can also be applied to models that include one- and two-axis countertwisting interactions and chaotic dynamics. This Letter offers a new perspective for advancing the application of nonlinear dynamics to enhance the parameter estimation precision in quantum systems.
one_liner: Saddle-point and separatrix dynamics let initially uncorrelated two-mode condensates attain Heisenberg-scaling metrology.
why_it_matters: The scheme offers nonlinear quantum enhancement across a broader parameter range than protocols requiring operation near a critical point.
detailed_summary: The protocol places spin-coherent states at saddle points or separatrices of a nonlinear two-mode Bose-Einstein-condensate phase space. Long-time scrambling amplifies spectral sensitivity to the estimated parameter, producing Heisenberg scaling of the quantum Fisher information within a finite parameter range. The analysis extends to one- and two-axis countertwisting models and chaotic dynamics.
main_result: Nonlinear evolution from classically special phase-space trajectories enables Heisenberg-scaling sensitivity without initially entangled states.
application_angle: The approach could broaden the operating range of interaction-enhanced atomic interferometers and nonlinear quantum sensors.

title: Optical Detection of Coherent Nuclear Spin Control in a Molecular System at Room Temperature
abstract: Molecular systems with optically addressable electron spins are emerging as versatile quantum sensing platforms, offering tunable qubit properties and molecular-scale spatial control. Owing to their longer lifetimes, coupled nuclear spins provide an attractive resource for enhancing sensing performance. For molecular spin systems, the ability to initialise, coherently control and readout nuclear spins at room temperature is crucial for realising such benefits. Here, we present the first optical detection of nuclear magnetic resonance and coherent nuclear spin control with a molecular system at room temperature. Specifically, we demonstrate optically detected Rabi oscillations of $^{14}$N nuclear spins in the photoexcited triplet state of the organic chromophore 6,13-diazapentacene. The strong hyperfine coupling between the electronic spin and $^{14}$N nuclei enhances the nuclear Rabi frequency, enabling fast coherent nuclear-spin rotations. This work lays the foundation for leveraging nuclear spins as memories for enhanced molecular-based quantum sensing.
one_liner: Room-temperature optical readout resolves coherent 14N nuclear-spin Rabi oscillations in an organic molecular triplet state.
why_it_matters: Fast, optically accessible nuclear control creates a route to long-lived quantum memories and enhanced sensing in tunable molecular platforms.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses the photoexcited triplet state of 6,13-diazapentacene to initialize, drive, and optically detect coupled 14N nuclear spins at room temperature. Optically detected NMR reveals coherent nuclear Rabi oscillations. Strong electron-nuclear hyperfine coupling increases the nuclear Rabi frequency and permits rapid coherent rotations.
main_result: The study demonstrates room-temperature optical detection of NMR and coherent 14N nuclear-spin control in a molecular platform.
application_angle: Coupled nuclear spins could serve as durable memories that extend interrogation and storage times in molecular-scale quantum sensors.

title: Architecting Instruction Execution for Scalable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
abstract: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires orchestrating millions of operations continuously across a tightly coupled classical-quantum control stack. A critical challenge in this orchestration is determining the optimal hardware-software boundary, i.e., the Quantum Instruction Set Architecture (QISA). We focus on cryogenic, fixed-connectivity qubit platforms, such as superconducting and topological Majorana qubits. For these, existing QISA choices either operate at too low a level, violating cryogenic thermal budgets at scale, or at too high a level, imposing unrealizable complexity on the control engine. To reason about these tradeoffs, we introduce the ARIES instruction set hierarchy, which categorizes QISAs into distinct abstraction levels. To systematically evaluate these levels, we develop an end-to-end evaluation toolflow featuring a cycle-accurate classical driver and hardware engine simulator. Using eight quantum applications across superconducting and topological qubit platforms, we measure instruction bandwidth, transceiver power dissipation, and measurement processing overheads. We demonstrate that while physical-level abstractions exceed the thermal limits of dilution refrigerators by orders of magnitude, canonical-level abstractions significantly underestimate hardware routing congestion and execution runtimes. Our Level 4 QISA (local logical operations) offers an optimal architectural balance. As quantum hardware platforms scale toward FTQC in the coming years, our findings provide concrete architectural guidance for the design of their classical control stacks and instruction interfaces.
one_liner: ARIES identifies local logical operations as the most balanced instruction abstraction for scalable fault-tolerant quantum control.
why_it_matters: The work quantifies how QISA design affects cryogenic power, instruction bandwidth, routing congestion, and runtime in large fault-tolerant machines.
detailed_summary: The authors introduce ARIES, a hierarchy of quantum instruction-set abstractions, and an end-to-end toolflow with cycle-accurate classical-driver and hardware-engine simulation. Eight applications are evaluated on superconducting and topological-qubit architectures using instruction bandwidth, transceiver power, measurement overhead, congestion, and runtime metrics. Physical-level interfaces exceed dilution-refrigerator thermal budgets by orders of magnitude, while canonical-level interfaces hide routing and execution costs.
platform_or_system: Cryogenic superconducting and Majorana-qubit control stacks
main_result: A Level 4 QISA based on local logical operations provides the best evaluated balance between cryogenic communication costs and control-engine complexity.
application_angle: The results give hardware architects concrete guidance for partitioning classical control and quantum execution in scalable fault-tolerant processors.

title: Programmable Floquet Response for Quantum Sensing
abstract: Quantum sensing is typically based on phase accumulation and is therefore fundamentally tied to the coherence time of the sensing system. Here we introduce an alternative sensing paradigm based on programmable Floquet locking in periodically driven two-level systems. We show that periodic control generates an effective Floquet locking field whose orientation and amplitude depend on global offset, allowing information to be encoded in the driven population relaxation dynamics, not in the integrated phase. By controlling transfer between distinct Floquet locking manifolds, external perturbations can be mapped onto engineered relaxation responses whose characteristics are programmable through the driving sequence. We numerically demonstrate this approach for both DC and frequency-selective AC sensing, and show that temporal encoding of the response can provide enhanced precision in the presence of slow instrumental fluctuations. These results illustrate the potential of programmable Floquet responses and open the way to exploring new sensing strategies in driven quantum systems.
one_liner: Programmable Floquet locking encodes DC or frequency-selective AC signals in driven-state relaxation instead of accumulated phase.
why_it_matters: Relaxation-based encoding could enable sensing protocols that are less directly constrained by conventional phase-coherence time and more robust to slow drift.
detailed_summary: Periodic control creates an effective Floquet locking field whose amplitude and orientation depend on a global offset. Perturbations are transferred between distinct locking manifolds and encoded into programmable population-relaxation responses rather than integrated phase. Numerical demonstrations cover DC and frequency-selective AC sensing, including temporal encoding under slow instrumental fluctuations.
main_result: The study numerically demonstrates programmable relaxation-based DC and AC sensing, with temporal response encoding improving precision under slow instrumental fluctuations.
application_angle: The method offers a configurable sensing modality for driven qubits where conventional phase accumulation is limited by coherence or low-frequency technical drift.

title: Programmable Hard-X-Ray Spectral Comb Generation via Laser-Compton Scattering
abstract: Independent control of line spacing and offset underpins programmable frequency-comb spectroscopy, yet it has not been established for hard-X-ray sources based on inverse Compton scattering after electron transport and angular collection. Self-consistent multi-particle tracking and Li'enard-Wiechert radiation calculations model a transported 10 pC beam and its angle-integrated spectrum near 11 keV. Laser pulse separation programs the comb spacing, while pulse-to-pulse phase translates the entire line grid at fixed spacing. The spacing model agrees within 0.52%, while transport and optics change the phase-transfer slope by less than 0.2%. At fixed electron spot size, the largest resolvable separation scales as the inverse square of normalized emittance; subnanometer bunches also produce a mode-locked train with 13.9 as spacing. This two-coordinate programmability enables phase-stepped multicolor measurements and offers routes to hard-X-ray Ramsey interferometry, coherent control of core and nuclear excitations, and attosecond nonlinear spectroscopy.
one_liner: Laser-Compton scattering enables independently programmable hard-X-ray comb spacing and spectral offset near 11 keV.
why_it_matters: Two-coordinate control could bring phase-stepped comb spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and attosecond measurements into the hard-X-ray regime.
detailed_summary: Self-consistent particle tracking and Liénard–Wiechert radiation calculations model a transported 10 pC electron beam and its angle-integrated spectrum near 11 keV. Laser-pulse separation controls comb spacing, while pulse-to-pulse phase shifts the line grid without changing that spacing. The spacing model agrees within 0.52%, the phase-transfer slope changes by less than 0.2% after transport and optics, and subnanometer bunches yield a mode-locked train with 13.9 as spacing.
main_result: Simulations establish independent control of hard-X-ray comb spacing and offset after realistic electron transport and angular collection.
application_angle: The source architecture supports phase-stepped multicolor spectroscopy, hard-X-ray Ramsey measurements, and coherent excitation of core or nuclear transitions.

title: Moving quantum sensors
abstract: We investigate whether controlled motion of a quantum sensor offers a metrological advantage in a field-detection task. We consider a localized field of known strength $B$ occupying an unknown contiguous region making up a fraction $1/N$ of the total search space, with a qubit sensor controlled for a total time $T$ to maximize the probability of detecting the field. We study the regime in which the characteristic timescale of the field is slow compared to the time to move the sensor between any two regions, and we distinguish classical motion, where the sensor follows a definite trajectory, from quantum motion, where the sensor can be in a coherent superposition of locations. For a single classically moving sensor, we derive an optimal multi-stop protocol and obtain the exact maximum detection probability. Allowing coherent spatial superposition maps the single-sensor problem onto Hamiltonian search and reduces the interrogation time for successfully detecting the field from $Θ(N/B)$ to $Θ(\sqrt{N}/B)$. We then extend the problem to $M$ sensors and identify a hierarchy of optimal time scalings for constant success probability determined by the available spatial and inter-sensor quantum resources. Unentangled coherently moving sensors achieve $T=Θ(\sqrt{N/M}/B)$ by searching disjoint regions in parallel, while entanglement among the sensors can further enhance the effective field coupling and achieve $T=Θ(\sqrt{N}/(MB))$. Matching lower bounds establish the optimality of these scalings in the presence of arbitrary controls and ancilla systems. Our results separate the roles of classical motion, spatial coherence, and entanglement in spatial field detection.
one_liner: Coherent sensor motion and entanglement provide provably optimal quantum speedups for locating a spatially confined field.
why_it_matters: The analysis isolates how spatial coherence, parallel sensors, and entanglement improve distributed field searches beyond classical scanning.
detailed_summary: The task is to detect a known-strength field occupying one unknown region among N using a qubit sensor under a total interrogation-time constraint. Coherent spatial motion maps the problem to Hamiltonian search and reduces the single-sensor scaling from Θ(N/B) to Θ(√N/B). With M sensors, unentangled coherent search achieves Θ(√(N/M)/B), while inter-sensor entanglement reaches Θ(√N/(MB)); matching lower bounds establish optimality.
main_result: Spatial superposition yields a quadratic search advantage, and entanglement supplies an additional M-fold enhancement of effective field coupling.
application_angle: The scaling laws guide the design of mobile or distributed quantum-sensor networks for locating sparse, spatially localized signals.

title: Principles and Techniques for Agentic Research in Experimental Physics
abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in physics research is increasingly common, yet few guidelines exist for its effective use. Starting with a principles-based approach, we outline a set of ten requirements for collaborative AI agents in experimental physics, spanning scientific norms, effective agent use, and domain expertise. We take a human-centered approach in which agents act as collaborators that amplify rather than replace the expertise of a human researcher (user) who directs the work and is responsible for its results. We then present a framework designed to enforce these requirements, detailing methods for improving off-the-shelf behavior of large language models (LLMs) with custom scaffolding and describing general-purpose scientific workflows and skills. In particular, we highlight the power of closed-loop campaigns where agents work iteratively toward a well-defined goal. We demonstrate the potential of this mode of research through six case studies in experimental physics, covering device design, hardware control, neural network optimization, physical model identification, and data analysis. All six case studies result in useful work products that add utility to our research, including a neural network architecture and solid-state quantum defect photodynamic model that substantially outperform our published work; a microwave waveguide design that extends a published design concept to a fabrication-ready device meeting our experimental constraints; a quantum control pulse sequence candidate that improves simulated performance by more than an order of magnitude; commissioning of an NMR spectrometer to $\sim$1~Hz frequency precision on live hardware; and finally a data-fitting pipeline that achieves, to our knowledge, the first reconstruction of the Ising microstate of an artificial spin-ice array from diffraction-limited magnetic imaging.
one_liner: A human-centered agent framework delivers useful experimental-physics outputs across design, control, modeling, and data analysis.
why_it_matters: Six case studies show how structured, closed-loop AI workflows can accelerate practical quantum and experimental research while retaining human responsibility.
detailed_summary: The paper specifies ten requirements for collaborative AI agents covering scientific norms, effective use, and domain expertise, then implements them through scaffolding, workflows, and reusable skills. Six case studies span device design, live hardware control, neural-network optimization, model identification, quantum pulse design, and magnetic-image reconstruction. Reported outputs include a fabrication-ready microwave waveguide, over an order-of-magnitude simulated pulse improvement, NMR commissioning to about 1 Hz precision, and artificial-spin-ice microstate reconstruction.
platform_or_system: Human-directed AI framework for experimental-physics workflows
main_result: Structured agents produced experimentally useful artifacts and, in several case studies, exceeded prior published modeling or optimization performance.
application_angle: The framework offers a practical pattern for accelerating laboratory design, commissioning, control optimization, and analysis without removing human oversight.

title: Revealing topological protection through unprotected operations in a Majorana parity qubit
abstract: A recent experiment reported coherent parity oscillations between minimal Kitaev chains, demonstrating a Majorana parity qubit (arXiv:2607.09511). Operations on this qubit are controlled by coupling two Kitaev chains and are intrinsically unprotected against noise in the coupling strength. Here we show how the exponential protection in the underlying chains can nevertheless be revealed through unprotected qubit operations. To this end, we develop an analytical theory of quasistatic dephasing for two coupled $N$-site Kitaev chains at the sweet spot. In Rabi experiments, protection can be resolved by adapting the operating point with chain length: depending on the coupling architecture, it appears as an exponentially increasing optimized number of coherent oscillations or as a longer coherence time. Ramsey experiments show an exponentially increasing coherence time, provided the chains can be sufficiently decoupled. Our analytical theory takes into account the non-Gaussian splitting statistics of the Kitaev chains, allowing us to quantitatively predict the scaling with chain length. Moreover, we determine how residual noise and imperfections limit the range of chain lengths over which this scaling can be observed. Our results show how qubit dynamics can be used to probe Majorana protection in experimentally realistic devices.
one_liner: Unprotected Rabi and Ramsey operations can expose exponential topological protection in coupled Majorana parity-qubit chains.
why_it_matters: The theory provides experimentally accessible signatures of Majorana protection despite noisy coupling operations and realistic device imperfections.
detailed_summary: The authors derive an analytical quasistatic-dephasing theory for two coupled N-site Kitaev chains at the sweet spot, including non-Gaussian chain-splitting statistics. In optimized Rabi protocols, protection appears through either exponentially more coherent oscillations or longer coherence, depending on the coupling architecture. Ramsey coherence also grows exponentially with chain length when the chains can be sufficiently decoupled, while residual noise and imperfections bound the observable range.
main_result: Properly chosen Rabi and Ramsey measurements reveal chain-length-dependent exponential protection even when the qubit operations themselves are unprotected.
application_angle: The protocols provide realistic dynamical tests for validating topological protection and diagnosing limiting noise in Majorana-qubit hardware.

title: Observation of Photon Bunching in Broadband Multimode Thermal Light Enabled by Temporal Imaging
abstract: Photons emitted by incoherent sources exhibit temporal bunching, a fundamental manifestation of Bose-Einstein statistics first observed by Hanbury Brown and Twiss (HBT). While intensity correlation measurements originated in astronomy and are now central across quantum technologies, biophysics, and spectroscopy, observing temporal bunching in broadband thermal light remains limited by detector temporal resolution. Conventional approaches - such as streak cameras or optical upconversion - introduce severe trade-offs in efficiency, bandwidth, or setup versatility. Here, we propose and demonstrate a third route: pre-detection temporal magnification of the optical field prior to measuring its intensity autocorrelation function in a conventional HBT setup. Using an electro-optic time lens with a temporal magnification of 660, we resolve the temporal intensity autocorrelation of broadband thermal light generated via non-degenerate spontaneous parametric down-conversion with a bandwidth of 250 GHz. This enables direct observation of thermal photon bunching on sub-3.5 picosecond timescales without narrow spectral filtering, establishing pre-detection temporal imaging as a general platform for broadband statistical optics, with applications spanning ultrafast quantum optics, biophysical imaging, and potentially stellar intensity interferometry.
one_liner: A 660× electro-optic time lens resolves photon bunching in 250 GHz thermal light on sub-3.5 ps timescales using conventional HBT detection.
why_it_matters: Pre-detection temporal magnification bypasses detector timing limits without narrow filtering, enabling efficient correlation measurements of broadband ultrafast light.
detailed_summary: The experiment temporally magnifies an optical field before sending it to a conventional Hanbury Brown–Twiss intensity-correlation setup. An electro-optic time lens providing 660× magnification resolves the autocorrelation of 250 GHz-bandwidth thermal light generated by non-degenerate spontaneous parametric down-conversion.
