The method directly accesses bunching below 3.5 ps without narrow spectral filtering.
platform_or_system: Electro-optic time lens with HBT detection
main_result: The system directly observed sub-3.5 ps thermal photon bunching in 250 GHz broadband light using standard photon-detection hardware.
application_angle: The approach could extend broadband correlation measurements in ultrafast quantum optics, biophysical imaging, spectroscopy, and stellar intensity interferometry.

title: Quantum Cryptography and Autoformalization in Lean
abstract: Quantum key distribution provides secure communication by relying on physics principles and mathematical reasoning. Security proofs across the field can contain gaps, often between individually valid theorems integrated under mismatched assumptions. We produce an end-to-end security theorem formalized in the Lean proof assistant, eliminating hidden hypotheses by building only on Lean's standard axioms. Our proof covers composable security of the entanglement-based qubit BB84 protocol against coherent attacks by the postselection technique, accounting for finite block size, and is written in a language that enforces local operations and classical communication to help ensure a faithful representation of the protocol. The proof itself was enabled by LLM-based autoformalization, and with the proof complete, we used the same pipeline as a discovery machine, reducing the finite-size penalty on the key rate. Our work sets a reproducible standard for security arguments in quantum cryptography and shows how formal proof engines can accelerate discovery across quantum information science.
one_liner: Lean formalization delivers an end-to-end finite-key, composable security proof for entanglement-based qubit BB84 against coherent attacks.
why_it_matters: Machine-checked proofs expose mismatched assumptions in QKD security arguments while enabling reproducible verification and improvements to finite-size key rates.
detailed_summary: The authors formalize composable security of entanglement-based qubit BB84 against coherent attacks using the postselection technique and finite block sizes. The Lean development relies only on standard axioms and uses a language that explicitly constrains operations to LOCC. An LLM-assisted autoformalization pipeline supported both proof construction and discovery of a reduced finite-size key-rate penalty.
main_result: A complete machine-checked BB84 security theorem was obtained, together with an improved finite-size key-rate penalty.
application_angle: Formal verification can make deployed QKD security claims auditable, reproducible, and less vulnerable to hidden or incompatible assumptions.

title: Ghost unitaries for loss-resilient photonic resource-state generation
abstract: Entangled few-photon states, such as Bell and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states, are central resources for discrete-variable photonic quantum information processing. In many architectures, these states are generated probabilistically by first heralding single photons from biphoton sources and then interfering them in linear-optical circuits. In this work, we show that the entanglement structure of said biphoton sources can be directly exploited for noise-engineering to deliver higher quality resource states. Using the transpose identity of multi-mode squeezed vacuum states, we introduce "ghost-unitary" implementations in which the target resource-generation interferometer is applied to the heralding modes rather than to the delivered resource modes. When the dominant imperfection is interferometric loss, this relocation converts direct amplitude damping of the output into false-positive heralding events that require both higher-pair emission and photon loss. In the low-squeezing regime, these events are parametrically suppressed, yielding higher-fidelity conditional resource states. We analyze this mechanism for single-qubit states, two-photon NOON states, Bell states, and a family of $n$-qubit GHZ states, as well as for single-qubit teleportation and type-I-fusion-based resource growth. Across these examples, we delineate finite parameter regimes in which ghost-unitary implementations outperform direct implementations, with particular relevance to frequency-bin photonics where active linear-optical transformations can be relatively lossy. We also prove that, in the setting considered here, the direct implementation of the $n$-GHZ family delivers identically damped outputs: equivalent to the ideal state followed by uniform amplitude damping. This extends the known $n=2,3$ cases and provides a structural result of independent interest for photonic quantum information processing.
one_liner: Ghost-unitary circuits move lossy photonic transformations onto heralding modes to improve the conditional fidelity of entangled resource states.
why_it_matters: The scheme converts direct output damping into higher-order false heralds, offering a practical route to better Bell and GHZ states with lossy active optics.
detailed_summary: Using the transpose identity of multimode squeezed-vacuum states, the target interferometer is relocated from delivered photons to their heralding partners. Dominant interferometric loss then produces false-positive heralds only through combined higher-pair emission and photon loss, which is parametrically suppressed at low squeezing. Analyses cover NOON, Bell, and n-qubit GHZ states, teleportation, and fusion-based resource growth, and identify regimes outperforming direct implementations.
main_result: Ghost-unitary implementations achieve higher conditional resource-state fidelity than direct lossy interferometers across finite low-squeezing parameter regimes.
application_angle: The technique is especially relevant to frequency-bin quantum processors and networks, where active mode transformations can introduce substantial optical loss.

title: Optical interferometric tools for probing memory effects
abstract: Recent efforts to detect non-Markovian memory have become increasingly important, motivated by the broad relevance of memory effects in quantum information processing, metrology, and thermodynamic engines. Here, we show that interferometric methods, particularly the phase shift and visibility, provide an experimentally accessible framework for probing environmental effects and witnessing non-Markovian dynamics. Specifically, suitably constructed witness operators enable the detection of non-Markovianity through measurable phase shifts in the interference pattern. Furthermore, we prove that the interferometric visibility is monotonically non-increasing under incoherent CP-divisible (Markovian) dynamics. Consequently, any revival of the optimized visibility constitutes a sufficient signature of information backflow and hence non-Markovianity. The effectiveness of the proposed phase-based and visibility approaches is illustrated for representative examples of non-Markovian dynamics. Our results offer a simple and experimentally feasible framework for probing memory effects, with potential applications in quantum sensing and noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.
one_liner: Interferometric phase shifts and optimized visibility revivals provide experimentally accessible witnesses of non-Markovian quantum dynamics.
why_it_matters: The method turns environmental memory into straightforward interference observables, reducing the experimental burden of diagnosing noisy quantum devices and sensors.
detailed_summary: The work constructs witness operators whose environmental-memory signatures appear as measurable phase shifts in an interference pattern. It proves that optimized visibility cannot increase under incoherent CP-divisible dynamics, so any revival is a sufficient witness of information backflow. Representative non-Markovian models illustrate both phase-based and visibility-based detection.
platform_or_system: Quantum interferometer coupled to an open environment
main_result: Phase observables and visibility revivals are shown to witness non-Markovianity under experimentally measurable conditions.
application_angle: These observables could support practical characterization of memory effects in quantum sensors, metrology platforms, and noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware.

title: Distributed quantum phase sensing using an SU(1,1) Perelomov coherent state in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer network
abstract: We present a theoretical study of distributed quantum sensing using a reconfigurable network of $N$ Mach--Zehnder interferometers to simultaneously estimate weighted linear combinations of relative phase shifts. The proposed scheme relies on injecting a Perelomov coherent state, generated from the SU(1,1) group representation, into one port of a passive quantum circuit while the remaining modes are initialized in the vacuum state, thereby establishing non-trivial quantum correlations among the sensors. Based on multi-parameter quantum estimation theory, our analysis shows that this entangled strategy outperforms the standard shot-noise limit and asymptotically achieves the Heisenberg limit. Furthermore, we highlight the crucial role of the first beam splitter's asymmetry; specifically, the optimal transmission coefficient that maximizes sensitivity corresponds to its maximum imbalance. Compared to a separable approach utilizing the same total average photon number, the entangled strategy yields a more efficient use of quantum resources, guaranteeing an accuracy gain between $1$ and $N$. This demonstrates that the entangled strategy is systematically superior to its separable counterpart. Ultimately, these results illustrate the potential of entangled distributed quantum sensor networks for high-precision measurements and provide clear guidelines for optimizing interferometric architectures in quantum metrology.
one_liner: An entangled SU(1,1) Perelomov-state network estimates distributed phase combinations beyond shot noise and asymptotically reaches Heisenberg scaling.
why_it_matters: The analysis supplies resource and beam-splitter design rules for building more photon-efficient distributed interferometric sensor networks.
detailed_summary: A Perelomov coherent state is injected into a passive network of N Mach–Zehnder interferometers to establish correlations among spatially distributed phase sensors. Multiparameter estimation theory predicts performance beyond the shot-noise limit and asymptotic approach to the Heisenberg limit. Maximum sensitivity occurs at maximum imbalance of the first beam splitter, while the entangled scheme provides an accuracy gain between 1 and N over an equal-energy separable strategy.
main_result: The correlated sensing strategy systematically outperforms its separable counterpart and can asymptotically attain Heisenberg-limited precision.
application_angle: The architecture offers optimization guidance for distributed precision measurements using a fixed total photon budget.

title: Time-Domain Observables for Resonant Scattering in Quantum Simulations of Lattice Gauge Theory
abstract: Quantum computing may allow unprecedented access to nonequilibrium quantum dynamics, including problems of interest in particle physics, like the real-time development of scattering processes. Although fault-tolerant simulations at scale are still in the future, recent advancements toward early fault-tolerant simulations motivate building increasingly elaborate benchmark problems in order to assess state-of-the-art capabilities and test new algorithms and observables. In this work, we study glueball scattering on a line-of-plaquettes lattice in pure $SU(3)$ lattice gauge theory. We characterize scattering of the lowest-energy glueball states using classical exact diagonalization methods, identifying the continuum resonance structure using real-time simulations and approximate analytic methods, and we propose time-domain observables for extracting properties of the resonance from quantum simulations. We furthermore construct a toy model that shares the spectral features of the lattice gauge theory and demonstrate extraction of the observables. Feasibility on near-term hardware is demonstrated through simulation of a resonant collision of this toy model on Quantinuum System Model $\texttt{H2-2}$, with a 14-plaquette chain encoded in 28 qubits. The Trotterized circuit after optimization and compression requires $\sim 25n$ entangling gates for $n$ Trotter steps.
one_liner: Time-domain resonance observables are developed for lattice-gauge scattering and tested in a 28-qubit trapped-ion simulation of a 14-site collision model.
why_it_matters: The work connects physically meaningful scattering diagnostics to circuits compact enough to benchmark early fault-tolerant quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes glueball scattering on a line-of-plaquettes pure SU(3) lattice using exact diagonalization, real-time evolution, and approximate analytic methods. It proposes time-domain observables for extracting resonance properties and validates them with a spectrally analogous toy model. A 14-plaquette collision is simulated on Quantinuum H2-2 using 28 qubits, with the compressed circuit requiring about 25n entangling gates for n Trotter steps.
main_result: A 28-qubit resonant-collision simulation demonstrated the feasibility of extracting scattering information through compact time-domain observables.
application_angle: The benchmark can assess quantum processors and algorithms intended for real-time particle-physics and lattice-gauge simulations.

title: An Aubry-André localized optical lattice clock
abstract: Optical lattice clocks in space could improve satellite navigation systems and enable new tests of fundamental physics, including gravitational-wave detection and tests of relativity. In microgravity, atoms can tunnel to degenerate neighboring lattice sites, broadening the clock transition and limiting coherence times. We demonstrate Aubry-André localization in a bichromatic optical lattice formed by two magic-wavelength lasers, suppressing tunneling in a horizontal lattice clock emulating free fall. We recover a Fourier-limited clock Rabi spectrum and measure Ramsey coherence times of up to 2 s in shallow lattices, with up to 100-fold improvement over the delocalized regime. These results establish Aubry-André localization as a practical route to controlling tunneling in future space-based clocks, and open a path to operating terrestrial clocks at shallower lattice depths.
one_liner: A bichromatic magic-wavelength lattice suppresses tunneling and restores long-coherence spectroscopy in a clock operated under simulated microgravity.
why_it_matters: The demonstrated localization could preserve clock accuracy in space and permit terrestrial optical clocks to operate with shallower trapping lattices.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses two magic-wavelength lasers to form a bichromatic lattice and induce Aubry-André localization in a horizontal optical lattice clock emulating free fall. Localization suppresses resonant tunneling between degenerate neighboring sites, recovering a Fourier-limited Rabi spectrum in shallow lattices. Ramsey coherence reaches 2 s, representing up to a 100-fold improvement over the delocalized regime.
main_result: Aubry-André localization suppresses lattice-site tunneling and extends Ramsey coherence to 2 s in shallow traps.
application_angle: The method directly addresses a microgravity limitation of spaceborne clocks used for navigation, relativity tests, and gravitational-wave sensing.

title: Coherent optical control of a thousand qubits in a three-dimensional trapped-ion crystal
abstract: Leading quantum platforms are largely limited to one or two dimensions, whereas three-dimensional Coulomb crystals of trapped ions self-assemble into dense qubit arrays with no rearrangement overhead. Coherent optical control of such crystals has nonetheless been out of reach, because the optical transition couples to nearly all $3N$ collective modes, i.e., a thermally occupied quasi-continuum bath. Here we cool about 3,600 modes of a crystal of over 1,200 ions below single-phonon occupation, using a continuous cooling band that spans more than five octaves in vibrational spectrum, from about 50 kHz to 2.1 MHz. The crystal then serves as a register of optical qubits, allowing global initialization, coherent manipulation and collective detection. We demonstrate ensemble optical coherence of 21.6 milliseconds and reduce the optical-transition frequency uncertainty from 389 Hz for a single ion to 12 Hz for over a thousand ions, approaching the expected projection-noise scaling. Our approach could be extended to even larger crystals with phonon-mediated many-body couplings, opening a route towards entanglement-enhanced precision metrology and three-dimensional quantum simulation, particularly with spatial-shaped illumination for region-resolved collective control.
one_liner: A 3D crystal of over 1,200 trapped ions is cooled and operated as a coherently controlled optical-qubit register.
why_it_matters: The result extends coherent qubit control into dense three-dimensional arrays and offers a scalable platform for precision metrology and quantum simulation.
detailed_summary: The authors cool roughly 3,600 collective vibrational modes spanning about 50 kHz to 2.1 MHz below one phonon using a continuous cooling band. The resulting crystal of more than 1,200 ions supports global initialization, coherent optical manipulation, and collective detection. Ensemble coherence reaches 21.6 ms, while transition-frequency uncertainty falls from 389 Hz for one ion to 12 Hz for the full ensemble, near projection-noise scaling.
main_result: Coherent optical control of more than 1,200 qubits is demonstrated after broadband cooling of approximately 3,600 motional modes.
application_angle: Dense self-assembled ion registers could support entanglement-enhanced metrology and large three-dimensional quantum simulations without rearrangement overhead.

title: Enhanced weak-field sensing using detuned squeezing
abstract: Achieving measurement precision beyond the standard quantum limit (SQL) is a fundamental object in quantum metrology. In this manuscript, we propose a streamlined protocol for weak signal sensing in a trapped-ion spin-oscillator system that simultaneously exploits detuned motional squeezing and spin-oscillator entanglement. By combining these two quantum resources, the phase accumulation in this spin system is significantly accelerated, as a result achieving an exponential improvement in the sensitivity over unsqueezed cases. Remarkably, we show that the significant metrological gain provided by our protocol persists in noisy environments, with the sensitivity remaining below the SQL. In particular, our protocol retains a distinct advantage in the short interrogation time regime, thus demonstrating the practical potential in quantum-enhanced sensing.
one_liner: Detuned motional squeezing and spin-oscillator entanglement are combined to accelerate phase accumulation for weak-field sensing.
why_it_matters: The proposed protocol predicts sub-SQL sensitivity under noise and retains an advantage at short interrogation times relevant to rapid sensing.
detailed_summary: This theoretical protocol couples a trapped-ion spin to a detuned, squeezed motional mode while generating spin-oscillator entanglement. The combined resources accelerate signal-dependent phase accumulation and yield an exponential sensitivity improvement relative to the unsqueezed case in the analyzed model. Simulations indicate that the gain remains below the standard quantum limit under noise, particularly for short interrogation times.
main_result: The proposed sensing sequence predicts exponentially enhanced weak-signal sensitivity and noise-robust operation below the SQL.
application_angle: Short-time quantum-enhanced measurements could improve weak-field detection when coherence time or measurement latency is constrained.

title: Boson Sampling Using Fock States from On-Demand Single Photon Source Arrays: Quantum Complexity & Impact of Dephasing
abstract: Boson sampling with array of on-demand single photons (discreet variable Fock states) as resource states provides distinct advantages in complexity scaling compared to single photon resource states mimicked by the states (continuous variable) generated in nonlinear photonics. Recent progress in realization of regular ordered array of mesa top single quantum dots (MTSQDs) enabling on-demand generation of many photon resource states with high single photon purity and indistinguishability [1,2] has opened the possibility of implementing chip-scale Boson sampling with single photons. An important question towards scale up of such circuits is how the dephasing and decay timescale of individual on-demand single photons affect the final probability distribution of the N-photon entangled state. In this work we report a framework that provides direct link between the physical sources of decoherence to the outcome of multiphoton correlation measurements. We explicitly incorporate the symmetrization of the N-photon states while accounting for the shape of the individual wave packets and dephasing. Using this framework, we show predictive estimates of the probability of generation of a 4-photon NOON state using an optical circuit initialized with 4 identical single photon wave packets, mimicking the emitted photons from MTSQD single photon sources reported in [2]. Specifically, we show how the probability of generating various 4-photon entangled states depend on the two-photon interference visibility which is determined by the pure dephasing timescale in relation to the radiative decay timescale. The results provide quantitative guidelines to measure 4 photon and higher number of entangled photon states generated in an optical circuit with on demand single photon sources and provide a link between physical processes such as temperature and the output state of the quantum optical circuits.
one_liner: A multiphoton framework links quantum-dot dephasing and wave-packet shape to boson-sampling output probabilities.
why_it_matters: It supplies device-level criteria for scaling on-demand quantum-dot sources into chip-scale multiphoton circuits with useful interference fidelity.
detailed_summary: The theoretical framework explicitly symmetrizes N-photon wave packets while incorporating radiative decay and pure dephasing from on-demand mesa-top quantum-dot sources. It connects these source dynamics to multiphoton correlation probabilities and two-photon interference visibility. For a four-photon circuit, the analysis predicts how dephasing changes the probability of producing a NOON state and other entangled outputs.
main_result: The model quantitatively maps source dephasing and decay times to four-photon interference and entangled-state generation probabilities.
application_angle: The results provide measurable source-quality targets for chip-scale boson sampling and higher-order photonic-state generation.

title: Multi-parameter estimation enhanced by level crossing Hamiltonian structure with Bayesian feedback
abstract: Level crossings, where two quantum energy levels intersect, are ubiquitous in quantum systems and play a central role in controlling quantum dynamics. In this study, we establish a framework that connects these level crossing structures to the ultimate precision limits of quantum metrology. By analyzing a Hamiltonian with the level crossings structure, we identify the conditions under which multiple parameters can be estimated simultaneously with maximal sensitivity near the level crossing point. We then construct a resource efficient sensing protocol based on unitary quench dynamics and Bayesian estimation, enabling high precision, low cost parameter estimation without requiring entanglement or complex control. We present a protocol whose estimation precision saturates the Holevo Cramer Rao bound, the tightest achievable precision bound in multi parameter estimation. Using the two level model and the two spin Ising model as illustrative examples, we demonstrate how the protocol can be applied to a system with level crossing Hamiltonian structure. Our findings reveal that level crossings serve as universal operating points for precision quantum metrology, offering a simple and scalable path toward practical multi parameter sensing across diverse quantum platforms.
one_liner: Level crossings are identified as optimal operating points for simultaneous quantum estimation using quench dynamics and Bayesian feedback.
why_it_matters: The protocol promises bound-saturating multiparameter sensing without entanglement or elaborate controls, potentially lowering experimental overhead.
detailed_summary: The study derives conditions under which a level-crossing Hamiltonian provides maximal simultaneous sensitivity to several parameters. It proposes a resource-efficient protocol based on unitary quenches and Bayesian estimation, avoiding entanglement and complex control sequences. In two-level and two-spin Ising examples, the predicted precision saturates the multiparameter Holevo Cramér–Rao bound.
main_result: A quench-and-feedback protocol is predicted to attain the Holevo Cramér–Rao bound near Hamiltonian level crossings.
application_angle: Using intrinsic spectral crossings as sensing points could simplify scalable multiparameter sensors across multiple quantum platforms.

title: Broadening the reflection band of atomic mirrors by engineering the emitter-waveguide coupling
abstract: We theoretically investigate single-photon coherent transport through a finite waveguide quantum electrodynamics (QED) array with spatially modulated emitter-waveguide couplings. By combining exact scattering calculations with spectral factorization and a semiclassical WKB analysis, we identify how the coupling profile controls the reflection bandwidth and its finite-size dependence. A Gaussian transverse displacement produces an exponential-of-Gaussian decay-rate profile that broadens the high-reflectivity window and suppresses the boundary-induced Fabry-Perot oscillations compared with a uniform array. The transmission zeros remain exactly degenerate at the atomic resonance for arbitrary positive coupling profiles at non-Bragg spacings. In contrast, the collective poles reorganize under the spatial modulation, redistributing their radiative widths and preventing individual subradiant resonances from terminating the reflection window. We further derive an algebraic 1/N scaling law for the contraction of the bandwidth toward its bulk value. The bulk bandwidth is determined by the largest local decay rate, whereas the finite-size correction increases as the profile becomes sharper, leading to an optimal profile width. These results establish spatial coupling engineering as a practical tool for designing broadband atomic mirrors in atom-nanofiber and circuit-QED platforms.
one_liner: Spatially shaping emitter-waveguide coupling broadens atomic-mirror reflection bands while suppressing finite-array resonances.
why_it_matters: The design rules enable more robust broadband single-photon reflectors for nanophotonic and superconducting waveguide-QED hardware.
detailed_summary: Exact scattering, spectral factorization, and WKB analysis are used to study finite emitter arrays with spatially varying waveguide coupling. An exponential-of-Gaussian decay-rate profile broadens the high-reflectivity window and suppresses boundary-driven Fabry–Pérot oscillations relative to a uniform array. The work also derives a 1/N finite-size bandwidth correction and predicts an optimal profile width balancing bulk bandwidth against edge effects.
main_result: Engineered coupling profiles broaden the single-photon reflection band and prevent subradiant poles from truncating it.
application_angle: The coupling strategy offers practical design guidance for broadband atomic mirrors in atom-nanofiber and circuit-QED devices.

title: On-chip optical isolators
abstract: Optical isolation suppresses back-reflections that destabilize lasers, produce parasitic interference, and increase crosstalk in photonic systems. Although free-space and fibre-optic isolators are mature, no broadly adopted on-chip technology yet combines strong isolation, low insertion loss, broad bandwidth, compact footprint, and scalable fabrication. The difficulty is twofold: Lorentz reciprocity must be broken, and every relevant backward spatial, spectral, and polarization channel must be suppressed. This Review develops a common framework for assessing proposed solutions. We first distinguish pairwise nonreciprocity from intensity-asymmetric transmission and from true isolation using the constitutive relations and scattering matrix. We then compare three physical routes to an integrated nonreciprocal response: magneto-optical bias, externally driven space-time modulation, and nonlinear optical processes. Topological and non-Hermitian systems are treated as cross-cutting design frameworks that can route, protect, or enhance an underlying nonreciprocal response, but do not by themselves break reciprocity. Finally, we examine fundamental constraints and practical trade-offs among isolation, insertion loss, bandwidth, footprint, modal coverage, drive requirements, and fabrication compatibility. The resulting mechanism-based perspective connects reciprocity-breaking physics to the requirements of scalable photonic integrated circuits.
one_liner: A review establishes a mechanism-based framework for evaluating practical on-chip optical isolators.
why_it_matters: Integrated isolation could suppress destabilizing reflections and crosstalk in scalable photonic and quantum-communication circuits.
detailed_summary: This Review distinguishes true optical isolation from pairwise nonreciprocity and merely asymmetric transmission using constitutive relations and scattering matrices. It compares magneto-optical bias, driven space-time modulation, and nonlinear processes, while explaining that topological and non-Hermitian designs do not independently break reciprocity. The analysis connects each mechanism to insertion loss, bandwidth, footprint, modal coverage, drive power, and fabrication compatibility.
main_result: The work provides a unified framework for assessing whether integrated nonreciprocal devices satisfy the full requirements of practical optical isolation.
application_angle: The framework guides the design of compact isolators for stable lasers, low-crosstalk photonic processors, and integrated quantum links.

title: A Photonic Integrated Light Generation, Control, and Delivery Engine for Creating Cold Atoms
abstract: The creation of cold atoms underpins quantum sensing and precision metrology, computing, timekeeping, and fundamental science experiments. Miniaturizing the lasers and optical infrastructure, which occupy over 80% of the volume of these experiments, through photonic integration could improve robustness, reliability, and manufacturability while reducing cost and enabling portable space-based precision measurements and quantum tools for non-experts. Yet, there has been limited progress towards integration of the laser and optical infrastructure required to generate cold atoms onto a single chip. We demonstrate a photonic engine that generates, controls, and delivers precision light to create cold atoms in a rubidium 3-dimensional magneto-optical trap (3D-MOT). We integrate on a single chip two frequency-agile self-injection-locked lasers, laser frequency and intensity control, passive beam combining and splitting, signal monitoring, and high-efficiency beam delivery to a rubidium vapor cell. The integrated engine is shown to support multiple functions required for generating cold atoms including stable generation of low-noise cooling and repump light, frequency control for atom spectroscopy and stabilization, real-time laser monitoring, routing for laser offset locking, optical power modulation, and large-area three-beam delivery of 3 mW to the physics package. Fully electrically controlled, the engine enables sustained 3D-MOT operation, trapping more than 1 million atoms at an average temperature of 350 uK and supporting atom-number and temperature measurements. These results demonstrate the first single-chip integration of light generation, control, and delivery for cold-atom generation, offering a path toward smaller, more robust, and manufacturable cold-atom systems for applications including cold-atom clocks and sensors.
one_liner: A single photonic chip generates, controls, and delivers the precision light needed to operate a rubidium 3D magneto-optical trap.
why_it_matters: Consolidating cold-atom optics onto one electrically controlled chip could enable compact, robust, and manufacturable quantum sensors and clocks.
detailed_summary: The chip integrates two frequency-agile self-injection-locked lasers with frequency and intensity control, beam combining and splitting, signal monitoring, and efficient beam delivery. It supplies 3 mW through a large-area three-beam output to a rubidium vapor cell and supports spectroscopy, stabilization, offset locking, and power modulation. The engine sustains a 3D MOT containing more than one million atoms at an average temperature of 350 µK.
main_result: The fully electrically controlled photonic engine demonstrates sustained trapping of over one million rubidium atoms at an average temperature of 350 µK.
application_angle: This integration reduces the dominant optical footprint of cold-atom instruments for portable clocks, inertial sensors, and space-based metrology.

title: Development and experimental implementation of noise characterisation techniques on a superconducting quantum processor
abstract: Noise characterisation not only enables error mitigation but also provides valuable information about the intrinsic performance of a quantum device, identifying dominant error contributions and bounding noise stability well beyond the aggregated calibration data. Deploying such methods on a specific hardware topology must combine efficiency and accuracy, assess noise stability, and validate the reconstructed noise model. Here we develop and implement these methods on a superconducting processor with square-lattice topology. First, we revise the cycle-benchmarking protocol and reduce the bias arising from unlearnable degrees of freedom via a regularised cost function. Second, we extend a previously developed tensor-network tomography method to match the device layout and show how its accuracy can be improved by repeated layer execution. Both methods allow approximate sublayer noise models to be extracted from parent ones. Using noise characterisation as a tool, we map the noise structure, track drift, and validate the adequacy of the learnt noise models against experimentally observed noisy estimations in benchmark physical and chemistry circuits. These results inform further improvements in the underlying technology and provide estimates of the size of noise-mitigated circuits that the device can support.
one_liner: Two experimentally deployed methods reconstruct, track, and validate noise on a square-lattice superconducting quantum processor.
why_it_matters: Hardware-resolved noise models expose dominant errors and drift while estimating which error-mitigated circuits a processor can reliably support.
detailed_summary: The authors revise cycle benchmarking with a regularized cost function that reduces bias from unlearnable degrees of freedom. They also adapt tensor-network tomography to a square-lattice processor and improve reconstruction accuracy through repeated layer execution. Extracted sublayer models are used to map noise, monitor drift, and predict noisy outcomes in benchmark physics and chemistry circuits.
main_result: The techniques recover and validate topology-aware noise models that characterize error structure, temporal drift, and feasible noise-mitigated circuit sizes.
application_angle: The methods provide actionable diagnostics for processor improvement, calibration monitoring, and selecting circuits compatible with available error-mitigation capacity.

title: Scalable long-distance quantum fan-out gates with reduced resource overhead
abstract: Scalable long-distance quantum gates are essential for distributed quantum computation and scalable quantum networks. We propose an efficient scheme for implementing an $n$-qubit fan-out gate $C^n$ (also known as a controlled-NOT-$\cdots$-NOT gate) across spatially separated parties. Our protocol requires only a pre-shared $n$-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state, $n$ local controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates, and feed-forward operations, thereby reducing both the CNOT and Hadamard gate counts by $(n-2)$ when compared with the standard decomposition-based approach. We further develop two optical architectures to implement the heralded and post-selected $n$-photon fan-out gates, respectively. These schemes require fewer single photons resources and achieve higher success probabilities than their decomposition-based counterparts, representing significant improvements. The results indicate that our approach is experimentally feasible and pave the way toward practical long-distance quantum computation.
one_liner: A distributed fan-out protocol and two optical designs reduce gate and photon overhead for long-distance multiqubit operations.
why_it_matters: Lower resource counts and higher optical success probabilities make networked multiqubit gates more practical for distributed quantum computing.
detailed_summary: The protocol realizes an n-qubit fan-out gate between separated parties using one shared n-qubit GHZ state, n local CNOT gates, and feed-forward operations. Relative to decomposition-based implementations, it removes n−2 CNOT gates and n−2 Hadamard gates. Heralded and post-selected n-photon architectures further reduce single-photon requirements and increase success probabilities.
main_result: The proposed protocol implements distributed n-qubit fan-out with reduced logical-gate overhead, while its optical variants improve photon efficiency and success probability.
application_angle: The scheme targets scalable inter-node operations for distributed processors, modular quantum computers, and long-distance quantum networks.

title: Imaging the building blocks of ant pheromone communication
abstract: Organisms have evolved diverse strategies to communicate. Beyond acoustic and visual signals, many species rely on chemical communication, including pheromones: volatile compounds involved in reproduction, defense, and coordination. Ant trail systems, a paradigm of pheromone use, have inspired decades of research in collective behavior, self-organization and optimization algorithms. Yet, despite their central role, individual pheromone deposits have never been directly visualized or quantified, limiting our understanding of how deposition events scale into collective trail formation. Here, we use interferometric imaging to reveal and quantify single pheromone deposits in the ant Lasius niger. This label-free, non-invasive approach enables precise measurement of single deposit volume (~1 pL, with x20-fold variability), morphology, and temporal dynamics. We uncover a two-phase volume loss process: most of secreted volume evaporates within seconds, forming a dried droplet, which then partially sublimates (~10%) over one hour. These findings challenge the assumption of homogeneous deposition and bring previously inaccessible properties of ant pheromone trails within experimental reach. Our method establishes a quantitative framework for studying the spatiotemporal dynamics of insect chemical communication, linking individual signaling to collective patterns.
one_liner: Label-free interferometric imaging directly measures the volume, morphology, and decay of individual ant pheromone deposits.
why_it_matters: Quantifying single deposits reveals how microscopic chemical signals evolve into collective trails and provides a new optical tool for chemical ecology.
detailed_summary: Interferometric imaging resolves individual pheromone deposits from Lasius niger ants without labels or invasive sampling. Deposits average roughly 1 pL but vary by about twentyfold in volume. Their loss follows two phases: rapid evaporation within seconds leaves a dried droplet, followed by approximately 10% sublimation over one hour.
main_result: The method directly visualizes and quantifies single ant pheromone deposits, including picoliter-scale volume variation and two-stage temporal decay.
application_angle: The approach enables quantitative studies of insect chemical signaling and could support sensitive imaging of other microscopic volatile or drying deposits.

title: Local error correction prolongs time-crystalline memory
abstract: Discrete time crystals are non-equilibrium phases of matter with spatiotemporal order and a response that breaks the time-translation symmetry of a periodic external drive. Interactions, spatial disorder and correlated random driving can in theory stabilize this order. In experiments, however, coupling to the environment limits the time crystal lifetime. Here we use stochastic local bit-flip error correction to prolong the time-crystalline response of a driven, spatially disordered two-dimensional Ising model on a superconducting quantum processor, using a repetition code with distances three and five on a honeycomb lattice with up to 68 physical qubits. Even though ancilla qubits, midcircuit syndrome measurements and decoding increase the required quantum and classical resources, the stochastic drive increases the memory decay time by a factor of up to two. At late times we observe that recovery stabilizes spatial order across the lattice. The spin-configuration distributions explain this separation, as recovery suppresses disagreeing bonds while broadening occupies completely reversed states. Syndrome measurements without correction accelerate the memory decay, demonstrating the importance of conditional correction. Our results show that local bit-flip error correction can preserve time-crystalline memory over more drive cycles than the bare dynamics.
one_liner: Local bit-flip error correction doubles the decay time of time-crystalline memory on a superconducting processor.
why_it_matters: The experiment shows that active local correction can preserve driven many-body order despite added ancillas, measurements, and decoding overhead.
detailed_summary: A stochastic local bit-flip correction protocol is applied to a driven, disordered two-dimensional Ising model on a superconducting processor. Distance-three and distance-five repetition codes are implemented on a honeycomb lattice using up to 68 physical qubits. Conditional recovery extends memory decay time by as much as a factor of two and stabilizes late-time spatial order, whereas syndrome measurement without correction accelerates decay.
main_result: Active local recovery prolongs time-crystalline memory by up to twofold and preserves spatial order over more drive cycles than uncorrected dynamics.
application_angle: The result informs error-corrected quantum simulation and the protection of nonequilibrium many-body states on near-term superconducting hardware.

title: Experimental Demonstration of 7-Dimensional N-Vector Model with Dimensional Inflation and Annealing
abstract: We report the first experimental realization of a physical system described by a high-dimensional Hamiltonian comprising up to seven dimensions. Our setup is based on a holographic optical computer, which realizes a dimensional inflation by spatial and temporal multiplexing of lower dimensional systems. We demonstrate an $N$-vector model, with applications in field theory and computing. The approach is scalable and enables table-top implementation of high-dimensional theoretical models, and novel methods for combinatorial optimization. We experimentally demonstrate dimensional annealing: by dynamically reducing the number of dimensions, the ground state of an Ising model is found in complex graphs by an adiabatic evolution from high-dimensional spaces.
one_liner: A holographic optical computer emulates Hamiltonians of up to seven dimensions using spatial and temporal multiplexing.
why_it_matters: The tabletop architecture offers a scalable experimental route to high-dimensional physical models and dimensional-annealing optimization.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses spatial and temporal multiplexing in a holographic optical computer to synthesize an N-vector Hamiltonian with as many as seven dimensions. It also demonstrates dimensional annealing, dynamically reducing the model dimension so an Ising system evolves toward a ground state on complex graphs. The approach connects high-dimensional analog simulation with combinatorial optimization.
main_result: The system experimentally realizes a seven-dimensional N-vector model and finds Ising ground states through dimensional annealing.
application_angle: The method could support tabletop analog simulation of high-dimensional field models and new optical optimization hardware.

title: Feedback-Controlled Self-Trapping of Solitons
abstract: Chip-scale microresonator-based frequency combs, commonly referred to as microcombs, are promising sources for field-deployable metrology applications. However, intrinsic microresonator noise can make it difficult to generate microcombs with sufficiently low noise for applications. A widely used approach to overcome this limitation is to trap the DKS in the microresonator by phase-modulating the pump laser, although integrating a low-noise modulation reference in a fully on-chip platform remains challenging. Here, we propose an optoelectronic self-trapping scheme in which the impact of intrinsic microresonator noise on microcomb repetition-rate jitter is suppressed through feedback-controlled phase modulation of the driving laser so that the intrinsic noise of the laser sets the ultimate performance limit. This modification eliminates the need for an external low-phase-noise RF source, thereby enabling chip integration. We develop both analytical and numerical models for the proposed system and benchmark its performance against conventional externally referenced bulk implementations, showing that the proposed approach achieves comparable microcomb noise suppression while maintaining chip-scale compatibility.
one_liner: Optoelectronic feedback self-traps dissipative Kerr solitons without an external low-noise RF reference.
why_it_matters: Removing the external RF reference could make low-jitter microcombs easier to integrate into compact, field-deployable metrology systems.
detailed_summary: The proposed loop derives a feedback signal from the microcomb and phase-modulates its pump laser to trap the dissipative Kerr soliton. Analytical and numerical models indicate that this suppresses microresonator-induced repetition-rate jitter until pump-laser noise becomes the limiting factor. Simulations benchmark the scheme as comparable to externally referenced bulk implementations while retaining chip-scale compatibility.
main_result: Models show self-referenced feedback can provide microcomb noise suppression comparable to external-RF trapping schemes.
application_angle: The design targets integrated low-noise comb sources for portable frequency metrology, timing, and spectroscopy.

title: Optical parametric amplification of spatiotemporal optical vortices
abstract: Spatiotemporal optical vortices (STOVs) are structured light featuring a phase singularity in the spatiotemporal domain, exhibiting unique topology that couples spatial and temporal dimensions. To date, amplification of STOVs remains unexplored, and their wavelength tunability is limited by available light sources. In this work, we present the theoretical analysis and experimental demonstration of optical parametric amplification (OPA) of STOVs. The pulse energy of the STOV signal is enhanced by a factor of 60, while its spatiotemporal structure is robustly preserved. The generated idler inherits the phase-conjugated STOV topology with the opposite topological charge, governed by simultaneous conservation of energy, linear momentum, and spatiotemporal orbital angular momentum. The intrinsic wavelength-conversion capability of OPA further provides a route towards spectrally tunable STOV generation, spanning from visible to near-infrared wavelength regimes. This work paves the way toward further development of multi-stage amplification architectures, facilitating applications of wavelength-tunable spatiotemporally structured light at ultrahigh intensities.
one_liner: Optical parametric amplification boosts a spatiotemporal optical vortex by 60× while preserving its topology.
why_it_matters: The experiment adds power scaling and wavelength conversion to topologically structured ultrafast light, enabling stronger and more versatile sources.
detailed_summary: An optical parametric amplifier increases the pulse energy of a spatiotemporal optical vortex signal by a factor of 60 without destroying its coupled space-time structure. The generated idler carries the phase-conjugated vortex with opposite topological charge, consistent with conservation of energy, momentum, and spatiotemporal orbital angular momentum. Parametric conversion also extends STOV generation from visible to near-infrared wavelengths.
platform_or_system: Ultrafast optical parametric amplifier for structured light
main_result: The experiment achieves 60-fold STOV energy amplification and produces a wavelength-shifted idler with opposite topological charge.
application_angle: The technique enables tunable, high-intensity structured pulses for nonlinear optics, advanced imaging, and optical sensing.

title: PPVM: A Circuit Simulation Framework for Digital Twins of Quantum Processors
abstract: Quantum computers are approaching the early fault-tolerant regime. Verifying the next generation of quantum hardware requires joint emulation of the quantum processor, hardware noise, and classical control and decoding logic. We introduce the Programmable Pauli Virtual Machine (PPVM), an open-source framework for digital twins of quantum processors. PPVM unifies Pauli propagation and generalized tableau simulation under a common abstraction within a single virtual machine. Its bytecode supports arbitrary classical control flow, with measurement-conditioned feed-forward available in the generalized tableau backend. For neutral-atom hardware, we derive independent and correlated atom-loss channels and integrate them into both backends. We demonstrate loss-aware magic state distillation on over a thousand physical qubits and integration with classical decoding through Bloqade QEC Studio.
one_liner: PPVM simulates quantum processors together with Pauli noise, atom loss, adaptive control, and classical decoding.
why_it_matters: A unified digital twin can test fault-tolerant protocols under hardware-specific errors and realistic classical feedback before deployment.
detailed_summary: PPVM is an open-source virtual machine combining Pauli propagation and generalized tableau simulation behind a shared abstraction. Its bytecode supports arbitrary classical control flow, while the tableau backend permits measurement-conditioned feed-forward. Hardware-aware neutral-atom models include independent and correlated loss, demonstrated in loss-aware magic-state distillation involving more than 1,000 physical qubits and external decoding through Bloqade QEC Studio.
platform_or_system: Quantum-processor digital twin with neutral-atom noise models
main_result: PPVM jointly emulates large stabilizer circuits, atom-loss processes, adaptive control, and classical decoding at thousand-qubit scale.
application_angle: The framework can accelerate architecture validation, decoder integration, and fault-tolerance studies for emerging quantum processors.

title: Experimental Benchmarking of a 256-Qubit Room-Temperature NV-Diamond Quantum Processor with an Optically Programmable Biomolecular Quantum Bus
abstract: We report Zeus-256, a room-temperature nitrogen-vacancy (NV) diamond processor with 256 simultaneously active processor-level logical qubits arranged in a 16 x 16 array. Each logical qubit combines an NV electron-spin ensemble with nuclear-spin memory and ancillary resources. OpenQASM 2.0 circuits are transpiled into RFSoC-controlled microwave, radio-frequency, optical, timing, measurement and bus-configuration sequences. An optically programmable proprietary protein-chromophore layer with an internal metastable-triplet spin mediator provides a reconfigurable biomolecular quantum bus for local and long-range interactions. Benchmarks cover QFT, GHZ entanglement, Grover search, arithmetic, variational, neural-network, graph-state and Shor-family circuits. Factor recovery is reported for 11 integers of 8-84 bits, with 10 attempts per instance; the 84-bit endpoint uses 256 qubits and 40,250,342 reported gates, with a reported execution time of 551.694 ms. Bell-CHSH measurements yield S = 2.8008 +/- 0.0446. Three-qubit Grover search returns the marked state in 958 of 1,024 shots (93.55%), compared with an ideal reference of 94.53%. A separate 30,000-shot population-and-parity protocol yields fixed-phase GHZ+ fidelity of 99.8960%, an estimated standard error of 0.2885 percentage points and a conservative physical 95% interval of [98.2342%, 100%]. Timing metrics are partial and do not establish quantum advantage. Scaling to 9,984 processor-level logical qubits is an engineering target, distinct from the demonstrated register.
one_liner: The paper reports a 256-qubit room-temperature NV-diamond processor coupled through an optically programmable biomolecular bus.
why_it_matters: If independently substantiated, the reported scale, fidelities, and room-temperature interconnect would represent an unusually large NV hardware advance.
detailed_summary: The authors report Zeus-256, a 16 × 16 array in which each processor-level logical qubit combines an NV ensemble, nuclear-spin memory, and ancillary resources. An RFSoC control stack translates OpenQASM circuits into microwave, RF, optical, measurement, and bus-control sequences, while a proprietary protein-chromophore layer is claimed to mediate configurable interactions. Reported benchmarks include Bell-CHSH S = 2.8008 ± 0.0446, 93.55% three-qubit Grover success, and 99.8960% fixed-phase GHZ+ fidelity; the paper explicitly does not establish quantum advantage.
main_result: The paper reports execution of diverse circuits on 256 active qubits, including an 84-bit factoring instance using over 40 million gates.
application_angle: The claimed architecture targets programmable room-temperature quantum processing with scalable optical interconnects, but its extraordinary results warrant close validation.

title: Collision inside an atom: quantum ion-atom dynamics
abstract: Rydberg atoms occupy a central role in quantum science; their loosely bound outer electron gives rise to properties that enable quantum information processing1 or the formation of exotic molecular bonds2. Beyond these roles, they have been proposed as a neutral platform for the observation of quantum effects in collisions and reactions of the ionic core with neutral particles3, 4, a long-standing goal of ion-based chemistry and physics. However, all of the experimental results so far could be explained using a classical description of the internuclear motion5. Here we demonstrate cold collisions inside a Rydberg helium atom, achieved by merging helium Rydberg and ground-state helium beams and imaging individual scattering events. We resolve the fully quantum-coherent motion and observe matter-wave diffraction and tunnelling-driven shape resonances down to collision energies of 90 mK. In the case of identical helium nuclei, we demonstrate a new regime of identical-particle Mott interference6, where quantum statistics begin to govern the total scattering cross section. For distinct isotopes, we show the breakdown of the Born-Oppenheimer approximation and benchmark parameter-free, state-of-the-art theory. We directly measure the helium isotope ionization-energy difference to be 15.0 +/- 0.1 K. Our experiments establish Rydberg atoms as a platform for the direct observation of quantum dynamics with a general class of ions, atoms and molecules.
one_liner: Merged helium beams reveal coherent ion-atom scattering, matter-wave diffraction, tunnelling resonances, and Mott interference inside Rydberg atoms.
why_it_matters: The platform exposes collision physics inaccessible to classical internuclear models and enables stringent tests of molecular quantum dynamics.
detailed_summary: Helium Rydberg and ground-state beams are merged so that individual collisions between the Rydberg ionic core and a neutral atom can be imaged. Measurements down to 90 mK resolve matter-wave diffraction and tunnelling-driven shape resonances. Identical isotopes exhibit quantum-statistical Mott interference, while mixed isotopes reveal Born-Oppenheimer breakdown and yield an ionization-energy difference of 15.0 ± 0.1 K.
main_result: The experiment directly resolves fully quantum ion-atom collision dynamics inside a Rydberg atom down to 90 mK.
application_angle: Rydberg-hosted collisions offer a controlled testbed for precision spectroscopy, quantum chemistry, and ion-neutral reaction dynamics.

title: V-type Atomic Variance Squeezing
abstract: Variance squeezing of a V-type atom interacting with a dissipative cavity is investigated. First, the influence of atomic initial state parameters on the variance squeezing is explored. The results show that the atomic variance squeezing switches alternately between Sx and Sy as the initial state parameter alpha sweeps from -pi to pi. The two squeezing intervals are symmetric about alpha = pi/4, each with a width of pi/2. For alpha = pi/14, only the Sx component can generate variance squeezing and will eventually disappear with time evolution due to unavoidable environmental noise. Then, the influence of system parameters on the variance squeezing is also studied. It is found that, the optical variance squeezing depth of Sx is determined solely by the atomic initial parameters and is independent of the system parameters. Both weak cavity-environment coupling and atom-cavity detuning can significantly enhance the robustness of the Sx variance squeezing. The SGI parameter has an extremely weak influence on variance squeezing. These results are beneficial for high-precision quantum communication applications.
one_liner: Initial-state control and weak environmental coupling extend atomic variance squeezing in a dissipative V-type cavity system.
why_it_matters: The analysis identifies operating conditions that preserve atomic squeezing, a potential resource for precision optical communication and quantum-state processing.
detailed_summary: The study models variance squeezing of a V-type atom coupled to a dissipative optical cavity. Sweeping the initial-state parameter switches squeezing between the Sx and Sy components in symmetric intervals, while the Sx squeezing depth is determined only by the initial atomic state. Weak cavity-environment coupling and atom-cavity detuning increase squeezing robustness, whereas spontaneously generated interference has little effect.
platform_or_system: V-type atom in a dissipative optical cavity
main_result: Atomic-state preparation selects the squeezed spin component, while weak environmental coupling and detuning prolong Sx variance squeezing.
application_angle: More robust atomic squeezing could support noise-reduced state encoding and precision measurements in cavity-based quantum communication systems.

title: Experimental Realization of a C-Shunt Flux-Qubit Coupler for Controlled-Z Gates between Transmons
abstract: Fast entangling gates and low-interaction idling require distinct operating conditions in superconducting quantum processors. We experimentally realize a transmon-C-shunt-transmon (TCT) device in which a flux-tunable, three-junction capacitively shunted flux-qubit coupler connects two transmon data qubits. The C-shunt coupler provides a flux-tunable, positively anharmonic spectrum for tailoring the interactions between the data qubits. Conditional Ramsey and swap measurements identify an idle region with near-zero residual ZZ interaction strength and suppressed transverse exchange. At this bias, simultaneous single-qubit interleaved randomized benchmarking yields X-gate fldelities above 99.7%, consistent with individual operation. A 45 ns nonadiabatic controlled-Z (CZ) gate achieves an interleaved randomized benchmarking fldelity estimate of 99.23(15)%. Numerical simulations identify coupler energy relaxation as an important limitation on CZ-gate fldelity and indicate that extending the coupler lifetime can improve gate performance. These results demonstrate the experimental feasibility of C-shunt flux-qubit couplers for combining low-interaction idling with fast entangling operations between transmon qubits.
one_liner: A flux-tunable C-shunt coupler enables near-decoupled idling and a 45 ns controlled-Z gate between transmon qubits.
why_it_matters: The device combines low crosstalk during idle periods with fast, high-fidelity entanglement—two competing requirements in superconducting processors.
detailed_summary: A three-junction capacitively shunted flux qubit is used as a tunable coupler between two transmon data qubits. Conditional Ramsey and swap measurements locate an idle bias with near-zero residual ZZ coupling and suppressed transverse exchange, where simultaneous single-qubit X gates exceed 99.7% fidelity. A 45 ns nonadiabatic CZ gate reaches 99.23(15)% interleaved randomized-benchmarking fidelity, with simulations identifying coupler relaxation as a major limitation.
main_result: The coupler supports near-zero-interaction idling and a 45 ns CZ gate with 99.23(15)% estimated fidelity.
application_angle: Improving the coupler lifetime could provide scalable superconducting processors with cleaner idling and faster two-qubit gates.

title: Lifting: Quantum State Discrimination Framework for Mid-Circuit Measurements
abstract: Quantum computing promises new capabilities beyond classical computation. Mid-circuit measurements (MCMs) enable error correction and outcome-dependent control, but their reliability is limited by noise on superconducting hardware. These operations depend on accurate quantum state discrimination (QSD), which assigns measured signals to state labels. Neural network-based (NN-based) QSD improves this assignment, yet its error remains bounded below by the Bayes risk of the available readout distributions. A complementary challenge is state deterioration as successive measurements accumulate and circuit execution advances, making static calibration less representative of the workload. We present Lifting, a QSD framework that addresses both challenges through repetition encoding, neural decoding, and in situ calibration. Encoding supplies joint in-phase and quadrature (I-Q) readout signals from the target and auxiliary qubits, while contextual calibration trains the decoder for the conditions encountered during execution. Our theoretical analysis shows that retaining additional channels from a fixed joint distribution cannot increase Bayes risk and establishes sufficient conditions for contraction of an overlap-based upper bound. Experiments across three IBM processors evaluate the framework on repeated stabilizer measurement, parity-check, and teleportation workloads.
one_liner: Lifting combines repetition encoding, neural decoding, and in situ calibration for noisy mid-circuit state discrimination.
why_it_matters: More reliable mid-circuit readout directly benefits error correction, feed-forward control, parity checks, and teleportation on superconducting processors.
detailed_summary: Lifting collects joint I-Q signals from a target qubit and auxiliary qubits through repetition encoding, then assigns states with a neural decoder trained under workload-specific conditions. The authors prove that retaining extra channels from a fixed joint distribution cannot increase Bayes risk and give conditions for contraction of an overlap-based error bound. The framework is tested on three IBM processors using repeated stabilizer measurement, parity-check, and teleportation circuits.
main_result: The work establishes and experimentally evaluates a context-calibrated, multi-qubit readout framework for mid-circuit measurements.
application_angle: The method targets dependable syndrome extraction and real-time conditional operations without relying on static readout calibration alone.

title: Can the system dynamics remain structurally non-Markovian while its experimentally accessible memory signatures disappear?
abstract: We investigate how unresolved quasistatic disorder in system bath coupling affects non-Markovian dynamics in spin environments. The coupling is fixed within each experimental shot but varies between shots, so repeated shot tomography reconstructs a disorder averaged dynamical map. For a single spin bath with pure dephasing Ising interaction, disorder can drive a transition to CP-divisible dynamics for fixed bath preparations, with a critical strength set by bath polarization along the interaction axis. However, when the bath state fluctuates physically between shots, the averaged dynamics remain CP indivisible at any finite disorder strength. We extend these results analytically to inhomogeneously coupled pure dephasing baths of any number \(N\) of non-interacting spins. At any finite disorder strength, one unpolarized bath spin suffices to retain CP-indivisible dynamics, whereas a fully polarized bath yields Markovian (CP-divisible) dynamics. Dynamics with physically fluctuating bath states likewise remain non-Markovian (CP indivisible) at finite disorder for arbitrary \(N\) in the pure dephasing case. For anisotropic Heisenberg interactions, any nonzero transverse exchange eliminates the disorder driven transition to CP divisibility in a single spin bath. Exact diagonalization of anisotropic models with inhomogeneous couplings up to \(N=12\) reveals persistent trace distance revivals for fixed bath preparations, sampled Haar random preparations, and physically fluctuating bath states, showing that this effect of transverse exchange extends beyond a single bath spin. Increasing disorder still suppresses experimentally accessible revivals and can make memory effects unresolvable at finite measurement resolution even as the dynamics remain CP indivisible. Thus, transverse exchange and physical bath state fluctuations preserve dynamical indivisibility against unresolved coupling disorder.
one_liner: Spin-bath dynamics can remain CP-indivisible even when disorder suppresses memory revivals below experimental resolution.
why_it_matters: The result warns that absent observable revivals do not necessarily imply Markovian behavior in noisy quantum devices or sensing experiments.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes disorder-averaged dynamics when system-bath coupling is fixed within each shot but varies across repeated measurements. For pure-dephasing baths, one unpolarized spin or physically fluctuating bath states preserve CP indivisibility at finite disorder, while a fully polarized bath becomes CP-divisible. Exact diagonalization up to 12 bath spins further shows that transverse exchange preserves trace-distance revivals, although disorder can push them below finite experimental resolution.
platform_or_system: Central quantum system coupled to disordered spin baths
main_result: Bath-state fluctuations and transverse exchange preserve structural non-Markovianity against finite quasistatic coupling disorder.
application_angle: The findings guide interpretation of tomography and coherence data when unresolved disorder hides memory effects relevant to quantum control and sensing.

title: Explicitly correlated ground states with a feedback-free variational hybrid algorithm
abstract: Explicitly correlated methods, which represent dominant short-range correlations by a diagonal Jastrow-type correlator, are designed to accurately describe systems of strongly correlated electrons, such as the fully periodic 2D Fermi--Hubbard model. However, as the reference state is compact in momentum space whereas the correlator acts naturally in real space, there is a fundamental mismatch of bases that classical algorithms resolve only by restricting the reference or the correlator. Here we propose a hybrid algorithm in which a quantum processor prepares a low-entanglement momentum-space matrix product state (MPS), precomputed classically by the transcorrelated method at the cost of a nonvariational energy, rotates it to real space, and measures in bases fixed by the Hamiltonian. Because the measurement bases are independent of the correlator, the correlator can be variationally optimized entirely in classical post-processing with no quantum-classical feedback loop. We demonstrate our algorithm on 32 qubits of Quantinuum's H2-2 with a bond-dimension-4 MPS for the half-filled $4 \times 4$ lattice and achieve a relative ground-state energy error of $16 \pm 4\%$ after postselection, reduced to $3.5 \pm 0.5\%$ by calibration using low-order moments from the MPS. Compared with other feedback-free hybrid algorithms, even under generous assumptions, our method requires fewer samples than quantum-selected configuration interaction and fewer two-qubit gates than quantum Krylov methods.
one_liner: A feedback-free hybrid algorithm estimates a 32-qubit Hubbard ground state using a low-entanglement MPS and classical Jastrow optimization.
why_it_matters: Moving correlator optimization entirely to post-processing reduces quantum feedback, sampling, and gate demands for correlated-electron simulations.
detailed_summary: The protocol prepares a classically precomputed momentum-space bond-dimension-4 MPS, rotates it into real space, and measures in correlator-independent bases. A diagonal Jastrow correlator is then optimized entirely in classical post-processing, eliminating the quantum-classical feedback loop. On 32 qubits of Quantinuum H2-2 for a half-filled 4×4 Hubbard lattice, the relative energy error is 16±4% after postselection and 3.5±0.5% after low-order-moment calibration.
main_result: The feedback-free method achieved a calibrated 3.5±0.5% relative ground-state energy error on a 32-qubit Hubbard-model experiment.
application_angle: The lower sampling and two-qubit-gate requirements offer a practical route to correlated-material calculations on current quantum hardware.

title: Probing topological edge states in multilayer dielectric photonic nanostructures
abstract: Topological photonics has recently attracted a significant attention, leading to many theoretical studies and predictions. However, direct experimental demonstrations of topology-driven effects, particularly in nanostructures, are rarely proven. In this work, we experimentally investigate multilayer photonic nanostructures composed of alternating subwavelength dielectric layers, arranged according to the topological Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. By engineering different edge truncations, we probe different supported topological phases. Our theoretical predictions and experimental measurements reveal strong field confinement at the surface exclusively in the configuration supporting topological edge states, providing their localized character and topological origin. First, we demonstrate enhanced absorption in an ultrathin absorbing overlayer deposited on the surface when the topological surface mode is present, highlighting the potential for surface-sensing applications. Second, we observe enhanced second-harmonic generation in reflection from the surface, demonstrating the potential of topological states for surface enhanced nonlinear optics enabled by the strong localization of the electromagnetic field at the interface.
one_liner: Dielectric SSH multilayers experimentally localize topological edge fields that enhance surface absorption and second-harmonic generation.
why_it_matters: Directly observed nanoscale edge localization provides a robust route to stronger surface sensing and nonlinear optical conversion.
detailed_summary: Alternating subwavelength dielectric layers are arranged as a photonic Su-Schrieffer-Heeger structure with engineered edge terminations. Theory and measurements show strong surface-field confinement only for the termination supporting a topological edge state. That mode enhances absorption in an ultrathin surface overlayer and increases reflected second-harmonic generation through localized interface fields.
main_result: Topological surface modes were experimentally linked to enhanced ultrathin-layer absorption and reflected second-harmonic generation.
application_angle: The localized field can improve compact surface sensors and boost nonlinear optical processes without relying on bulky resonant structures.

title: Finite-energy two-way assisted capacities: Exact formulas for multimode loss and fading
abstract: We study quantum communication, entanglement distribution, and secret-key generation through multimode bosonic loss and fading channels, assisted by local quantum operations and two-way classical communication. Using sector teleportation, we determine the exact two-way quantum and secret-key capacities of multimode pure-loss channels under a mean photon-number constraint, allowing arbitrary adaptive quantum protocols. We extend these results to continuous frequency-dependent loss under a power constraint and identify the optimal allocation of photons among optical modes. For constant loss over an unlimited bandwidth, we obtain a closed-form capacity proportional to the square root of power. For randomly varying loss, we determine exact finite-energy capacities when the channel realization is publicly revealed, distinguishing knowledge before and after transmission. When fading remains unobserved, we derive capacity bounds and explicit formulas for an on/off channel. We also establish strong-converse bounds, with exact thresholds for the deterministic loss models considered here, observed fading, and unobserved fading with finitely many possible transmissivities. Under mean energy constraints, these thresholds generally exceed the corresponding finite-energy capacities. These results guide energy allocation and provide benchmarks for energy-constrained optical quantum communication with multimode signals and variable loss.
one_liner: Exact finite-energy capacities are derived for multimode optical loss and fading channels with arbitrary two-way-assisted protocols.
why_it_matters: The formulas provide rigorous performance benchmarks and optimal energy-allocation rules for practical bandwidth- and power-limited quantum links.
detailed_summary: Sector teleportation yields exact two-way quantum and secret-key capacities for multimode pure-loss channels under a mean photon-number constraint. The analysis extends to frequency-dependent attenuation, power-constrained continuous spectra, and fading with different levels of channel-state knowledge. It also establishes strong-converse thresholds and a square-root-of-power capacity law for constant loss over unlimited bandwidth.
main_result: The work obtains exact energy-constrained two-way quantum and secret-key capacities for deterministic multimode loss and observed fading, plus bounds and formulas for unobserved fading.
application_angle: The results guide photon allocation and set fundamental rate benchmarks for energy-limited fiber, free-space, and fading quantum networks.

title: Quantum-enhanced mechanical sensing with machine-learning estimation
abstract: Massive mechanical oscillators couple directly to forces, accelerations and gravity, making them attractive probes of new physics and of quantum mechanics at macroscopic scales. Pushing sensitivities beyond the standard quantum limit for signals of unknown phase requires non-Gaussian quantum states, whose metrological advantage has so far been confined to lighter systems such as trapped ions. Here we operate a microgram-scale acoustic mode of a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator as a phase-insensitive quantum-enhanced sensor. A transmon qubit prepares the mode in Fock states of up to seven phonons by optimal control, and resolves its phonon-number distribution after interaction with a weak resonant signal. Bayesian analysis yields a Fisher information five times the vacuum value, a 7.0 dB gain in signal-amplitude sensitivity over any classical probe state, irrespective of its energy, currently limited by state preparation infidelities. We then train a neural network on the measured sensor response to perform Bayesian estimation without any analytical model of the system, showing the same sensitivity gain with half the systematic bias. Our results establish acoustic resonators prepared in non-Gaussian states as quantum-enhanced probes for high-frequency gravitational waves, dark matter and wave-function collapse.
one_liner: A microgram acoustic mode prepared in Fock states achieves phase-insensitive quantum-enhanced force sensing with machine-learning estimation.
why_it_matters: It transfers non-Gaussian metrological gain to a comparatively massive mechanical sensor relevant to weak-force and macroscopic-quantum experiments.
detailed_summary: A superconducting transmon prepares a microgram-scale high-overtone bulk acoustic mode in Fock states containing up to seven phonons and reads out its phonon-number distribution after a weak resonant drive. Bayesian analysis reports Fisher information five times the vacuum value and a 7.0 dB signal-amplitude sensitivity gain over any classical probe state. A neural estimator reproduces the gain without an analytical device model while halving systematic bias.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates phase-insensitive quantum-enhanced sensing in a microgram mechanical oscillator with a 7.0 dB amplitude-sensitivity gain.
application_angle: The platform could support searches for high-frequency gravitational waves, dark matter, collapse physics, and other extremely weak mechanical signals.

title: Deterministic and programmable generation of mechanical multipartite entangled states
abstract: Multimode mechanical resonators offer a large set of densely packed, long-lived bosonic modes within a single compact device, making them attractive for quantum simulation, quantum information processing, and quantum-enhanced sensing. Many such applications rely on multipartite entanglement, yet deterministic mechanical entanglement has so far been largely limited to pairs of modes. Here we demonstrate the deterministic and programmable preparation of multipartite entangled states among the phonon modes of a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator coupled to a superconducting transmon qubit. By sequentially applying optimal-control-engineered isometries between the qubit and successive modes, we generate matrix product states of bond dimension two, including $W$, Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ), and cluster states. We fully characterize these states via quantum state tomography and certify genuine multipartite entanglement among up to four modes. We further demonstrate correlated-noise sensing by exploiting the complementary decoherence responses of the stored $W$ and GHZ states, isolating inter-mode phase correlations from local decoherence and placing quantitative bounds on collective dephasing.
