Our results establish a scalable approach to preparing multipartite entangled states in mechanical systems, with promising applications in multiparameter sensing and tests of quantum mechanics with massive objects.
one_liner: Programmable qubit-mediated control deterministically creates W, GHZ, and cluster states across up to four mechanical modes.
why_it_matters: This expands deterministic mechanical entanglement beyond mode pairs and enables compact multimode resources for sensing and bosonic information processing.
detailed_summary: Optimal-control isometries sequentially transfer quantum correlations from a superconducting transmon to phonon modes of a high-overtone bulk acoustic-wave resonator. The protocol generates bond-dimension-two matrix product states, including W, GHZ, and cluster states, and tomography certifies genuine entanglement among as many as four modes. Comparing W- and GHZ-state decoherence also isolates intermode phase correlations and constrains collective dephasing.
platform_or_system: Multimode BAW resonator coupled to a transmon
main_result: The authors deterministically and programmably prepare and verify genuine multipartite entanglement across up to four mechanical modes.
application_angle: The method offers scalable mechanical resources for multiparameter sensing, correlated-noise spectroscopy, quantum simulation, and macroscopic-quantum tests.

title: Information-theoretic measures of electron correlation in a double quantum dot
abstract: In this work, we investigated how variations in spatial confinement affect the electron correlation between two electrons in a symmetric double quantum dot. In strong confinement regime, the ground-state energy can be obtained using the Hartree-Fock method neglecting the electron-electron repulsion term. Under a weaker confinement, the FCI method provides a more accurate description. Using the mutual information as a measure of correlation, we determine the confinement regions where electronic motion is uncorrelated. We conjecture that the Shannon entropy can serve as a qualitative guide to to study the electron correlation. We identified an approximately linear relationship between mutual information and relative correlation energy.
one_liner: Information-theoretic metrics map how spatial confinement controls two-electron correlation in a symmetric double quantum dot.
why_it_matters: The reported relation between mutual information and correlation energy may provide a compact diagnostic for tuning interacting semiconductor quantum devices.
detailed_summary: The study compares Hartree–Fock and full-configuration-interaction descriptions of two electrons in a symmetric double quantum dot as confinement is varied. Mutual information identifies regimes where electron motion is effectively uncorrelated, while Shannon entropy is proposed as a qualitative correlation indicator. An approximately linear relationship is found between mutual information and relative correlation energy.
main_result: The calculations identify confinement-dependent correlation regimes and an approximately linear link between mutual information and relative correlation energy.
application_angle: These metrics could help characterize and tune electron interactions in quantum-dot hardware without relying solely on energy-based correlation measures.

title: $\mathsf{EFI}\Leftrightarrow\mathsf{1PRS}$
abstract: A series of recent works has established EFI pairs as the "minimal" assumption for quantum cryptography. Recently, Cavalar et al. [CCC+26] showed that EFI pairs are equivalent to non-uniform expanding single-copy pseudorandom state generators (1PRS), and obtained a non-uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. We remove the non-uniformity in their construction and prove that EFI pairs are equivalent to expanding 1PRS. As a corollary, we obtain the first uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. Together with the equivalence of statistically verifiable one-way state generators and commitments proved by Batra and Jain [BJ24], this gives a quantum analogue of the classical equivalence between one-way functions, commitments, and pseudorandom generators.
one_liner: EFI pairs are proved equivalent to uniform expanding single-copy pseudorandom-state generators.
why_it_matters: The equivalence sharpens the minimal assumptions underlying quantum cryptography and supplies its first uniform meta-complexity characterization.
detailed_summary: The paper removes the non-uniformity from an earlier construction connecting efficiently samplable, statistically far but computationally indistinguishable state pairs to expanding single-copy pseudorandom-state generators. It proves a uniform equivalence between EFI pairs and expanding 1PRS. Combined with prior results on one-way state generators and commitments, this yields a quantum counterpart of classical equivalences among one-way functions, commitments, and pseudorandom generators.
main_result: The work establishes the uniform equivalence of EFI pairs and expanding 1PRS and derives the first uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs.
application_angle: The result clarifies which computational assumptions suffice for commitments and pseudorandom quantum-state primitives used in secure quantum protocols.

title: Gaussian entanglement and quantum communication: geodesic optimization and multimode bounds
abstract: Loss and noise limit the use of light to distribute entanglement, transmit quantum information, and establish secret keys. Gaussian states have a compact description in terms of means and covariance matrices, but their entanglement still requires global optimization. We develop a framework for computing Gaussian-restricted versions of the relative entropy of entanglement and Rains entanglement. An integral representation reveals a convex geometry under matrix geometric means and reduces Gaussian Rains entanglement to relative entropy minimized over Gaussian states with positive partial transpose. We obtain unique optimal reference states and additivity for independent Gaussian input states. Our convex-majorization algorithm has an explicit geometric convergence rate, uniform in the faithful regularization parameter and valid for pure input states. Controlled numerical integration and approximate convex subproblem solutions give a bit-complexity bound that is polynomial in accuracy bits for each fixed rational input covariance matrix, with explicit dependence on covariance size. These calculations bound extractable entanglement and, through the relative entropy of entanglement, extractable secret key. Teleportation simulation, energy allocation, and a convex optimization of passive-basis loss cores give bounds on quantum and private communication under an input-energy constraint, allowing arbitrary two-way classically assisted protocols. Two- and three-mode examples compare the bounds with achievable rates, including matching pure-loss benchmarks. Finally, we separate the Gaussian-restricted quantities from their unrestricted counterparts and give a photon-number truncation method with controlled error for computing the latter.
one_liner: Geodesic convex optimization makes Gaussian entanglement measures computable and yields multimode bounds on energy-constrained quantum links.
why_it_matters: The framework supplies scalable, certified upper bounds for entanglement, secret-key extraction, and two-way-assisted optical communication.
detailed_summary: An integral representation exposes convex geometry under matrix geometric means and reduces Gaussian Rains entanglement to optimization over Gaussian positive-partial-transpose states. The authors prove uniqueness and additivity, give a geometrically convergent algorithm with bit-complexity guarantees, and handle pure inputs through controlled regularization. Teleportation simulation and optimized energy allocation then produce multimode bounds on quantum and private communication, with controlled photon-number truncation for unrestricted quantities.
main_result: The paper develops certified algorithms for Gaussian entanglement measures and converts them into energy-constrained bounds for arbitrary two-way-assisted quantum and private communication.
application_angle: These tools enable quantitative evaluation and optimization of realistic multimode optical links when loss, energy budgets, and passive mode mixing matter.

title: Logical gate set tomography
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) can strongly suppress noise, but predicting whether a computation succeeds requires understanding not only how much effective noise persists after QEC, but what form that noise takes. To thoroughly characterize this noise, we introduce logical gate set tomography (``logical GST''). Logical GST produces detailed representations of noisy logical operations that can be used to derive higher-level metrics, such as gate fidelity and diamond distance, and to test for non-Markovian and coherent logical errors. We use logical GST to obtain the first full, self-consistent characterization of a universal single-qubit logical gate set, implemented in the seven-qubit Steane code using Quantinuum System Model H1, a 20-qubit trapped-ion quantum processor. In the experimental data from H1, logical GST identified predominantly logical Pauli-stochastic errors, found no evidence of logical non-Markovianity, and detected weak potential signatures of coherent logical error. By contrast, higher-shot datasets generated with Quantinuum's detailed system emulator, identify mechanisms for weak but statistically significant logical non-Markovianity and strong evidence of coherent logical error. Finally, we use logical GST to perform error attribution with the system emulator, revealing how specific physical error sources shape logical error mechanisms.
one_liner: Logical gate set tomography fully characterizes a universal logical-qubit gate set on Quantinuum’s trapped-ion H1 processor.
why_it_matters: It reveals the form and physical origins of residual logical errors, enabling more reliable fault-tolerant performance predictions than fidelity alone.
detailed_summary: The authors introduce logical gate set tomography, a self-consistent method for reconstructing noisy logical preparations, measurements, and gates after quantum error correction. They apply it to a universal single-qubit gate set encoded in the seven-qubit Steane code on Quantinuum System Model H1. Hardware data show predominantly Pauli-stochastic logical noise, while higher-statistics emulator studies expose coherent errors, weak non-Markovianity, and links between physical error sources and logical mechanisms.
main_result: The work delivers the first full, self-consistent experimental characterization of a universal single-qubit logical gate set.
application_angle: Logical GST can guide hardware debugging, decoder improvement, and realistic forecasting of fault-tolerant algorithm performance.

title: The cost of classically simulating quantum communication is as high as it could be
abstract: A long-standing open question is to characterize the classical communication cost of simulating the correlations arising from measurements on finite-dimensional quantum systems. We consider this question in the prepare-and-measure scenario. First we construct a classical simulation model involving a finite average number of bits of one-way communication that simulates exactly the correlations arising from arbitrary $d$-dimensional quantum states and arbitrary measurements. Second, we show that no classical simulation protocol involving a finite average message dimension can exist for $d\geq 4$, hence strengthening a recent result of de Gois, Santos and Vieira. Our first result relies on a more general simulation theorem which can be applied to certain continuous variable (i.e. infinite-dimensional) quantum systems, and even beyond quantum theory, e.g. to generalized probabilistic theories. In particular, we show that multimode Gaussian states of bounded average energy and general Gaussian measurements admit an exact classical simulation with a finite expected number of bits. Overall, our results show that the classical simulation cost of quantum communication is essentially as high as it could be.
one_liner: Exact classical simulation of finite-dimensional quantum communication is possible with finite expected bits but not finite average message dimension.
why_it_matters: The result sharply separates finite expected communication from finite-dimensional messages and establishes near-maximal classical simulation complexity.
detailed_summary: The paper constructs an exact one-way classical simulation for arbitrary finite-dimensional prepare-and-measure quantum correlations using a finite expected number of communicated bits. It also proves that, for dimension d at least 4, no exact protocol can have finite average message dimension. A broader theorem covers bounded-energy multimode Gaussian states with general Gaussian measurements and extends to some generalized probabilistic theories.
main_result: Quantum prepare-and-measure correlations admit exact finite-expected-bit simulation, yet require unbounded message dimension for systems of dimension four or greater.
application_angle: The bounds clarify the classical resources needed to reproduce quantum communication links and help identify operational quantum advantages.

title: A modular quantum computer based on Cornucopia codes
abstract: Ultra-high-rate quantum error correction codes store many logical qubits in a single code block with few physical qubits. A fault-tolerant quantum computer, however, also requires a universal set of logical operations on individually addressable logical qubits, and the ancilla overhead of these operations may erode the advantage of the high encoding rate. Here, we propose the Cornucopia architecture, in which a universal set of logical operations is implemented at low overhead for the Cornucopia codes. In particular, we focus on the [[2844,1426,18]] Cornucopia code as an example and introduce a modular quantum computer built from such code blocks connected by bridges. Each block stores 1,426 logical qubits and serves as a universal logical processor. Exploiting the code's translation symmetry, we construct a family of reusable gadgets that individually address 1,422 logical qubits within each block. These gadgets support three universal logical instruction sets: basic, high-throughput and fixed-extractor. Excluding magic-state factories, a module with sufficient workspace to execute any instruction in the basic set requires an average of 4.1 physical qubits per logical qubit, compared with 3.0 for memory alone. The architecture thus preserves the resource advantage of ultra-high-rate quantum memory while enabling universal logical computation, providing a route towards low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computers.
one_liner: A modular Cornucopia-code architecture enables universal logical computation while retaining ultra-high-rate quantum-memory efficiency.
why_it_matters: It addresses the control and ancilla overhead that can otherwise erase the physical-qubit savings of high-rate error-correcting codes.
detailed_summary: The proposed architecture uses [[2844,1426,18]] Cornucopia-code blocks connected by bridges, with each block acting as a universal processor for 1,426 logical qubits. Translation symmetry enables reusable gadgets that individually address 1,422 logical qubits and support three instruction-set variants. Excluding magic-state factories, a basic universal module averages 4.1 physical qubits per logical qubit, versus 3.0 for memory alone.
main_result: The architecture combines individually addressable universal logical operations with an average cost of 4.1 physical qubits per logical qubit for the basic instruction set.
application_angle: It offers a resource-efficient blueprint for scaling modular fault-tolerant quantum computers with dense logical-qubit storage.

title: Federated Unlearning of Quantum Data via Classical Shadows
abstract: Quantum federated learning trains a quantum neural network (QNN) across nodes that hold quantum data, such as the states of quantum sensors. To forget data, unlearning methods for quantum models replay them, and federated unlearning from stored updates removes whole nodes only. Quantum data cannot be replayed, since a state is consumed when measured and cannot be cloned. We propose Shadow-based Data Erasure (SHADE), in which each node records a classical shadow of every training state, a few randomized single-qubit measurements taken at training time. The gradient and curvature of a QNN on a state are expectations of observables, so SHADE estimates them for the forget data from the shadows at any later parameters and removes their effect by a federated Newton correction. Only classical estimates cross the network. We prove that the shadow size needed for a target unlearning error grows exponentially in the size of the backward light cone of the measured observable and not in the number of qubits. In simulation with 50 nodes and on edge boards, SHADE matches the forget accuracy of retraining within 0.5 points, without replay and in under 0.2 s.
one_liner: SHADE uses classical shadows and a federated Newton correction to erase consumed quantum training data without replay.
why_it_matters: It enables data-level unlearning for distributed quantum-sensor models despite the no-cloning rule and destructive quantum measurements.
detailed_summary: Each federated node records randomized single-qubit classical-shadow measurements of its quantum training states, allowing later estimates of QNN gradients and curvature. SHADE removes selected data through a federated Newton correction while exchanging only classical estimates. Across simulations with 50 nodes and edge-board tests, it approaches retraining forget accuracy within 0.5 percentage points in under 0.2 seconds; shadow cost scales with backward-light-cone size rather than total qubit count.
main_result: SHADE achieves replay-free quantum-data erasure with near-retraining accuracy and sub-0.2-second execution in the reported tests.
application_angle: The method supports fast privacy, consent-revocation, and data-governance workflows for distributed quantum sensing and edge learning.

title: Selective Control and Imaging of Higgs and Goldstone Modes with a Quantum Simulator
abstract: We realize the mesoscopic Bose-Hubbard model at unit-filling on a two-dimensional array of transmon qubits and selectively excite collective modes associated with amplitude or phase fluctuations of the superfluid order parameter. We identify these modes respectively as the Higgs and Goldstone modes using complementary local observables, extracted from measuring the number of particles on each site. Modulation of the coupling between sites excites the Higgs mode, which we detect via the density of doubly occupied sites. In contrast, modulation of the local chemical potential with an appropriately chosen spatial profile excites the lowest-frequency Goldstone mode, which we detect via changes in the local density. The two modes have different symmetries and do not couple to one another. By varying the system geometry, we characterize the impact of finite system size on the evolution of both modes. In the thermodynamic limit, decay into a continuum of lower-energy excitations can obscure the Higgs response. In our mesoscopic system, however, the finite system size leads to spectral gaps and allows us to detect the Higgs mode as a coherent, long-lived excitation. Our work demonstrates how finite quantum simulators can isolate and probe physical phenomena that become difficult to resolve in the thermodynamic, large-scale limit.
one_liner: A 2D transmon quantum simulator selectively excites and images coherent Higgs and Goldstone modes in a mesoscopic Bose-Hubbard system.
why_it_matters: Finite-size spectral gaps expose collective modes that become difficult to resolve in bulk systems, expanding quantum simulators’ spectroscopic reach.
detailed_summary: The experiment realizes a unit-filled mesoscopic Bose-Hubbard model on a two-dimensional transmon array. Coupling modulation excites the amplitude-like Higgs mode, detected through double occupancy, whereas patterned chemical-potential modulation excites the phase-like Goldstone mode, detected in local density. Geometry-dependent measurements show that finite-size gaps isolate a coherent, long-lived Higgs response and preserve the modes’ distinct symmetries.
main_result: The simulator selectively controls and locally images distinct Higgs and Goldstone collective modes, including a long-lived finite-size Higgs excitation.
application_angle: The approach provides a programmable platform for resolving elusive many-body dynamics and benchmarking analog quantum simulators through local observables.

title: Beyond the lemon: Spectra of random Lindblad operators with a Hamiltonian component
abstract: Generators of continuous-time quantum Markovian evolution, known as Lindblad operators, play a key role in the theory of open quantum systems. The question of how to define and characterize random Lindblad operators has attracted considerable attention in recent years. Purely dissipative random Lindbladians have been extensively studied using toolboxes of free probability and non-Hermitian random matrix theories, which helped, among other results, to uncover a characteristic lemon-like spectral support. In this work, we focus on random Lindbladians with a Hamiltonian component. We analyze three ensembles of increasing complexity, designed to illustrate the joint effects of dissipative and Hamiltonian dynamics. While the first two ensembles allow for an exact analytic treatment with standard probabilistic and free-probability methods, the generic case of independently random Hamiltonian and dissipative components requires a novel framework that combines operator-valued free probability with sequential noise averaging. For this ensemble, our approach preserves the underlying tensor-product structure of the Lindblad operator and derives a general equation for the spectral boundary. We characterize the effect of Hamiltonian-induced spectral squeezing and explain how the spectral support changes with the relative Hamiltonian strength and the rank of the dissipative component.
one_liner: A new free-probability framework predicts spectra of random Lindbladians with coupled Hamiltonian and dissipative dynamics.
why_it_matters: Its spectral-boundary equations clarify how coherent evolution reshapes relaxation spectra in complex open quantum systems.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes three ensembles of random Lindblad generators containing Hamiltonian and dissipative components. For the generic independently random case, it combines operator-valued free probability with sequential noise averaging while retaining the Lindbladian tensor-product structure. The resulting boundary equation describes Hamiltonian-induced spectral squeezing and its dependence on coherent strength and dissipator rank.
main_result: The authors derive a general spectral-boundary equation for random Lindbladians with independent Hamiltonian and dissipative components.
application_angle: The theory can inform modeling of relaxation, stability, and decoherence spectra in complex driven-dissipative photonic and quantum platforms.

title: Gap-Priced $|T\rangle$-States: Dynamic $|T\rangle$ Post-Selection and Budget-Aware Factory Provisioning
abstract: Magic $|T\rangle$-state preparation dominates the cost of fault-tolerant quantum computation on surface codes, yet cultivation and distillation are typically provisioned statically, leaving much of the program's error budget unused. We present Gap-Priced $|T\rangle$ States (GP$|T\rangle$-S), a lattice surgery scheduler and factory allocator that co-optimizes both methods under a total $T$-error budget. GP$|T\rangle$-S uses the complementary gap of each cultivated state as a fidelity estimate and dynamically adjusts the cultivation gap cutoff, converting budget slack into speed by giving the scheduler control over the cultivation post-selection. GP$|T\rangle$-S also characterizes distillation factories by size, $|T\rangle$-state production rate, and budget slack, and introduces cultivating factories that embed cultivation within routing channels, achieving fidelities otherwise requiring two-level distillation at a single-level footprint. GP$|T\rangle$-S organizes these characterizations into a factory catalog, and performs distillation factory allocation over this catalog in tandem with the gap cutoff using dynamic-programming to achieve one of i) minimum spacetime volume, ii) minimum execution time, or iii) minimum space overhead, all within a user-provided $T$-error budget. Across sixteen benchmarks under high and low $T$-error budgets of $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-5}$ respectively, GP$|T\rangle$-S consistently outperforms cultivation-only and single-factory baselines without exceeding the budget, achieving a 5.5$\times$ geometric mean speedup in logical cycle count and a 3.4$\times$ geometric mean reduction in space-time volume.
one_liner: A budget-aware scheduler dynamically combines cultivated and distilled T states to reduce fault-tolerant quantum-computing overhead.
why_it_matters: Adaptive use of the available error budget could substantially reduce the time and hardware footprint of surface-code quantum computation.
detailed_summary: GP|T⟩-S jointly selects cultivation post-selection thresholds and distillation-factory configurations under a user-defined total T-state error budget. Its catalog includes cultivating factories embedded in routing channels and supports optimization for spacetime volume, runtime, or space. Across 16 benchmarks at error budgets of 10^-3 and 10^-5, it reports 5.5× geometric-mean fewer logical cycles and 3.4× lower spacetime volume than cultivation-only and single-factory baselines.
main_result: Dynamic T-state post-selection and factory allocation achieve 5.5× mean speedup and 3.4× mean spacetime-volume reduction without exceeding the error budget.
application_angle: The method can guide resource-efficient provisioning of magic-state factories in large-scale fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Leakage benchmarking with decohering subgroups in the presence of preparation and measurement errors
abstract: A common problem with physical qubits is that the state can leak outside the computational subspace. To characterize the problem, it is desirable to measure both the leakage probability and the fidelity of gates inside the computational subspace. Randomized benchmarking is a readily accessible method for estimating average gate fidelities and can be modified to account for leakage. However, in the presence of state preparation and measurement errors (SPAM) there are parameter degeneracies, and fidelities and leakage become underdetermined. We study the example of qudits with any number of leakage levels under the assumption of gate-independent noise. We show that randomized benchmarking sequences with leakage level decoherence can be analyzed as a Markov process with noisy classical preparations and measurements. This result generalizes to randomized benchmarking with random gates from an arbitrary group that contains a phase-decohering subgroup. We characterize the parameter degeneracy in inferring the Markov process, preparations and measurements. Based on this characterization we develop a measurement and inference method taking advantage of known conservative bounds on SPAM to constrain fidelity, leakage and other parameters of the Markov process, state preparations and measurements. As part of our study, we experimentally implemented the measurement method for a qubit defined on the one-excitation subspace of two transmons, for which there are two leakage levels. We determined confidence intervals accounting for parameter degeneracy for a number of performance parameters of the system. For leakage and fidelity, we compare these intervals to those obtained for several conventional methods for leakage benchmarking.
one_liner: A leakage-benchmarking method uses SPAM bounds to extract defensible fidelity and leakage intervals despite inference degeneracies.
why_it_matters: It enables more reliable characterization of multilevel hardware when leakage and imperfect preparation or measurement cannot be independently identified.
detailed_summary: The authors map randomized benchmarking with decohering leakage levels to a Markov process with noisy classical preparation and measurement. They characterize the resulting parameter degeneracies and use conservative prior bounds on SPAM to constrain gate fidelity, leakage, transition parameters, and readout. The protocol is demonstrated on a logical qubit encoded in the one-excitation subspace of two transmons with two leakage levels.
main_result: The method produces confidence intervals for leakage and fidelity that explicitly account for otherwise underdetermined SPAM parameters.
application_angle: It offers an experimentally accessible diagnostic for validating gates and tracking leakage in superconducting and other multilevel quantum processors.

title: A note on the A.C. spectrum of limit-periodic Jacobi matrices
abstract: We show that limit-periodic Jacobi matrices in the weak exponential class $EC(η)$ have purely absolutely continuous spectral type when $η$ is sufficiently large, depending only on the $R$-boundedness constant. The proof first establishes homogeneity of the spectrum from the weak exponential approximation rate. A closure theorem for reflectionless Jacobi matrices then transfers reflectionlessness from the periodic approximants to the limit, and a theorem of Poltoratski and Remling rules out singular spectrum on a homogeneous set.
one_liner: The work proves purely absolutely continuous spectra for a class of rapidly approximable limit-periodic Jacobi matrices.
why_it_matters: The result advances mathematical spectral theory, though it has no direct experimental quantum-photonics or hardware demonstration.
detailed_summary: The paper proves that limit-periodic Jacobi matrices in a weak exponential approximation class have purely absolutely continuous spectral type when the approximation rate is sufficiently large. The argument establishes spectral homogeneity, transfers reflectionlessness from periodic approximants through a closure theorem, and invokes a Poltoratski–Remling result to exclude singular spectrum. The contribution is theoretical and does not present a photonic device or experiment.
main_result: Sufficiently rapid weak-exponential periodic approximation guarantees a purely absolutely continuous spectrum under the stated boundedness condition.
application_angle: The theorem may inform mathematical models of wave propagation in quasiperiodic media, but its near-term application relevance is indirect.

title: Retrieving Metrological Information from Noisy Squeezed Spin States via Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Frequency inhomogeneity can obscure the metrological advantage of squeezed spin states, making the choice of readout crucial. We study interacting spin-1/2 ensembles with static local frequency disorder and optimize a common collective readout over independent disorder realizations. Using Bayesian optimization of the full measurement-outcome distribution, we identify observables combining dipole and quadrupole operators that yield greater classical Fisher information than the optimized dipole readout considered here. For ensembles of up to 17 spins, their disorder-averaged CFI surpasses the standard quantum limit at both disorder strengths studied, including a regime where the dipole readout remains below it. For the larger ensembles studied, fixing the encoding axis to the direction that maximizes the disorder-averaged quantum Fisher information retains nearly the same performance. These results identify a route to extracting metrological information from frequency-disordered spin ensembles through the choice of collective observable.
one_liner: Bayesian optimization finds collective spin readouts that recover sub-SQL sensitivity from frequency-disordered squeezed states.
why_it_matters: Optimized observables can preserve useful quantum-enhanced sensitivity when inhomogeneous broadening defeats conventional collective-spin readout.
detailed_summary: The study considers interacting spin-1/2 ensembles with static local frequency disorder and optimizes a shared collective measurement across disorder realizations. Bayesian optimization over the full outcome distribution identifies observables combining dipole and quadrupole operators. For ensembles up to 17 spins, the disorder-averaged classical Fisher information remains above the standard quantum limit at both tested disorder strengths, including one where optimized dipole readout is sub-SQL.
main_result: Dipole–quadrupole collective observables recover disorder-averaged classical Fisher information above the standard quantum limit for ensembles of up to 17 spins.
application_angle: The approach could improve sensing with spin-squeezed atomic, solid-state, or molecular ensembles affected by static frequency inhomogeneity.

title: A compact six-beam 3D magneto-optical trap based on multifunctional metasurface chips
abstract: Magneto-optical traps (MOTs), indispensable to cold-atom-based quantum computing and quantum precision measurement, are increasingly desired in compact and stable form. Particularly, the six-beam 3D-MOT, distinguished by symmetric geometry and superior trapping performance, finds particularly broad applications. Conventional implementations, however, rely on complex and bulky free-space optics, hindering miniaturization, practical assembly, and long-term stability. Here, we demonstrate a compact six-beam 3D-MOT system that employs two multifunctional optical metasurface chips to implement the optical-field functionalities required for cooling and trapping atoms. By combining two metasurface chips and a vacuum cell, a photonic-integrated cell module (PICM) is implemented as the core assembly and the volume is only" 73*73*107 mm^3" . In success, 1.3 * 10^3 Rb atoms are trapped and cooled to the temperature of ~183 μK. It should be noticed that the laser beam is guided to the metasurface through optical fiber, thus such fully fiber-coupled architecture enables straightforward and stable operations. We believe that this work would pave a practical route toward compact and portable 3D-MOT.
one_liner: Two multifunctional metasurface chips form a fiber-fed six-beam 3D MOT that traps 1.3×10^3 rubidium atoms at about 183 μK.
why_it_matters: Replacing bulky free-space optics with metasurfaces advances compact, stable cold-atom sources for portable sensors and quantum systems.
detailed_summary: The authors integrate two multifunctional metasurface chips with a vacuum cell to generate the optical fields required for a symmetric six-beam 3D magneto-optical trap. The resulting photonic-integrated cell module occupies 73×73×107 mm³ and is fed by optical fiber. It traps approximately 1.3×10^3 rubidium atoms and cools them to roughly 183 μK.
main_result: A compact, fully fiber-coupled metasurface module demonstrates six-beam trapping of 1.3×10^3 Rb atoms at approximately 183 μK.
application_angle: The architecture supports miniaturized cold-atom clocks, inertial sensors, magnetometers, and neutral-atom quantum-computing platforms.

title: Shot- and Noise-Aware Pauli Correlation Encoding for Max-Cut Experiments on IBM Heron Quantum Processor
abstract: Pauli correlation encoding (PCE) encodes $m$ binary variables in the signs of $k$-body Pauli correlators of $n=O(m^{1/k})$ qubits, and trains a parameterized circuit on a relaxed loss of sharpness $α$. The strongest published schedules sharpen this loss aggressively and are benchmarked with exact expectation values, whereas a quantum computer estimates correlators from a finite number of shots. We show that the sharpness is a hidden shot budget. Since the expected sign of a correlator estimated from $S$ shots, $\mathrm{erf}(c\sqrt{S/2})$, agrees with $\tanh(0.851\sqrt{S}\,c)$ to within $0.019$, the edge term of the relaxed loss at $α=0.851\sqrt{S}$ approximately equals, up to a constant, minus twice the cut expected from decoding $S$ shots. This explains why schedules tuned with exact expectation values lose their advantage at realistic budgets, and yields a shot-aware schedule whose final sharpness is set by the shot budget. On five G-set graphs with $800$ variables on $13$ qubits, this schedule outperforms every published schedule at its target budget in all $150$ paired comparisons of the decoded circuit output, owing to the sharpness at $1.6\times10^4$ shots and mostly to switching off the regularization at $10^3$; after a classical bit-swap search, it remains the best on average at $1.6\times10^4$ shots. Device noise damps the correlators by a factor $s$, which amounts to a smaller shot budget $s^2S$. On the IBM Heron processor ibm_fez, an all-to-all ansatz of the type used for the best published G-set results compiles to $835$ CZ gates and decodes to a random cut, while our $96$-CZ hardware-native circuit, trained in simulation and sharpened to $α\simeq0.65\,s\sqrt{S}$, retains up to $0.919$ of the best-known cut. For new circuits, a damping and an offset calibrated on other circuits of the same graph predicted the decoded cuts at $10^3$ shots to within $0.002$.
one_liner: A shot- and noise-aware Pauli-correlation schedule preserves strong Max-Cut solutions on IBM Heron with a hardware-native circuit.
why_it_matters: Matching optimization sharpness to finite-shot statistics and device damping makes compressed quantum encodings more useful on current hardware.
detailed_summary: The paper interprets the sharpness parameter in Pauli correlation encoding as an implicit shot budget and derives a schedule scaled to finite sampling. On five 800-variable G-set graphs encoded with 13 qubits, the schedule wins all 150 paired comparisons against published schedules at their target budgets. On ibm_fez, a 96-CZ hardware-native circuit retains up to 0.919 of the best-known cut, whereas an 835-CZ all-to-all ansatz decodes to a random cut.
main_result: A 96-CZ noise-aware circuit achieved up to 91.9% of the best-known Max-Cut value while a deeper 835-CZ ansatz produced random-quality cuts.
application_angle: The calibration and scheduling strategy provides a practical route to running compressed combinatorial-optimization experiments on noisy processors.

title: A Reconstruction of Michelson Interference from On--Off Detection Statistics
abstract: This paper reconstructs the Michelson interference phenomenon based solely on the binary (on-off) statistics of a single-photon counter and macroscopic path-difference data, without the a priori assumptions of complex wave superposition or prior spectral information. In contrast to the conventional approach that assumes light as a continuous complex wave function and considers interference between them, this study focuses on the algebraic properties inherent in discrete detection statistics. We verify that the discrete response data collected across various path differences form a positive semi-definite matrix, and apply Herglotz's theorem to this result. Consequently, we show that the harmonic form of the interference fringe is not a consequence of adopting a wave model as an axiom, but rather it is uniquely decomposed into a cosine average of wavenumbers dictated by testable algebraic constraints satisfied by the statistical data. Through this approach, the logical basis of the interference phenomenon can be described by the characteristics of the binary data itself, perfectly aligning with the modern optical experimental environment that relies entirely on discrete event statistics.
one_liner: Michelson fringes are reconstructed from binary photon-counting data without assuming complex-wave superposition or prior spectral information.
why_it_matters: The work derives interference structure from experimentally testable statistical constraints, offering a detection-centric foundation for optical interferometry.
detailed_summary: The study uses on-off statistics from a single-photon counter measured across macroscopic path differences. It verifies that the resulting discrete response data form a positive semidefinite matrix and applies Herglotz's theorem to obtain a unique cosine-average decomposition over wavenumbers. Thus, harmonic interference emerges from algebraic constraints on detection statistics rather than an assumed complex-wave model.
main_result: Michelson interference is reconstructed directly from binary detection statistics as a uniquely constrained cosine average of wavenumbers.
application_angle: The framework supports model-light analysis of event-based interferometric measurements when spectral information is unavailable.

title: Cryogenic Multiplexing Control Chip for Superconducting Quantum Processor
abstract: This paper proposes a scheme and design of cryogenic multiplexing control chip (MCC) which enables one microwave cable to control many superconducting qubits. Designed based on adjustable inductor, MCC is a non-reciprocal device which generates microwave signals between 4 and 8 GHz and constructs XY control circuit to operate qubits. The effects of filters, isolators, power splitters, qubits and load impedance on MCC are analyzed in the frequency-domain simulation. And in time-domain simulation, the response time, Gaussian pulses, single-sideband, amplitude and frequency compensation of MCC are examined. The MCC can be integrated with the superconducting qubits on the same package at 20 mK temperature stage, and output specific microwave pulses used to drive the superconducting qubits without crosstalks. The MCC can greatly reduce the number of microwave control lines and is beneficial to the development of large-scale superconducting quantum processor.
one_liner: A cryogenic multiplexing chip is designed to generate 4–8 GHz qubit-control pulses for many superconducting qubits through one microwave cable.
why_it_matters: Integrating multiplexed control at 20 mK could reduce cryostat wiring and control-line scaling pressure in large superconducting processors.
detailed_summary: The proposed nonreciprocal multiplexing control chip uses adjustable inductors to synthesize 4–8 GHz microwave signals and implement XY control. Frequency-domain simulations include filters, isolators, splitters, qubits, and load impedance, while time-domain studies examine Gaussian pulses, single-sideband operation, response time, and compensation. The design is intended for same-package integration with qubits at the 20 mK stage.
main_result: Simulations indicate that one cryogenic multiplexing chip can deliver targeted microwave control pulses to multiple qubits without crosstalk.
application_angle: The approach could substantially reduce microwave cabling and enable denser control architectures for scalable superconducting processors.

title: Dynamical Decoupling of Nonclassical States in a Biased-Noise Spin Qudit
abstract: Encoding quantum information in $d$-dimensional systems (qudits) with $d>2$ offers appealing new directions for resource-efficient quantum computing. However, protecting the coherence of nonclassical qudit resource states remains an open challenge. Dynamical decoupling (DD) is a well-established technique for extending coherence, but its application to qudits is hindered by the quadratic scaling of the decoupling sequence overhead with the dimension $d$. As a result, demonstrations of qudit DD have so far been limited to low-dimensional qudits. Here, we show that noise-biased qudits enable a nontrivial reduction of this overhead, for example, from quadratic to linear. We perform qudit DD on a model $d=8$ qudit, the nuclear spin of an antimony donor in silicon. We benchmark DD performance on highly nonclassical states such as uniform superpositions, cat states, and Haar random states and measure coherence improvements up to a factor $5$ to $10$. For a spin-cat error correction code, continuous DD extends the coherence time of the logical superposition $|+\rangle_L$ to $225$~ms, compared to $19$~ms under free evolution and $85$~ms with a Hahn echo. This improvement shows that DD sequences tailored to a system's noise bias can significantly enhance the lifetime of encoded logical qubits.
one_liner: Noise-tailored dynamical decoupling extends coherence of nonclassical states in an eight-level antimony nuclear-spin qudit by up to 5–10×.
why_it_matters: Exploiting biased noise reduces decoupling overhead from quadratic toward linear scaling while protecting encoded qudit resources in silicon.
detailed_summary: The experiment implements dynamical decoupling on the d=8 nuclear spin of an antimony donor in silicon. Noise-biased sequences reduce the control overhead and improve coherence by factors of 5–10 for uniform superpositions, cat states, and Haar-random states. For a spin-cat code, continuous decoupling extends the logical |+⟩ coherence to 225 ms, versus 19 ms under free evolution and 85 ms with Hahn echo.
platform_or_system: Antimony donor nuclear-spin qudit in silicon
main_result: Bias-tailored continuous decoupling preserves a spin-cat logical superposition for 225 ms and protects diverse nonclassical d=8 states.
application_angle: The method offers a lower-overhead route to longer-lived logical qubits and high-dimensional quantum memories in donor-spin hardware.

title: Void-Free Through-Glass Vias for Multilayer Surface-Electrode Ion Traps
abstract: Through-substrate interconnects are a key technology for scaling surface-electrode ion traps (SEITs) toward large electrode counts and complex architectures. Dielectric substrates such as fused silica offer superior RF performance compared to silicon, but the reliable fabrication of void-free through-glass vias (TGVs) remains challenging. In this work, we demonstrate a SEIT fabricated on a fused silica substrate incorporating TGVs. The via-holes are formed using Selective Laser-Induced Etching and subsequently metallized with gold by electroplating. A patent-pending geometry-assisted bottom-up plating approach enables void-free filling using constant-current electroplating without electrolyte additives or pulsed deposition schemes. Electrical characterization across multiple wafers confirms a TGV-level yield above 98.8 %, demonstrating the robustness and reproducibility of the developed TGV technology. The TGVs are combined with multilayer SEIT fabrication, enabling vertical signal routing to all electrodes while maintaining an unaffected trapping surface without wire bonds. To interface the trap with external control electronics, a glass interposer providing signal fan-out to a larger pitch is designed and fabricated. The trap chip and the interposer are integrated using thermocompression bonding, forming a compact chip-to-chip assembly. The presented technology demonstrates the first fully integrated multilayer SEIT on fused silica incorporating void-free TGVs.
one_liner: Void-free gold through-glass vias achieve over 98.8% via-level yield in a fully integrated multilayer fused-silica surface ion trap.
why_it_matters: Reliable vertical routing removes wire bonds from the trapping surface and supports denser, cleaner ion-trap electrode architectures.
detailed_summary: Via holes are formed in fused silica by selective laser-induced etching and filled with gold using geometry-assisted bottom-up constant-current electroplating. Electrical tests across multiple wafers show a via-level yield above 98.8%. The vias route signals vertically to every electrode, while a thermocompression-bonded glass interposer fans the connections out to external electronics.
main_result: The authors demonstrate the first fully integrated multilayer fused-silica surface ion trap with void-free through-glass vias and greater than 98.8% via yield.
application_angle: The fabrication stack enables compact, high-electrode-count ion-trap modules without surface wire bonds, aiding scalable trapped-ion processors.

title: Quantum-enhanced Search for Galactic Dark Photons Using Cat-State Cavities
abstract: We present a quantum-enhanced search for the Galactic dark-photon background (GDPB), a relativistic and anisotropic vector field that can be produced by dark-matter decay or annihilation in the Milky Way halo. We reinterpret an existing quantum-enhanced dark-photon dataset obtained with a superconducting circuit QED platform originally developed for wave-like dark-photon dark-matter searches, consisting of a high-$Q$ niobium cavity in the $\mathrm{TM}_{010}$ mode dispersively coupled to a transmon qubit. By preparing four-component cat states and performing repeated quantum non-demolition parity measurements, analyzed with a hidden Markov model, we extract photon-transition probabilities for multiple cat amplitudes and integration times. The coupling to the GDPB is governed by a polarization- and angle-dependent cavity overlap function, which predicts a distinctive diurnal modulation of the excitation rate for both longitudinal and transverse polarizations. From the absence of such modulation, we set 90\% confidence-level bounds on the kinetic-mixing parameter $ε$ for two benchmark production mechanisms (parametric and cascade decay) over the relativistic mass range $m_X \ll ω_c$.
one_liner: Cat-state cavity data are reanalyzed to search for diurnally modulated Galactic dark-photon signals with quantum nondemolition measurements.
why_it_matters: The study repurposes quantum-enhanced circuit-QED sensing to constrain relativistic dark photons with polarization-sensitive daily signatures.
detailed_summary: The analysis uses an existing dataset from a high-Q niobium TM010 cavity dispersively coupled to a transmon qubit. Four-component cat states and repeated quantum nondemolition parity measurements yield photon-transition probabilities, extracted with a hidden Markov model across several cat amplitudes and integration times. No predicted polarization- and angle-dependent diurnal modulation is observed, enabling 90% confidence bounds on kinetic mixing for parametric- and cascade-decay scenarios.
main_result: The absence of diurnal excitation modulation sets quantum-enhanced 90% confidence bounds on relativistic Galactic dark-photon kinetic mixing.
application_angle: The technique broadens quantum-sensor searches beyond wave-like dark matter to anisotropic relativistic backgrounds.

title: Quantum-enhanced phase interrogation of a fiber-optic strain sensor
abstract: Fiber-optic sensors enable high-sensitivity measurements of various physical parameters. Here, we demonstrate a quantum-enhanced interrogation of an all-fiber-optic Fabry-Perot resonator, employing entangled two-photon interference to probe directly strain-induced optical phase shifts. The resonator is interrogated by a narrow-linewidth laser that is frequency-locked to its resonance mode, thereby exploiting the cavity's inherent sensitivity to variations in the fiber length. To access the phase fluctuations transferred to the interrogation field due to external perturbations on the sensor, we implement an in-fiber Mach-Zehnder interferometer readout. This configuration allows the sensor to operate both with classical coherent light and with entangled photon pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion. Harnessing two-photon entangled states corresponding to an N = 2 NOON state, we experimentally demonstrate a reduction of the measurement noise below the standard quantum limit. These results provide clear evidence of the quantum advantage in enhancing fiber-optic sensors under practical constraints on optical power.
one_liner: Entangled photon pairs interrogate an all-fiber Fabry–Perot strain sensor with phase-measurement noise below the standard quantum limit.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates practical quantum advantage in fiber sensing under optical-power constraints using an all-fiber architecture.
detailed_summary: A narrow-linewidth laser is locked to an all-fiber Fabry–Perot resonance so that strain-induced fiber-length changes appear as optical phase shifts. An in-fiber Mach–Zehnder interferometer reads out the transferred phase fluctuations using either coherent light or entangled photon pairs from spontaneous parametric down-conversion. With an N=2 NOON state, the experiment reduces measurement noise below the standard quantum limit.
main_result: Two-photon entangled interrogation achieves sub-standard-quantum-limit phase readout of strain in an all-fiber resonator.
application_angle: Quantum-enhanced interrogation can improve low-power fiber sensors for structural monitoring and other photon-budget-limited measurements.

title: Scalable Tomography of Coherent Noise via Stabilizer-Code Polarization
abstract: Coherent errors accumulate linearly rather than diffusively, making them invisible to Pauli-twirl-based char- acterization. It poses a central challenge for quantum error correction, yet its characterization typically requires multi-qubit process tomography whose cost grows exponentially with system size. We show that measurement- free error correction projects arbitrary few-qubit coherent noise onto a fixed single-logical-qubit effective chan- nel, enabling tomography at constant cost. Exploiting the polarization effects of bit-flip and phase-flip codes, we construct a concatenated effective-channel fingerprint and prove, by a parity-based contradiction argument, that the observation map is globally injective over a prescribed coherent-noise family; hence the underlying noise parameters are uniquely recovered without any sparsity or low-rank assumptions. The recovered coherent noise model can be fed into decoding algorithms; relative to independent noise priors, we expect this to reduce the logical error rate for surface-code decoders. The protocol offers a scalable route to coherent-noise identification whenever the noise admits a moderate-dimensional parameterization.
one_liner: Stabilizer-code polarization maps few-qubit coherent noise to a single-logical-qubit channel that can be characterized at constant cost.
why_it_matters: The protocol could make coherent-error identification scalable and provide better noise priors for quantum-error-correction decoders.
detailed_summary: The authors use measurement-free error correction to project parameterized few-qubit coherent noise onto a fixed effective channel acting on one logical qubit. Concatenated bit-flip and phase-flip codes create a channel fingerprint whose observation map is proved globally injective for the prescribed noise family. Thus, the underlying coherent-error parameters can be uniquely recovered without sparsity or low-rank assumptions and without exponentially scaling process tomography.
main_result: The method identifies moderate-dimensional coherent-noise models through constant-cost logical-channel tomography.
application_angle: Recovered noise parameters could inform surface-code decoding and hardware calibration to reduce logical errors caused by coherent accumulation.

title: Acoustic scattering from quantum dynamics
abstract: Scattering of sound waves propagating in a compressible fluid is linked to the quantum dynamics generated by a class of non-Hermitian Hamiltonian operators. The scattering amplitude is expressed in terms of the corresponding evolution operator. This is used to provide a new proof of the reciprocity theorem in acoustic scattering, conduct analytic low-frequency acoustic scattering calculations, and study the scattering of sound waves by a finite planar array of delta-function point scatters embedded in an infinite acoustic slab. A detailed discussion of acoustic scattering properties of a homogeneous acoustic slab including a pair of delta-function point scatters on one of its faces is provided.
one_liner: Acoustic-wave scattering is reformulated through evolution under a class of non-Hermitian quantum Hamiltonians.
why_it_matters: The quantum-dynamical formulation supplies analytical tools for reciprocal acoustic structures, low-frequency scattering, and engineered slab arrays.
detailed_summary: The work expresses the acoustic scattering amplitude of a compressible fluid in terms of an evolution operator generated by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. This correspondence yields a new proof of acoustic reciprocity and supports analytic low-frequency calculations. It is applied to finite planar arrays of delta-function scatterers and to a homogeneous slab carrying two point scatterers on one face.
main_result: A non-Hermitian evolution-operator framework reproduces reciprocity and enables analytic treatment of structured acoustic scattering.
application_angle: The framework may aid the design and analysis of acoustic slabs, metasurfaces, and compact arrays of engineered scatterers.

title: Single and coupled quantum van der Pol oscillators: Wigner-function dynamics, exact qutrit solutions, and synchronization
abstract: We study quantum van der Pol oscillator in which single-photon pumping competes with a nonlinear two-photon dissipative channel to produce a quantum limit cycle, and the question of how two such oscillators with non-identical intrinsic frequencies synchronize in the sense of phase locking when coupled dissipatively to one another. For a single oscillator, starting from a Lindblad description of the dynamics, we derive the exact Wigner-function evolution equation, and show that its Fokker--Planck approximation admits in the appropriate regime an equivalent classical Itô stochastic description that reproduces remarkably well the full Lindblad dynamics. Notably, the stochastic approach provides an efficient means of capturing system dynamics in the semiclassical regime, where a large number of energy eigenstates contribute and direct numerical simulations become computationally demanding. Restricting to the three lowest Fock states and using a parity symmetry, we obtain in closed form the stationary-state density matrix and its Wigner-function representation that displays pronounced nonclassical features. For two non-identical oscillators, we study the full Lindblad dynamics numerically and characterize synchronization through the stationary-state order parameter as a function of frequency mismatch and dissipative coupling. We find that increasing the effective nonlinear dissipative strength suppresses the synchronized region. Restricting the two oscillators to the three-level qutrit subspace, a parity symmetry reduces the stationary-state problem to an exact $41$-dimensional linear system, allowing to compute the synchronization order parameter. In this reduced description, results in the limit of large dissipation agree closely with those from the full dynamics, while exhibiting in the limit of small dissipation a double-peak synchronization structure accompanied by a phase reversal.
one_liner: Quantum van der Pol oscillators are analyzed from exact qutrit steady states to semiclassical dynamics and dissipative synchronization.
why_it_matters: The results clarify how nonlinear dissipation controls synchronization in open quantum oscillators relevant to photonic and circuit platforms.
detailed_summary: For one oscillator, the authors derive the exact Wigner-function evolution and show that an Itô stochastic approximation closely reproduces full Lindblad dynamics in the semiclassical regime. A three-Fock-state truncation yields closed-form stationary density matrices with nonclassical Wigner features. For two detuned oscillators, full and qutrit-reduced calculations show that stronger nonlinear dissipation suppresses synchronization, while weak dissipation produces a double-peaked structure and phase reversal.
platform_or_system: dissipative quantum van der Pol oscillators
main_result: The study provides exact reduced solutions and maps how detuning, coupling, and nonlinear loss shape quantum phase locking.
application_angle: These models can guide synchronization and control of coupled nonlinear resonators in photonic, electromechanical, or superconducting hardware.

title: Deterministic and Programmable Fusion for Scalable Generation of Photonic Graph States
abstract: Entanglement in multiphoton graph states is an important resource with various applications, such as measurement-based quantum computing and memory-less quantum repeaters. While some primitive instances have been successfully prepared, scalable generation of large-scale graph states with programmable connections remains an outstanding challenge. Fusion provides a promising "divide-and-conquer" approach by linking smaller resource states into larger, more complex graphs. However, its practical scalability has been limited by the probabilistic nature of conventional fusion protocols, which necessitates extensive hardware overhead and feed-forward resources to achieve deterministic outcomes. Here, we introduce and experimentally demonstrate a deterministic fusion operation with built-in error mitigation, capable of connecting small time-bin-encoded cluster states--originally generated on-demand from a quantum emitter--into larger, reconfigurable photonic graph states of increased sizes. The fusion operation is realized by nondestructively projecting pairs of flying microwave photonic qubits into Bell states using superconducting circuits with in-situ programmability. Crucially, the protocol features active reset and reuse of matter qubits during graph state generation, thereby circumventing the coherence constraints of the quantum emitter and enabling the generation of genuine multipartite entanglement across 13 photonic qubits. Our results establish a scalable framework for photonic graph-state synthesis, paving the way for fault-tolerant measurement-based quantum computation and distributed quantum networks.
one_liner: Programmable superconducting fusion deterministically joins emitter-generated time-bin clusters into graph states containing 13 microwave photons.
why_it_matters: Deterministic fusion with reusable matter qubits removes major probabilistic and coherence bottlenecks in scalable photonic graph-state generation.
detailed_summary: Small time-bin cluster states are generated on demand by a quantum emitter and connected using nondestructive Bell-state projections on pairs of flying microwave photons. Superconducting circuitry provides in-situ programmability, built-in error mitigation, and active reset and reuse of matter qubits. The experiment produces reconfigurable graph states with genuine multipartite entanglement across 13 photonic qubits.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates deterministic programmable fusion and genuine 13-photon multipartite entanglement.
application_angle: The architecture targets scalable resource-state production for fault-tolerant measurement-based computing and memory-free quantum repeaters.

title: Photon Demultiplexing Using Spatial Routing
abstract: Spatial sectioning of the far-field noncollinear field from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) is a promising approach for multiparty quantum communication. Although demonstrations with six pairs of users have been reported, the fundamental limits remain unknown. These include the maximum number of channels, the required degree of channel optimization, and the dependence on input parameters. In this paper, we provide a practical framework that answers these questions by connecting input parameters and invoking a design theorem. For a representative configuration, we realize 12 user-pair channels with routing consistency exceeding $0.9999$ at a $12\%$ reduction in photon flux. We further show that sectioning improves the accidental-coincidence budget linearly with the number of channels $N$, allowing the aggregate key rate to scale with the user count. These results provide a design strategy for spatial-division multiplexing of entangled photons analogous to the channel-spacing standards used in wavelength-division networks.
one_liner: Spatial routing of noncollinear SPDC emission creates 12 entangled user-pair channels with consistency above 0.9999.
why_it_matters: A practical channel-design rule enables scalable spatial multiplexing of entangled photons while improving the network-wide coincidence budget.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a design framework connecting SPDC input parameters to the maximum channel count and required spatial optimization. In a representative configuration, far-field sectioning supports 12 user-pair channels with routing consistency exceeding 0.9999 while reducing photon flux by 12%. The accidental-coincidence budget improves linearly with channel number, allowing aggregate key rate to grow with user count.
main_result: The proposed spatial demultiplexer achieves 12 highly consistent user-pair routes and predicts linearly improving coincidence tolerance with channel count.
application_angle: The approach offers a standards-like design strategy for high-user-count entanglement distribution and spatially multiplexed quantum-key networks.

title: Observation of correlations beyond the single-particle picture in fermionic counting statistics
abstract: The analysis of charge fluctuations in a mesoscopic device can shed light on the fundamental question of whether or not a single-particle picture of electron transport is appropriate, even in the presence of Coulomb interaction. It has been shown on general grounds that mapping the interacting system onto a fermionic single-particle description is subject to strict constraints on the charge-transfer statistics. These constraints can be formulated in terms of a sign rule for the factorial cumulants of the full counting statistics. We report here on the experimental observation of a sign-rule violation in a most elementary model system, i.e. a single-level quantum dot, and provide theoretical modeling that can quantitatively reproduce the experimental data. This reveals the presence of correlations introduced by electron-electron interaction.
one_liner: Charge-counting measurements in a single-level quantum dot reveal factorial-cumulant signatures incompatible with independent electrons.
why_it_matters: The observed sign-rule violation provides a direct experimental diagnostic of interaction-induced correlations in mesoscopic transport.
detailed_summary: The experiment measures charge-transfer fluctuations in a single-level quantum dot and tests constraints imposed by any fermionic single-particle description. Its factorial cumulants violate the expected sign rule, demonstrating that independent-particle transport cannot explain the statistics. A model incorporating electron-electron interactions quantitatively reproduces the observed data.
main_result: A factorial-cumulant sign-rule violation experimentally exposes electron-electron correlations beyond a single-particle transport model.
application_angle: Full counting statistics can serve as a sensitive benchmark for interactions, noise, and correlated dynamics in quantum-dot devices.

title: Preservation of photon statistics upon selective molecular modulation in hollow-core fibers
abstract: Preserving the underlying statistical properties of light during frequency transduction is essential for interfacing spectrally disparate quantum systems. To do this successfully, the process needs to be highly efficient, broadband and noiseless. Despite significant progress in this field, satisfying all these conditions remains challenging. Recently, molecular modulation-based transduction in hollow-core fibers has emerged as a promising approach, where biphoton correlations were proven to be preserved during frequency up-conversion. However, beyond this previous demonstration of correlation-maintaining conversion, whether molecular modulation can preserve more general statistical properties of light remains experimentally unexplored. Here, we demonstrate the conservation of photon-number statistics during selective frequency transduction by Raman molecular modulation in a hydrogen-filled hollow-core fiber. As a proof of concept, weak 585-nm signals are selectively converted to 773 nm in the near-infrared and to 471 nm in the blue spectral region with near-unity efficiencies. Phase matching between the generated coherence waves and the transitions of interest is achieved through the effective dispersion of the system, enabling independent selection of the frequency up- and down-conversion processes. The preservation of the photon-number statistics of the shifted signals, along with the large frequency shifts, broad tunability and compatibility with quantum-optical fields, provides a versatile fiber-based platform for quantum frequency transduction. In particular, the demonstrated interfacing between visible and near-infrared wavelengths using low pump energies and low gas pressures offers a route towards connecting spectrally distinct quantum systems, including quantum emitters, sensors and atomic quantum memories, within hybrid quantum networks.
one_liner: Hydrogen-filled hollow-core fiber preserves photon-number statistics while selectively shifting 585-nm light to 773 or 471 nm.
why_it_matters: Near-unity, low-noise conversion across large spectral gaps could connect visible emitters and sensors to near-infrared memories and network channels.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses Raman molecular modulation in a hydrogen-filled hollow-core fiber to convert weak 585-nm signals selectively to 773 nm or 471 nm. Effective-dispersion engineering phase-matches the desired coherence wave and independently selects up- or down-conversion. The shifted fields retain their photon-number statistics while reaching near-unity conversion efficiency.
main_result: Selective visible-to-near-infrared and visible-to-blue conversion achieves near-unity efficiency while preserving photon-number statistics.
application_angle: The fiber platform could spectrally interface quantum emitters, optical sensors, and atomic memories in hybrid quantum networks.

title: Hyperentanglement in intermediate phase-space planes: benchmarking a photon-pair source for quantum key distribution
abstract: We characterize a source of photon pairs simultaneously entangled in polarization and in the transverse spatial degree of freedom, with the spatial measurements performed in intermediate planes of the fractional Fourier transform. The source consists of two crossed type-I crystals in a non-collinear geometry, such that the transverse variables carry information about the crystal of origin. Detection in the crystal plane reveals this information completely and destroys the polarization entanglement, so that a scheme using the near and far fields as conjugate spatial bases cannot support a parallel polarization channel. In intermediate planes both spatial bases combine position and momentum, such that the which-crystal information is partially erased, and the polarization entanglement survives in all four combinations of spatial bases. Applying Bell and Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen criteria to the same photon pairs certifies both degrees of freedom simultaneously. We evaluate quantum bit error rates and asymptotic secret key rates in each degree of freedom, and find that the source delivers two simultaneously usable channels per photon pair.
one_liner: Intermediate fractional-Fourier planes enable simultaneous polarization and spatial entanglement channels from the same photon pairs.
why_it_matters: Two usable degrees of freedom per photon pair can raise QKD information capacity without requiring a proportional increase in transmitted photons.
detailed_summary: Crossed type-I crystals generate photon pairs entangled in polarization and transverse spatial variables, but crystal-plane detection exposes the source crystal and destroys polarization entanglement. Measurements in intermediate fractional-Fourier planes partially erase this which-crystal information, preserving polarization entanglement for all four spatial-basis combinations. Bell and EPR tests certify both degrees of freedom, while QBER and asymptotic key-rate calculations show two simultaneously usable QKD channels per pair.
main_result: The source supports simultaneous polarization and spatial QKD channels when spatial measurements use appropriately chosen intermediate phase-space planes.
application_angle: Hyperentangled encoding offers a practical route to increasing secret-key throughput per detected photon pair.

title: Mechanical trisqueezing in circuit quantum acoustodynamics with SNAIL devices
abstract: Continuous-variable quantum information processing with mechanical oscillators requires a uni- versal gate set, including a genuine non-Gaussian evolution. While circuit quantum acoustodynamics (cQAD) experiments have realized bilinear and quartic (four-wave mixing) operations by coupling mechanical modes to transmon qubits, the intrinsic Kerr nonlinearity of these devices precludes access to odd-order effective Hamiltonians such as trisqueezing. Here we propose a cQAD architec- ture in which a mechanical mode, hosted in a high-overtone bulk acoustic-wave resonator (HBAR), is coupled to a superconducting nonlinear asymmetric inductive element (SNAIL). By combining the cubic nonlinearity of the SNAIL with parametric flux driving, we engineer a three-wave mixing interaction that generates trisqueezed mechanical states, producing the characteristic triangular, star-shaped Wigner function with negative regions indicative of non-Gaussianity. We derive the effective trisqueezing Hamiltonian from the full circuit model, identify the drive frequencies and flux modulation required to isolate the desired interaction from competing terms, and quantify the achievable coupling strengths for parameters compatible with current fabrication capabilities. Our results establish a hardware-efficient route to non-Gaussian resource generation in mechanical quantum systems, extending the toolbox of cQAD toward universal continuous-variable quantum computation and enhanced quantum-limited sensing.
one_liner: A SNAIL-coupled acoustic resonator architecture enables cubic interactions for generating non-Gaussian trisqueezed mechanical states.
why_it_matters: The proposal supplies a missing odd-order operation for mechanical continuous-variable processors and may enhance quantum-limited sensing.
detailed_summary: The proposed circuit couples a high-overtone bulk acoustic-wave resonator mode to a superconducting SNAIL element. Combining the SNAIL's cubic nonlinearity with parametric flux modulation isolates an effective three-wave-mixing Hamiltonian that produces trisqueezed mechanical states. Circuit-level analysis identifies suitable drives and predicts triangular Wigner functions with negative regions using fabrication-compatible parameters.
main_result: The architecture theoretically generates non-Gaussian mechanical trisqueezing at coupling strengths compatible with current superconducting-device fabrication.
application_angle: It provides a hardware-efficient non-Gaussian resource for universal continuous-variable processing and mechanically enhanced quantum sensing.

title: Advances in quantum optomechanical control based on cavity cold-atom systems
abstract: Cavity optomechanics represents a frontier research direction in quantum science and technology, centered on the control and exploration of interactions between electromagnetic fields and mechanical motion. Rooted in quantum mechanics, this field realizes efficient coupling and precise manipulation of optical fields and mechanical vibrations through the structural design and precise regulation of optical microcavities and mechanical oscillators, thereby revealing and harnessing novel quantum phenomena. In recent years, cavity optomechanics has evolved into an interdisciplinary frontier integrating quantum optics, condensed matter physics, and quantum precision measurement, exhibiting profound application in both fundamental physics research and quantum information science. With advancements in technologies such as nanomanufacturing and laser cooling, optomechanical interactions have been successfully demonstrated in various experimental systems. Among these platforms, cavity cold-atom systems stand out as one of the ideal platforms for implementing quantum optomechanics. Featuring exceptional environmental isolation, long quantum coherence times, and strong light-matter interaction, these systems provide a crucial testbed for exploring strong and even ultrastrong optomechanical coupling effects as well as rich nonlinear quantum phenomena. This paper reviews the recent progress in optomechanical control and manipulation based on cavity cold-atom systems. We first outline the fundamental principles of standard cavity optomechanical systems. Then, we describe the experimental realization of linear and nonlinear optomechanical couplings in cold-atom systems. After that, we focus on the representative applications of this platform in high-precision quantum sensing, quantum memory, and the preparation of macroscopic nonclassical states. Finally, we give an outlook and challenges in this field.
one_liner: This review surveys linear and nonlinear quantum optomechanical control using cold atoms coupled to optical cavities.
why_it_matters: Cold-atom cavities combine long coherence, strong light-matter coupling, and isolation for sensing, memories, and macroscopic-state engineering.
detailed_summary: The review introduces standard cavity-optomechanical principles and maps them onto cold-atom cavity platforms. It surveys experimental realizations of linear and nonlinear optomechanical coupling, including regimes enabled by strong light-matter interaction and long atomic coherence. Representative applications include precision sensing, quantum memory, and preparation of macroscopic nonclassical states, followed by outstanding challenges.
main_result: The article consolidates experimental progress and control methods for linear and nonlinear optomechanics in cavity cold-atom systems.
application_angle: The reviewed platform supports precision metrology, coherent information storage, and controlled generation of nonclassical many-body states.

title: Strong subadditivity of topological entropy on the torus: Rényi order and non-Abelian structure
abstract: We classify strong subadditivity for the canonical topological Rényi functional at finite positive orders on an unpunctured torus in the topological quantum field theory of any finite unitary modular tensor category. Universal validity means validity for all pure ground states and all regular region pairs with transverse or disjoint boundaries and compatible corner rounding. At von Neumann order one, the inequality holds universally. For each fixed order strictly between zero and one, universal validity is equivalent to pointedness, meaning that every simple anyon type has quantum dimension one. For every nonpointed category and each finite positive order other than one, we construct a violating pure state and an allowed pair. For a fixed pointed category and fixed order above one, universal validity is equivalent to a same-order modular Fourier entropy bound for every pure state. Global homological constraints on actual unions and intersections and established weighted modular uncertainty prove the order-one theorem. For parallel annuli at fixed flux distribution, the order-one functional is affine in their positive count.
