At other orders, unequal quantum dimensions on the occupied support induce strict curvature that suitable overlapping regions convert into negative deficits. Under the boundary-charge cutting prescription, the von Neumann theorem extends to arbitrary logical density matrices in the same ground space.
one_liner: Topological Rényi strong subadditivity on a torus holds universally at order one but generally fails for non-Abelian anyon theories.
why_it_matters: The classification gives entropy-based constraints and diagnostics for topological ground spaces relevant to fault-tolerant quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The work classifies strong subadditivity of a canonical topological Rényi functional for ground states on an unpunctured torus. Universal validity holds at von Neumann order one; for orders between zero and one it is equivalent to the underlying modular tensor category being pointed. For nonpointed categories, including non-Abelian structures with unequal quantum dimensions, the authors construct violating states and regions at every finite positive order except one.
platform_or_system: Topological ground space on a torus
main_result: Universal strong subadditivity is proved at Rényi order one and shown to fail away from order one for every nonpointed modular tensor category.
application_angle: The results sharpen entropic tools for characterizing anyonic topological phases proposed for intrinsically fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Near-field contributions to cavity-mediated radiative heat transfer
abstract: Embedding materials in optical cavities has emerged as a powerful strategy for controlling their physical properties. In this context, increasing attention has been devoted to the thermal Purcell effect, which describes how the radiative heat transfer between a material and its photonic environ- ment can be modified by the electromagnetic boundary conditions imposed by the cavity. Here, we investigate near-field effects in cavity-mediated radiative heat transfer in planar cavities composed of realistic, dissipative gold mirrors, extending previous work that considered ideal mirrors. We iden- tify the conditions under which near-field effects lead to a substantial enhancement of heat transfer between the material and a photonic thermal bath relative to free space, owing to the strong modi- fication of the photonic local density of states by evanescent modes within the cavity. In particular, we find that radiative heat flow can be enhanced by several orders of magnitude in cavities ranging from nanometer to micrometer scales, depending on the absorber frequency and dipole orientation. These findings suggest that near-field effects may be relevant to polariton chemistry experiments and other systems operating within this cavity length-scale regime. Our results add to the idea that cavities can modify material properties not only by engineering vacuum fluctuations in the strong light-matter coupling regime, but also by controlling radiative dissipation and heat transfer.
one_liner: Evanescent cavity modes can enhance radiative heat transfer by orders of magnitude between an absorber and a thermal photonic bath.
why_it_matters: Accounting for dissipative mirrors and near fields is essential when designing nanoscale cavities for thermal control and polariton experiments.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes radiative heat exchange in planar cavities formed by realistic dissipative gold mirrors rather than ideal reflectors. Evanescent modes strongly reshape the photonic local density of states and can enhance heat flow by several orders of magnitude over free space. The enhancement depends on cavity spacing from nanometers to micrometers, absorber resonance, and dipole orientation.
main_result: Near-field cavity modes are predicted to produce orders-of-magnitude radiative heat-transfer enhancement across experimentally relevant cavity lengths.
application_angle: The results inform thermal management and dissipation engineering in polariton chemistry and other nanoscale cavity-photonics experiments.

title: A low-cost compact muon detector for millikelvin operation
abstract: Ionizing radiation produces correlated errors in superconducting qubits, posing some challenges to quantum error correction. In addition, it causes background events in other superconducting cryogenic devices, such as kinetic inductance detectors and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors. Cosmic muons are a component of this background that can only be partly shielded against at ground level, but can be tagged by an independent detector inside the cryostat, so that the affected data can be vetoed, or the muon tags incorporated into error correction. We present a low-cost, compact muon detector consisting of two plastic scintillator modules, each read out by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), operated in coincidence. We characterize the SiPMs from room temperature down to 10 mK, including the breakdown and upper-limit voltages that define the operating bias range. Operated as a muon counter, the detector measures a coincidence rate that, as expected, is independent of temperature within uncertainties and agrees with analytical and Monte Carlo predictions. Below approximately 8 K, each muon event produces two pulses, one narrow and one broad, an effect that, to our knowledge, has not been reported before. Coincidences with an independent muon detector outside the cryostat confirm that muons are still counted reliably in this regime. By studying the appearance of double pulses as a function of temperature and magnetic field up to 4.5 T, we find a behavior consistent with the phase diagram of a type-II superconductor. This links the double pulses to a superconducting material in the SiPM, likely an adhesion layer or diffusion barrier introduced during manufacturing. The mechanism by which the superconducting state produces the second pulse is not yet understood.
one_liner: A compact scintillator–SiPM coincidence detector reliably tags cosmic muons inside a cryostat down to 10 mK.
why_it_matters: Cryogenic muon tagging could help veto radiation-induced events or inform error correction in superconducting qubits and photon detectors.
detailed_summary: The detector uses two plastic-scintillator modules with SiPM readout in coincidence and was characterized from room temperature to 10 mK. Its measured muon rate remains temperature-independent within uncertainty and agrees with analytical and Monte Carlo estimates. Below about 8 K, muons generate an unexplained second broad pulse consistent with a superconducting SiPM layer, yet external-detector coincidences confirm reliable counting.
platform_or_system: Cryogenic plastic-scintillator and SiPM muon counter
main_result: The system reliably detects cosmic muons at 10 mK and reveals a previously unreported low-temperature double-pulse response.
application_angle: It provides an inexpensive in-cryostat radiation tag for vetoing or correcting correlated faults in superconducting quantum hardware and cryogenic photodetectors.

title: Loss-Tolerant Measurement-Device-Independent QKD over Untrusted Repeaters via High-Dimensional Time-Bin Multiplexing
abstract: We propose a loss-tolerant measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol using time-bin-multiplexed single photons entangled with local qubits stored in nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers. In each round, Alice and Bob each send a single multiplexed photon to an untrusted intermediary, Charlie. Each photon first becomes entangled with Charlie's NV-center qubits; Charlie then performs entanglement swapping between his NV qubits to establish EPR pairs between Alice's and Bob's local qubits. With $d$ time bins per photon, $\log_2 d + 1$ EPR pairs can be generated per transmitted photon, substantially increasing the probability of EPR-pair creation under limited channel bandwidth. To further mitigate the effects of prolonged memory storage, the protocol employs a memory-insensitive (MI) architecture, where multiple banks of qubits and multiplexed photon routing reduce the effective memory lifetime requirements. This approach enhances loss tolerance, enabling higher secret key rates and secure key distribution over longer distances compared to conventional single-photon protocols. Using the Lo-Chau EPR-QKD framework and Shor-Preskill reduction, we prove that the protocol is secure without trusting intermediate nodes, making it suitable for quantum networks with untrusted repeaters.
one_liner: A time-bin-multiplexed MDI-QKD protocol uses NV memories and untrusted repeaters to improve loss tolerance and key rates.
why_it_matters: The design targets secure long-distance quantum networking without trusted intermediate nodes while reducing channel-bandwidth and memory-lifetime constraints.
detailed_summary: Alice and Bob transmit time-bin-multiplexed single photons that become entangled with NV-center qubits at an untrusted intermediary. Entanglement swapping then establishes remote EPR pairs, with d time bins yielding log2(d)+1 pairs per transmitted photon. A multi-bank, memory-insensitive architecture reduces effective storage-time requirements, while security follows from the Lo-Chau framework and Shor-Preskill reduction.
platform_or_system: Time-bin photonics with NV-center quantum memories
main_result: The proposed protocol increases EPR-pair generation and predicted secret-key performance over conventional single-photon schemes while retaining security against untrusted repeaters.
application_angle: It offers a route to bandwidth-efficient, long-distance QKD networks that tolerate high channel loss and limited quantum-memory coherence.

title: From Single-Particle Thermal Asymmetry to Collective Control: Janus Plasmonic Colloids for Photothermal Applications
abstract: Janus nanoheaters provide a route to break the spatial symmetry of thermoplasmonic heating and generate directionally biased thermal gradients at the nanoscale. However, in realistic photothermal scenarios, nanoheaters rarely act as isolated objects, but rather operate within colloidal assemblies where collective thermal and electromagnetic effects reshape the local temperature landscape. Here, we investigate how the intrinsic thermal asymmetry of a single Janus plasmonic nanoheater is transformed when moving from isolated particles to planar random arrays under continuous-wave illumination. Using coupled electromagnetic and steady-state heat-transfer simulations, we first quantify the finite spatial range over which the single-particle Janus signature remains detectable. We show that neighboring nanoheaters introduce two competing effects: a nearly symmetric collective thermal background that screens and homogenizes the Janus factor, and short-range neighbor-induced asymmetries that partially compensate this screening when interparticle distances become comparable to the spatial extent of the single-particle thermal anisotropy. We derive a closed-form analytical model for the array-averaged Janus factor as a function of nanoparticle number and surface density. The model predicts the screening-dominated regime from single-particle quantities and identifies deviations associated with near-field neighbor-induced contributions at higher densities. These results demonstrate a central trade-off for biomedical photothermal applications in continuous-wave operation: collective heating is required to reach relevant temperature increments, but it progressively erases the directional Janus character by thermal homogenization. Our framework provides a practical route to predict and rationally design the spatial temperature distribution in plasmonic assemblies of Janus particles.
one_liner: Simulations and an analytical model show how collective heating reshapes directional temperature gradients in Janus plasmonic arrays.
why_it_matters: The work exposes a design trade-off between achieving useful bulk heating and preserving nanoscale thermal directionality in photothermal systems.
detailed_summary: Coupled electromagnetic and steady-state thermal simulations track the asymmetric heating signature from an isolated Janus nanoheater into random planar arrays. Neighboring particles create a largely symmetric thermal background that screens directionality, while short-range interactions partly restore asymmetry at high density. A closed-form model predicts the array-averaged Janus factor from particle number, surface density, and single-particle properties.
platform_or_system: Planar arrays of Janus plasmonic nanoheaters
main_result: The study quantifies thermal-asymmetry screening in particle ensembles and supplies an analytical model for predicting the array-averaged Janus factor.
application_angle: The framework can guide nanoparticle density and spacing choices for spatially controlled biomedical heating, therapy, and photothermal imaging.

title: A hybrid quantum interferometer bridging Hong-Ou-Mandel and N00N-state interference
abstract: Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference offers robustness in high-noise environments due to its phase-insensitive nature, while N00N-state interference provides enhanced phase sensitivity for precision measurements in low-noise settings. However, their realizations have typically required separate experimental platforms. Here, we report a single hybrid quantum interferometer that can dynamically transition between HOM and N00N-state interference by adjusting two time delays, $τ_1$ and $τ_2$. This tunability enables operation in phase-insensitive, phase-sensitive, or hybrid modes within a unified setup, as confirmed by theoretical analysis and experimental demonstration. Our system offers a versatile platform with potential for quantum sensing applications, paving the way for integrated quantum technologies capable of adapting to diverse noise conditions.
one_liner: One tunable interferometer switches between robust HOM interference, phase-sensitive N00N interference, and hybrid operation.
why_it_matters: Combining complementary two-photon interference modes in one platform enables sensors that can adapt their sensitivity to changing phase noise.
detailed_summary: The interferometer is controlled through two time delays, τ1 and τ2, which tune the system among HOM, N00N-state, and intermediate hybrid regimes. Theory and experiment confirm both phase-insensitive interference suited to noisy conditions and phase-sensitive interference suited to precision measurements. The unified optical layout removes the need for separate platforms for the two modalities.
main_result: The experiment dynamically transitions between HOM and N00N-state interference within a single apparatus by adjusting two temporal delays.
application_angle: A reconfigurable interferometer could support quantum sensors that trade robustness for enhanced phase sensitivity as environmental noise changes.

title: Photoacoustic-guided reflection-mode wavefront shaping through dynamic biological tissue
abstract: Strong optical scattering limits the depth at which light can be focused and used for imaging in biological tissue. Photoacoustic (PA)-guided wavefront shaping enables non-invasive light focusing in scattering media, but most existing implementations require optical and acoustic access from opposite sides of the sample and a rigidly aligned free-space optical path, which have confined these demonstrations to thin or static samples. Here, we combine a real-valued intensity transmission matrix (RVITM) algorithm with a photoacoustic guidestar (PA-RVITM) in a reflection-mode configuration. Modulated light is delivered through a flexible multimode fiber passing through the central aperture of a focused ultrasound transducer, enabling optical illumination and acoustic detection from the same side of the sample without a free-space combiner. Fiber integration preserved the wavefront shaping performance, and the reflection-mode PA-RVITM system achieved sub-second wavefront optimization with a ~14-fold PA signal enhancement through a diffuser. In ex vivo chicken breast tissue, the enhancement decreased with tissue thickness, reaching ~3.5 through a 2-mm chicken breast layer, with a speckle decorrelation time of ~450 ms. By performing an independent RVITM optimization at each scan position, our system enabled photoacoustic microscopy of a black nylon wire through the same layer, reducing the imaged line width from ~141 μm to ~102 μm, close to the nominal diameter of ~100 μm. This work advances PA-guided wavefront shaping toward a compact, same-side implementation for future biomedical therapeutic and imaging applications.
one_liner: A fiber-integrated reflection-mode system rapidly focuses light through dynamic tissue using a photoacoustic-guided transmission matrix.
why_it_matters: Same-side optical and acoustic access makes wavefront shaping more compatible with compact biomedical imaging and therapeutic instruments.
detailed_summary: The system combines a real-valued intensity transmission matrix with a photoacoustic guidestar in a reflection-mode geometry. Light is delivered through a multimode fiber placed in the aperture of a focused ultrasound transducer, permitting same-side illumination and detection. It achieves sub-second optimization, about 14-fold enhancement through a diffuser, and about 3.5-fold enhancement through 2 mm of chicken tissue, improving a wire image from roughly 141 μm to 102 μm width.
main_result: The platform demonstrates sub-second wavefront optimization and near-nominal-resolution imaging through a 2-mm ex vivo tissue layer.
application_angle: Its compact same-side geometry advances deep-tissue optical focusing for photoacoustic microscopy, targeted therapy, and minimally invasive biomedical probes.

title: Demonstration of a mobile ion-trap quantum device
abstract: Trapped-ion devices are being investigated for transportable applications, including the transfer of exotic charged particles between laboratories and the development of portable quantum technologies. To date, ion transport has been demonstrated only in magnetic (Penning) traps, whereas radiofrequency (Paul) traps are the predominant platform in quantum science. Here, we report the first transport of a few thousand ions confined in a linear Paul trap over distances of several kilometers, with transport durations of 15 and 45 min. These results establish a foundation for mobile trapped-ion quantum devices capable of operating while in motion and may enable the transport of exotic ions in Paul traps between experimental facilities.
one_liner: A linear Paul trap transported thousands of confined ions over several kilometers during journeys lasting up to 45 minutes.
why_it_matters: This first mobile demonstration with a Paul trap extends the dominant trapped-ion quantum platform toward field deployment and inter-laboratory transport.
detailed_summary: A few thousand ions were confined in a linear radiofrequency Paul trap while the apparatus traveled several kilometers. Successful runs lasted 15 and 45 minutes, showing that confinement can survive macroscopic transport and motion. The result extends mobile ion trapping beyond previously demonstrated magnetic Penning traps.
main_result: The experiment achieves the first kilometer-scale transport of thousands of ions confined in a linear Paul trap.
application_angle: Mobile Paul traps could enable portable quantum instruments and transfer exotic ions between facilities without changing trapping architecture.

title: Petz Recovery through a Single Polar Transformation for Approximate Quantum Error Correction
abstract: The Petz recovery map provides a near optimal decoder for approximate quantum error correction, but its inverse square-root normalization complicates circuit implementation. We use the polar structure of the Petz recovery isometry to implement recovery through a single quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). We give explicit block-encoding circuits and an extended recovery isometry that yields approximate Petz recovery without postselection. We bound the diamond distance between the approximate and ideal Petz encoding-recovery channels in terms of a spectrum-weighted loss, which provides a channel specific objective for optimizing the QSVT angles. Uniform polynomial approximation yields an asymptotic error bound that decays exponentially with the number of QSVT iterations, at a rate controlled by the smallest nonzero scaled singular value. Applications to Haar-random encoding and the Hayden-Preskill protocol illustrate the tradeoff between circuit depth and recovery accuracy and place existing scrambling decoders within a common Petz recovery framework.
one_liner: A single-QSVT construction implements approximate Petz recovery without postselection and with exponentially improving accuracy.
why_it_matters: The method turns a near-optimal but implementation-heavy recovery map into explicit circuits with a tunable depth–accuracy tradeoff for approximate QEC.
detailed_summary: The authors exploit the polar structure of the Petz recovery isometry to replace inverse-square-root normalization with a single quantum singular value transformation. They provide explicit block encodings and an extended recovery isometry that avoids postselection. A diamond-distance bound connects recovery error to a spectrum-weighted loss, while uniform polynomial approximation gives exponential error decay with QSVT iteration count.
main_result: Approximate Petz recovery is implemented by one QSVT sequence with explicit circuits, no postselection, and exponentially decaying approximation error.
application_angle: The construction offers a circuit-level route to practical approximate decoders for noisy quantum processors and scrambling-based recovery protocols.

title: Intermediate memory costs of quantum channel synthesis with a protected subsystem
abstract: A quantum memory can preserve a subsystem perfectly while discarding information needed by a later operation. We study the total intermediate dimension required for channel synthesis when the first stage protects a $b$-dimensional subsystem and has a prescribed noncommutative graph imposing full confusability on an $a$-dimensional control register. For a finite family of classically controlled branches, exact synthesis is possible if and only if the target graph contains the prescribed graph of the first stage. For every feasible family, we construct a single processor that implements all branches exactly. The processor uses pairwise nonorthogonal pure program states in a register of dimension at most $a$. A target graph may be realizable with a carrier of dimension $b$, while synthesizing a channel with that graph can require dimension $ab$. We also characterize the closure of the attainable channels, distinguishing exact synthesis from arbitrarily accurate approximation. Finally, for a family built from the trine communication task, a four-dimensional carrier permits exact synthesis with quantum programs under output depolarization. At the same total carrier dimension and without free shared randomness, classical programs have optimal normalized diamond error $(1-η)/4$, where $0\leqη\leq1$ is the depolarization strength. For $η<1$, the gap persists under sufficiently small perturbations of the target branches.
one_liner: Exact protected-subsystem channel synthesis can require an intermediate quantum memory of dimension ab even when the target carrier needs only b.
why_it_matters: It quantifies hidden memory costs in staged quantum communication and identifies a robust advantage of nonorthogonal quantum programs over classical ones.
detailed_summary: The work characterizes exact two-stage channel synthesis when the first stage preserves a b-dimensional subsystem and imposes full confusability on an a-dimensional control register. Feasibility is equivalent to containment of the prescribed noncommutative graph in the target graph, and a universal processor using nonorthogonal program states of dimension at most a is constructed. A trine-task example shows exact synthesis with a four-dimensional carrier using quantum programs, whereas classical programs retain normalized diamond error (1−η)/4 without free shared randomness.
main_result: The study proves exact feasibility conditions, an ab intermediate-memory requirement in some cases, and a perturbation-robust quantum-program advantage.
application_angle: The bounds guide memory sizing and program-register design for modular quantum communication processors and staged channel implementations.

title: Quantum Partial Information Decompositions, an Operational Order on Ensembles, and Direct Quantifications of Objective Information
abstract: The partial information decomposition (PID) framework is an extension of classical information theory that enables a systematic analysis of the structure of information in multipartite systems. We advance a simple extension of this framework enabling the construction of multipartite quantum PIDs (QPIDs); generalizing recent, exclusively bipartite, extensions. We construct two QPIDs of the Holevo quantity. First a naive QPID based on the classical minimum mutual information. Second a sophisticated QPID enabled by our development of an operational partial order on quantum ensembles in terms of ensemble (inter-)convertability. Finally, as a concrete example of how QPIDs can be applied, we investigate objectivity scenarios; using our Holevo QPIDs to directly quantify objective information in extended graph states. These findings ultimately establish a foundation upon which generic multipartite QPIDs can be systematically constructed, introduce an operational partial order on ensembles, advance QPIDs as interesting objects of study in their own right, and demonstrate their immediate applicability to problems in quantum information.
one_liner: Multipartite quantum partial information decompositions are developed to quantify redundant, unique, and synergistic Holevo information.
why_it_matters: The framework can directly measure how objective information is distributed across multiple quantum subsystems, including extended graph states.
detailed_summary: The authors extend partial information decomposition to multipartite quantum systems and construct two decompositions of the Holevo quantity. The more operational construction rests on a new partial order defined by convertibility between quantum ensembles. Applied to extended graph states, the resulting quantities directly resolve the structure of objective information shared among subsystems.
platform_or_system: Multipartite quantum ensembles and graph states
main_result: Two multipartite Holevo-information decompositions are constructed, including one based on an operational ensemble-convertibility order.
application_angle: These tools could analyze how measurement records or environmental fragments redundantly encode sensing-relevant information across distributed quantum systems.

title: Boundary-induced geometrical frustration in a square Rydberg-atom lattice
abstract: We study geometric defects in square-lattice Rydberg-atom arrays induced by lattice-size parity in the striated density-wave phase. While odd-sized lattices select a single striated domain, even-sized lattices seed incompatible domains at the four corners, resulting in a π/2-rotation invariant state with a geometrical defect emanating from the lattice center. At larger detunings, we instead identify a π-rotation-invariant state with two domains nucleated by opposite corners and separated by a one-dimensional diagonal defect. We probe the state-preparation protocol on the Aquila atomic quantum processor and benchmark it with equilibrium and real-time dynamics tensor-network simulations. Our results assess the role of boundaries and lattice size in determining the global ordering in programmable quantum matter.
one_liner: Square Rydberg arrays exhibit parity-selected domains and central or diagonal defects seeded by competing boundary conditions.
why_it_matters: Aquila experiments and tensor-network benchmarks show how finite-array geometry controls ordered states in programmable neutral-atom hardware.
detailed_summary: In the striated density-wave phase, odd square lattices select one domain, whereas even lattices nucleate incompatible domains at their corners. The even arrays support either a fourfold-symmetric central defect or, at larger detuning, two domains separated by a one-dimensional diagonal defect. The preparation protocol is probed on the Aquila processor and compared with equilibrium and real-time tensor-network simulations.
main_result: The study observes and models boundary-induced, parity-dependent domain structures and geometrical defects in programmable Rydberg arrays.
application_angle: Understanding these finite-size effects can improve array-layout choices and state-preparation protocols for neutral-atom simulators and processors.

title: Quantum prepare-and-measure scenarios: concepts and methods
abstract: Prepare-and-measure scenarios are among the simplest and most widely used settings for quantum communication. A sender prepares a physical system in one of several possible states, which a receiver then measures. Despite this simple structure, these scenarios offer a rich framework for exploring the differences between classical and quantum communication, revealing quantum advantages, and developing protocols for quantum cryptography and device certification. In this tutorial, we give a ground-up introduction to prepare-and-measure scenarios and the methods used to study them. We introduce different frameworks for constraining and characterising communication, with an emphasis on semi-device-independent approaches to quantum information. We also cover modern convex-optimisation techniques for characterising the correlations achievable in these scenarios and illustrate how these tools can be applied in practice. Our aim is to give newcomers the conceptual and technical foundations needed to approach the current literature and apply prepare-and-measure methods in their own research. We conclude with a discussion of open problems and directions for future work.
one_liner: A tutorial unifies prepare-and-measure quantum communication, semi-device-independent models, and convex methods for correlation analysis.
why_it_matters: It provides an accessible technical toolkit for designing and certifying quantum communication protocols with limited device assumptions.
detailed_summary: The tutorial develops prepare-and-measure scenarios from their basic operational structure through classical and quantum communication constraints. It emphasizes semi-device-independent formulations and introduces convex-optimization techniques for characterizing attainable correlations. Worked applications connect the formal tools to quantum advantages, cryptography, and device certification, followed by open research directions.
main_result: The paper provides a unified conceptual and computational introduction to analyzing prepare-and-measure correlations under varied device assumptions.
application_angle: The methods support practical protocol development, security analysis, and certification when full device characterization is unavailable.

title: Alternating Squeezing and Photon Subtraction for Optical Cat-State Generation
abstract: Schrödinger cat states are important non-Gaussian resources for quantum information processing and quantum-enhanced metrology. Although photon subtraction from squeezed vacuum states has proven useful for generating such states in the optical domain, scaling to large amplitudes while maintaining high fidelity and heralding probability remains challenging. To address these obstacles, we analyze alternating squeezing and photon-number-subtraction operations. Rather than optimizing for a single heralding outcome, we formulate cat-state generation as a fidelity-constrained multibranch problem, jointly optimizing the total probability of all photon-number outcomes satisfying a prescribed fidelity threshold at one common experimental setting. Already for plain photon subtraction, this provides a more operational measure of the usable generation probability and can favor parameter configurations that differ from single-branch optima. Considering experimental constraints on available squeezing and photon-number-resolving capability, we demonstrate improvements in fidelity and success probability compared with plain photon subtraction, without necessarily increasing the required squeezing resources. Without restrictions on photon-number resolution, we find that the optimal architecture of the alternating scheme reduces to one of two single-subtraction endpoint configurations, depending on the available squeezing resources. When photon-number resolution is additionally limited, genuinely alternating branches can become advantageous. We derive analytical expressions for the conditional states, cat-state fidelities, and heralding probabilities, enabling efficient multibranch optimization and a systematic analysis of resource trade-offs, sensitivity to experimental parameter deviations, and heralding loss. Together, these results identify the architecture best suited to a given resource budget.
one_liner: Jointly optimized squeezing and photon subtraction improve the usable fidelity and heralding probability of optical cat-state generation.
why_it_matters: The multibranch treatment identifies experimentally useful architectures under realistic squeezing, detector-resolution, parameter-error, and loss constraints.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate cat-state preparation as a fidelity-constrained multibranch optimization that sums all acceptable photon-number heralding outcomes at one experimental setting. Analytical conditional states, fidelities, and probabilities enable systematic comparisons between plain and alternating squeezing–subtraction schemes. Endpoint single-subtraction configurations are optimal with unrestricted number resolution, while genuinely alternating branches can win when detector resolution is limited.
main_result: Alternating squeezing and subtraction can raise cat-state fidelity and total heralding probability without necessarily requiring more squeezing.
application_angle: The resource-aware optimization can guide laboratory sources of non-Gaussian states for photonic quantum computing and quantum-enhanced metrology.

title: The Lovász number is not alone: a continuum of Rényi points in the entanglement-assisted spectrum of graphs
abstract: Li and Zuiddam's entanglement-assisted asymptotic spectrum of graphs consists of the normalized graph parameters that are additive under disjoint unions, multiplicative under strong products and monotone under entanglement-assisted cohomomorphisms; the entanglement-assisted Shannon capacity is their pointwise minimum. To our knowledge, the Lovász number $\vartheta$ was its only known element. We find a continuum of others. Three quantities of Duan and Winter, $\log_2\vartheta$, the minimal Holevo capacity $C_{\min}$ and the logarithm of the no-signalling simulation cost $Σ$, are the smallest information radii of classical-quantum channels compatible with a graph, measured with Petz-Rényi divergences of orders $0$, $1$ and $2$. At order zero this is due to Schrijver (as credited by Dalai) and to Duan and Winter; at order one it is the min-max formula for the Holevo capacity. Interpolating in the order gives a family $\vartheta_α$, $0\leα\le2$, and we prove that every member lies in the spectrum. The main step, multiplicativity under strong products for channels that need not factor, follows from an exact nesting identity for compressions. Sandwiched Rényi radii of order $β\in[1/2,\infty]$ give the same family, at $α=2-1/β$. On the five-cycle the family takes every value in $[\sqrt5,5/2]$. A Hilbert-Schmidt inequality for the pentagon gives $C_{\min}(C_5)=\log_2(5/2)$, proving a conjecture of Duan and Winter. We also settle the two open links of their inequality chain: the graph-level no-signalling simulation rate always equals its single-letter value $\log_2Σ(G)$, and a 32-vertex graph from the Mermin-Peres magic square has $C_{\min}<\log_2Σ$, certified in exact rational arithmetic. Finally, $Σ$ never exceeds the projective rank of the complement; a rank inequality for the same square makes this strict on a 1440-vertex graph.
one_liner: A continuum of Rényi-based graph parameters expands the entanglement-assisted spectrum beyond the Lovász number.
why_it_matters: The results sharpen mathematical limits on entanglement-assisted communication and distinguish channel capacity from simulation cost.
detailed_summary: The authors construct a family of graph parameters θ_α for 0≤α≤2 using Petz-Rényi information radii of compatible classical-quantum channels and prove that every member belongs to the entanglement-assisted asymptotic spectrum. The family connects the Lovász number, minimal Holevo capacity, and no-signalling simulation cost, while an exact compression-nesting identity establishes strong-product multiplicativity. They also resolve conjectures and separations using the five-cycle and Mermin-Peres magic-square graphs.
main_result: A continuous Rényi family is proven to lie in the entanglement-assisted graph spectrum, with new exact equalities and strict separations among operational bounds.
application_angle: The framework provides tighter tools for bounding entanglement-assisted zero-error communication rates and channel-simulation resources.

title: Syndrome-Resolved Decoding of Qubit Readout Errors
abstract: Readout errors in superconducting qubits include incorrect state assignment, bit flips within the computational subspace, and leakage to non-computational states. These errors require different mitigation strategies, yet conventional measurement fidelity and repeatability metrics do not resolve their individual contributions. Previous repeated-readout studies have shown that temporal correlations reveal additional information about readout errors. Here we introduce the Readout Error Decoder (RED), which converts repeated thresholded binary records into a channel-resolved error budget. Controlled error injections validate the channel-specific response of the decoder. We demonstrate RED on both fluxonium and transmon qubits and across distinct leakage-lifetime regimes. RED identifies the error channels limiting readout performance without requiring dedicated discrimination of non-computational states, providing a basis for targeted readout optimization across different qubit modalities.
one_liner: Repeated binary measurements are decoded into separate assignment, computational bit-flip, and leakage error contributions.
why_it_matters: Channel-resolved diagnostics can direct readout improvements more effectively than aggregate fidelity or repeatability metrics.
detailed_summary: The Readout Error Decoder converts repeated thresholded binary records into an error budget separating incorrect assignment, computational-subspace flips, and leakage. Controlled error injections validate its channel-specific response. Measurements on fluxonium and transmon qubits show that RED remains informative across different leakage-lifetime regimes without dedicated non-computational-state discrimination.
main_result: RED identifies the individual error channels limiting superconducting-qubit readout from repeated binary records.
application_angle: The method supports targeted calibration and hardware optimization using standard thresholded readout data.

title: Perfect and peak state transfer on IBM quantum hardware
abstract: We run continuous-time quantum walks with perfect and peak state transfer on a present-day superconducting quantum processor, IBM Quantum's $156$-qubit Heron device ibm_kingston, deliberately without error correction or error mitigation. Perfect state transfer and its relaxations have been studied extensively in algebraic graph theory, where one can prove exactly which graphs move a quantum state from one vertex to another with probability one (or with the largest probability the graph allows, in the case of peak state transfer), and at what time. Our experiments cover perfect state transfer on the hypercubes $Q_2 = C_4$ and $Q_3$, and on the Hamming-weighted paths $\mathrm{HP}_n$, the equitable-partition quotients of the hypercubes $Q_n$, for $n$ up to $20$; peak state transfer on the $X_n$ family for $n$ up to $11$; and, for comparison, moving the state along a path of qubits by a sequence of SWAP gates.
one_liner: Perfect and peak quantum state transfer protocols are executed on IBM's 156-qubit Heron processor without mitigation or correction.
why_it_matters: The experiments test analytically designed quantum-walk transport protocols directly on present-day superconducting hardware.
detailed_summary: Continuous-time quantum walks were implemented on IBM's 156-qubit ibm_kingston processor without error correction or mitigation. Experiments cover perfect transfer on Q2, Q3, and Hamming-weighted paths up to n=20, plus peak transfer on X_n graphs up to n=11. Sequential SWAP-based transport provides a hardware-level comparison.
main_result: Graph-engineered continuous-time quantum walks realize perfect or peak state-transfer protocols across several graph families on current IBM hardware.
application_angle: The work informs hardware-efficient quantum routing and transport protocols based on engineered interaction graphs.

title: A Rydberg atom array coupled to a high-cooperativity optical cavity
abstract: Integrating Rydberg-state control of atom-atom interactions with cavity control of atom-light interactions enables the combination of local entangling operations with photon-mediated long-range coupling, measurement, and communication. Such integration is challenging because electric fields generated by charges on cavity optics and by cavity-stabilizing actuators may disturb Rydberg-state coherence. Here, we couple a Rydberg tweezer array to a high-cooperativity optical cavity, suppressing the electric fields produced by cavity length actuation so that the residual field variation of about $3~\mathrm{mV/cm}$ rms does not limit Rydberg coherence. We demonstrate two capabilities that neither system provides alone. First, we use Purcell-enhanced fluorescence to read out atoms directly in the ground-Rydberg basis within $7.5~μ\mathrm{s}$, well within the Rydberg-state lifetime, with ground- and Rydberg-state detection infidelities of $3\%$ and $5\%$, respectively, and with low atom loss. Second, we use Rydberg-Rydberg interactions to control collective light-atom scattering into the cavity mode. Specifically, we drive blockaded Rabi oscillations between a state with two ground-state atoms, which scatter collectively with a superradiant or subradiant rate controlled by the atomic positions, and an entangled state with a single Rydberg excitation, which scatters like a single atom. These capabilities open routes toward networked Rydberg processors, mid-circuit measurements in analog quantum simulators, and many-body quantum optics with entangled emitters coupled collectively to light.
one_liner: A Rydberg tweezer array is integrated with a high-cooperativity cavity for fast state readout and interaction-controlled scattering.
why_it_matters: The hybrid platform combines local Rydberg entangling interactions with cavity-mediated measurement, networking, and long-range optical coupling.
detailed_summary: A Rydberg atom array is coupled to a high-cooperativity optical cavity while suppressing actuator-induced electric-field variation to about 3 mV/cm rms. Purcell-enhanced fluorescence reads out the ground-Rydberg basis in 7.5 μs with 3% and 5% detection infidelities, respectively. Rydberg blockade also controls collective cavity scattering between superradiant or subradiant ground-state configurations and a singly excited entangled Rydberg state.
platform_or_system: Rydberg tweezer array in a high-cooperativity optical cavity
main_result: The system demonstrates fast ground-Rydberg readout and Rydberg-controlled collective light scattering in one integrated platform.
application_angle: It enables mid-circuit measurement, networked Rydberg processors, and many-body quantum optics with collectively coupled emitters.

title: Practical wavelength selection for quantum-augmented networks over shared optical fiber
abstract: In a quantum augmented network, sharing optical fiber with classical traffic requires quantum wavelength selection to balance logical fidelity, block acceptance, and classical data reception. Here we develop a wavelength-selection framework for an error-corrected three-stage quantum communication protocol. Under a thermal-background model with independent errors, an ideal one-photon receiver, and ideal recovery, we derive an accepted qubit channel and a key-independent lower bound on logical entanglement fidelity. Combining this bound with block acceptance gives an entanglement-fidelity yield bound, which we maximize over evaluated wavelengths subject to fidelity and classical link-budget requirements. For the Steane [[7,1,3]] code at 5 km per traversal and -10 dBm per classical channel, the largest fidelity certificate occurs near 1537 nm, whereas the largest yield bound occurs near 1551 nm. Along the 1.25 Gb/s classical link budget with 0.2% base error, the optimized yield bound falls below 10^-6 near 10 km per traversal, while fidelity remains certified at 0.99 or higher at longer spans. These results distinguish fidelity and yield constraints and identify certified operating regions for quantum-augmented networks sharing optical fiber.
one_liner: A wavelength-selection framework balances logical fidelity, accepted-block yield, and classical reception on shared fiber.
why_it_matters: It exposes a practical tradeoff: the wavelength maximizing certified fidelity can differ from the one maximizing usable quantum throughput.
detailed_summary: The authors derive an accepted logical-qubit channel and a key-independent lower bound on entanglement fidelity for a three-stage, error-corrected communication protocol. For a Steane [[7,1,3]] code with 5 km traversals and -10 dBm classical channels, certified fidelity peaks near 1537 nm while the yield bound peaks near 1551 nm. Under the stated 1.25 Gb/s link assumptions, optimized yield drops below 10^-6 near 10 km per traversal even as fidelity remains at least 0.99 over longer spans.
platform_or_system: Quantum and classical channels sharing telecom fiber
main_result: Optimization identifies distinct wavelengths and operating regions for maximum logical-fidelity certification and maximum accepted-qubit yield.
application_angle: The framework helps network designers choose wavelengths and span limits for error-corrected quantum links coexisting with classical traffic.

title: Agent-assisted experimental strategy transfer across quantum processors
abstract: Progress in quantum hardware requires a growing volume of experiments across diverse devices, straining the capacity of human experts. Automation remains challenging because device differences and drift can render workflows developed on one processor unsuitable for another. Here we present an agent-assisted experimental strategy for conducting experiments across three-qubit nuclear magnetic resonance processors. Developed on one processor and applied sequentially to four others, the strategy uses an agent to assess experimental evidence, select subsequent measurements and adapt procedures, with operators providing instrument preparation and physical intervention. Using three-qubit Grover state preparation as a common task, each deployment combined device-specific calibration, control-pulse optimization and measurement. The experimental strategy was refined through sequential deployment, and all four processors ultimately produced outputs dominated by their respective marked states. The marked-state populations of the reconstructed dominant eigenstates ranged from \(0.910\) to \(0.959\), with relative deviations below \(3.8\%\) from the ideal value of 0.945. These results demonstrate that an agent-assisted experimental strategy can be reused and refined across processors to realize a common quantum task, providing a basis for scaling experimental practice beyond individual devices.
one_liner: An agent-guided experimental strategy transfers Grover-state preparation across four distinct three-qubit NMR processors.
why_it_matters: Reusable, evidence-driven automation could reduce expert workload when calibrating and operating heterogeneous or drifting quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: An experimental agent assesses evidence, selects measurements, and adapts calibration, pulse optimization, and measurement procedures, while operators handle instrument preparation and physical intervention. A strategy developed on one three-qubit NMR processor was sequentially refined and deployed on four others. All devices produced outputs dominated by their marked Grover states, with dominant-eigenstate populations of 0.910–0.959 and deviations below 3.8% from the ideal 0.945.
main_result: A reusable agent-assisted workflow successfully adapted Grover-state preparation to four processors with device-specific calibration and control.
application_angle: The approach offers a path toward scalable experimental operations across heterogeneous quantum processors without fully autonomous laboratory control.

title: Stitched surface codes: planar concatenation through GHZ corridors
abstract: We present a fault-tolerant quantum-memory architecture that concatenates four distance-t rotated surface-code patches with the [[4,2,2]] outer code, encoding two logical qubits at code distance d = 2t in a physical footprint of N < 2(2t+1)^2 qubits on a square lattice with nearest-neighbor connectivity. The outer-code stabilizer generators XXXX and ZZZZ, each of physical weight 4t, are measured in situ via verified Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) ancillae distributed through narrow corridors between adjacent patches, without lattice surgery or long-range gates. The outer-code gadgets introduce hyperedge fault mechanisms, but by design each decomposes into graphlike components, so the complete syndrome is decoded by a single minimum-weight-perfect-matching pass. Circuit-level simulations show logical error rates that scale as p^t, consistent with distance-2t protection. Finally, we implement the construction experimentally on a 105-qubit Willow superconducting processor in both the ZZ and XX memory bases. With the correlated-matching decoder, increasing the code distance from d = 4 to d = 6 reduces the block logical error rate by a factor of 1.52. The construction thus provides a near-term testbed for concatenated architectures beyond the standard surface code.
one_liner: A stitched surface-code memory uses verified GHZ corridors to concatenate four patches without lattice surgery or long-range gates.
why_it_matters: The 105-qubit Willow experiment offers a hardware-tested route beyond standard surface codes using only square-lattice nearest-neighbor connectivity.
detailed_summary: Four rotated distance-t surface-code patches are concatenated with a [[4,2,2]] outer code, yielding two logical qubits with distance 2t and fewer than 2(2t+1)^2 physical qubits. Verified GHZ ancillae measure the weight-4t outer stabilizers through narrow corridors, while engineered hyperedge faults remain compatible with a single minimum-weight perfect-matching decode. Circuit-level simulations show p^t logical-error scaling, and experiments on 105 superconducting qubits cover both ZZ and XX memory bases.
main_result: Increasing code distance from 4 to 6 reduced the block logical error rate by a factor of 1.52 with correlated matching.
application_angle: The architecture provides a near-term, nearest-neighbor-compatible testbed for concatenated fault-tolerant quantum memories beyond conventional surface codes.

title: When do quantum views help? Complementary classical-quantum representations in multi-view fusion
abstract: Recent studies have reported promising results from quantum machine learning in drug discovery, healthcare, materials science and cybersecurity. Research includes comparisons with classical machine learning algorithms and the development of sequential hybrid pipelines. We propose that fusion can improve prediction when classical and quantum representations capture complementary predictive relationships. Our classical-quantum multi-view framework preserves the full classical input alongside simulated quantum features. Concatenation and attention combine the views; single-view comparisons, replacement and masking controls assess both views' contributions. Controlled angular-polynomial experiments distinguish targets adequately represented by a single view from those that depend on complementary angular and polynomial relationships. For these mixed targets, fusion improves prediction by combining the relevant feature sets, while matched classical representations recover the same benefit, linking the improvement to their complementary predictive content. Controlled classification tests further show that gains depend on alignment between the chosen representation and the target, and on a suitable fusion rule. Benchmark validation shows improved mean predictive performance over classical baselines on Wine, Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer, three-class Fashion-MNIST and Steel Plates Faults within the evaluated protocols. Classical replacement and masking controls remain competitive, classical baselines lead on Digits and Covertype, and outcomes with missing or corrupted views depend on the available inputs. These findings support evaluating quantum representations for their complementary predictive contribution and matching the representation and fusion strategy to the target relationships.
one_liner: Classical-quantum multi-view fusion helps when its two feature representations encode complementary relationships aligned with the target.
why_it_matters: The controls show that gains arise from useful complementary features rather than quantum processing alone, sharpening how hybrid models should be evaluated.
detailed_summary: The framework retains the full classical input while adding simulated quantum features, then combines the views through concatenation or attention. Synthetic angular-polynomial tasks and masking, replacement, and single-view controls isolate when complementary representations improve prediction. Several evaluated benchmarks improve over classical baselines, but matched classical features can recover the benefit and classical models remain stronger on Digits and Covertype.
main_result: Fusion improved mean prediction on several evaluated datasets when classical and quantum views captured complementary target-aligned structure.
application_angle: The framework supplies practical controls for deciding whether hybrid quantum models add useful sensing or classification features in real data workflows.

title: Optimising multipartite entanglement manipulation in quantum networks
abstract: Long-range, genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) between distant parties in a quantum network is a crucial resource for distributed quantum information processing. Through controlled manipulation of short-range GME states in the network via stochastic local operations aided by classical communication (SLOCC), long-range GME can be established between selected target nodes on demand. Optimizing such multipartite entanglement distribution protocols under constraints imposed by the network architecture, target-node set, and available resource budget is a key challenge in resource-efficient manipulation of GME. We present a general operational framework for manipulating GME in quantum networks by classifying the relevant networking operations into three broad primitives-inflation, deflation, and purification-reflecting their effect on the proliferation of GME through general bounds and illustrative examples. We show how these primitives can be combined to construct a broad class of multipartite quantum repeater protocols, enabling their systematic optimization, and demonstrate the framework with a simple example. Applying our approach to networks of Dür-Cirac-Tarrach states reveals a rich landscape of achievable end-to-end GME and accessible entanglement classes. More generally, our framework provides a systematic approach to the construction and optimization of multipartite quantum repeater protocols for scalable and resource-efficient GME distribution in quantum networks.
one_liner: A framework organizes multipartite entanglement networking into inflation, deflation, and purification primitives for protocol optimization.
why_it_matters: It turns long-range genuine multipartite entanglement distribution into a systematic resource-allocation problem for scalable quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The authors classify network operations by how they expand, contract, or purify genuine multipartite entanglement and derive general bounds with illustrative examples. These primitives can be composed into multipartite repeater protocols and optimized under topology, target-node, and resource constraints. Application to Dür-Cirac-Tarrach states exposes multiple reachable end-to-end entanglement classes.
main_result: The framework systematically constructs and optimizes protocols for distributing long-range genuine multipartite entanglement between selected network nodes.
application_angle: It supports resource-efficient design of distributed quantum computing and communication networks that require shared multipartite states.

title: Crossovers between Time-Bin and Energy-Time Entanglement in Homodyned Resonance Fluorescence
abstract: We theoretically investigate photonic entanglement generated by homodyning resonance fluorescence from a two-level emitter with a phase-locked laser field. Under weak excitation, increasing the relative laser-field amplitude produces crossovers from time-bin to energy--time and back to time-bin entanglement. The intermediate energy--time regime occurs near amplitude matching, where destructive interference suppresses the single-photon component, allowing the two-photon contributions to dominate the coincidence signal. We evaluate the resulting photon statistics and first-order coherence and characterize the entanglement through violations of the CHSH Bell inequality in a Franson interferometer. This scheme provides a route to controlling photonic entanglement through linear optics and coherent interference.
one_liner: Coherent homodyning tunes resonance fluorescence between time-bin and energy-time photonic entanglement regimes.
why_it_matters: The proposal controls the entanglement type using only a phase-locked field, linear optics, and interference around emitter-laser amplitude matching.
detailed_summary: A phase-locked laser field is coherently combined with weakly excited resonance fluorescence from a two-level emitter. Near amplitude matching, destructive interference suppresses the single-photon component so that two-photon coincidences dominate, producing an intermediate energy-time regime between two time-bin regimes. Photon statistics, first-order coherence, and predicted CHSH violations in a Franson interferometer characterize the crossovers.
main_result: Varying the coherent-field amplitude produces controllable time-bin–energy-time–time-bin entanglement crossovers with predicted Bell violations.
application_angle: The scheme could provide a simple tunable source of photonic entanglement formats for interferometric quantum communication.

title: Accurate gap control of 3D-integrated superconducting quantum circuits using asymmetric indium architecture and multi-angle flip-chip bonding
abstract: Flip-chip 3D integration is a key enabling technology for overcoming the routing and layout constraints of planar superconducting quantum processors, but it requires accurate and uniform control of the inter-chip spacing while preserving qubit coherence. In conventional processes, thick indium bumps are deposited symmetrically on both chips, while dedicated spacers are introduced to limit the residual tilt. Here, we present a flip-chip bonding process based on an asymmetric indium architecture, combining $20\,μ\mathrm{m}$ thick indium bumps on the control chip with $200\,\mathrm{nm}$ thin indium pads on the qubit chip. Using electrical and microwave measurements, we demonstrate low resistance and low loss indium interconnects, and show that transmon qubits integrated with this process reach relaxation and coherence times of $T_1=(159\pm14)\,μ\mathrm{s}$ and $T_{\mathrm{2,echo}}=(294\pm42)\,μ\mathrm{s}$, respectively, comparable to planar devices. Combined with a multi angle compression procedure that suppresses systematic tilt, this approach reduces the average post bonding tilt to $(20\pm12)\,μ\mathrm{rad}$. These results establish an asymmetric indium architecture combined with multi angle compression as a robust, coherence preserving route toward 3D-integrated superconducting quantum processors.
one_liner: Asymmetric indium bumps and multi-angle compression deliver low-tilt 3D integration while preserving superconducting-qubit coherence.
why_it_matters: The process addresses a central packaging bottleneck by combining uniform chip spacing, low-loss interconnects, and planar-class transmon coherence.
detailed_summary: The process pairs 20-μm indium bumps on the control chip with 200-nm pads on the qubit chip, avoiding symmetric thick deposits and dedicated spacers. Electrical and microwave tests indicate low-resistance, low-loss interconnects. Multi-angle compression reduces systematic tilt while integrated transmons retain relaxation and echo-coherence times comparable to planar devices.
main_result: The bonded devices achieved 20±12 μrad average tilt, T1=159±14 μs, and T2,echo=294±42 μs.
application_angle: This coherence-preserving packaging method can relieve routing and layout constraints in larger superconducting quantum processors.

title: Periodic conditional measurements on a photonic chip
abstract: Quantum measurements not only extract information but also reshape quantum evolution through measurement backaction. Here, we investigate periodic conditional measurements, in which coherent evolution is repeatedly interrupted by local measurements. We show that the bright and dark modes of the conditional evolution operator provide a unified spectral description of both the post-selected final state along no-detection trajectories and the statistics of detection events. Using a three-dimensional photonic chip, we demonstrate on-demand state engineering through dark-mode preservation and bright-mode selection, enabling the protection of topological corner states and excited-state shelving. We further observe the predicted transition of the total detection probability on an effectively infinite one-dimensional lattice and identify its microscopic origin in Floquet near-dark modes. These results establish periodic conditional measurements as a general framework for engineering conditional quantum states and manipulating event-detection statistics in monitored quantum dynamics.
one_liner: Periodic conditional measurements on a 3D photonic chip engineer quantum states through selectable bright and dark evolution modes.
why_it_matters: The experiment turns measurement backaction into a programmable tool for protecting localized states and controlling detection-event statistics.
detailed_summary: Repeated local measurements interrupt coherent evolution, with the conditional evolution operator's bright and dark modes governing no-detection states and event statistics. A three-dimensional photonic chip demonstrates dark-mode preservation and bright-mode selection for topological corner-state protection and excited-state shelving. The experiment also observes a transition in total detection probability on an effectively infinite one-dimensional lattice and links it to Floquet near-dark modes.
main_result: Periodic measurements enabled on-demand state engineering, topological-state protection, excited-state shelving, and control of detection statistics.
application_angle: Measurement-driven mode selection offers a hardware-accessible method for state preparation and robust control in monitored photonic quantum systems.

title: Limits of adaptive two-way linear postprocessing in six-state quantum key distribution
abstract: Two-way classical communication improves the noise tolerance of quantum key distribution, but the limits of adaptive parity processing remain unclear. For the six-state protocol with equal three-basis error rate $p\in[p_*,1/2]$, where $p_*=(5-\sqrt5)/10\simeq27.64\%$, we construct a single compatible collective attack that defeats a broad class of linear postprocessing. Each public message may be a linear function of the sender's raw key, chosen adaptively from the public history. For every finite input length and every accepted transcript of positive probability, Eve's optimal probability of recovering any linear function of Alice's raw key is at least Bob's. Consequently, reliable agreement on a linear final key is incompatible with secrecy. The same conclusion holds for arbitrary publicly seeded privacy amplification after reliable recovery of a linear candidate. The proof conditions on the complete transcript, which restricts the two raw keys to affine subspaces. A local degradation of Eve's state, a known Rényi-entropy comparison, and a coset-probability inequality then give the recovery comparison. Both inequalities are proved in self-contained appendices. The result allows block splitting, regrouping, nonzero-syndrome selection, and adaptive linear reconciliation.
one_liner: A collective attack sets a sharp limit on adaptive two-way linear postprocessing for noisy six-state QKD.
why_it_matters: The result rules out secrecy from a broad family of practical reconciliation strategies above a 27.64% equal-basis error rate.
detailed_summary: For equal three-basis error rates from about 27.64% to 50%, the authors construct one compatible collective attack that defeats a broad class of adaptive linear postprocessing. Conditioned on any accepted finite-length transcript, Eve can recover every linear function of Alice's raw key with probability at least as high as Bob. The no-go result also covers block regrouping, syndrome selection and publicly seeded privacy amplification applied after recovery of a linear candidate.
main_result: Reliable agreement on a linear final key is shown to be incompatible with secrecy throughout the stated high-error regime.
application_angle: The bound identifies when increasingly elaborate two-way linear reconciliation cannot rescue six-state QKD security.

title: Practical Fidelity Estimation for Noisy Quantum Devices Using Direct and Survival-Probability-Based Protocols
abstract: Reliable characterization of quantum states and quantum processes is central to the development of scalable quantum computing. Standard characterization techniques such as full quantum state tomography become rapidly impractical as system size increases. In this work we present two software-oriented fidelity estimation protocols that avoid full tomographic reconstruction while remaining experimentally relevant for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. The first protocol is direct fidelity estimation (DFE), where the fidelity between a target state and an experimentally prepared state is estimated from importance-sampled Pauli measurements. The second protocol is a survival-probability-based method that reconstructs fidelity from experimentally accessible moments of a noisy evolution and its approximate inverse, and is intrinsically robust against state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) errors. We discuss the theoretical basis of both approaches, analyze their noise sensitivity, and present numerical evidence on representative multiqubit states under depolarizing, dephasing, and amplitude-damping channels. For DFE we show that attenuation-aware correction improves robustness against measurement noise. For the survival-probability approach we show that an $L_2$-optimized expansion substantially outperforms naive Taylor truncation in high-noise regimes.
one_liner: Two tomography-free protocols estimate state fidelity on noisy multiqubit devices using sampled Pauli data or survival probabilities.
why_it_matters: The methods reduce characterization overhead while addressing measurement noise and SPAM errors on near-term quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The study compares direct fidelity estimation from importance-sampled Pauli measurements with a moment-based survival-probability protocol using noisy evolution and an approximate inverse. Numerical tests cover multiqubit states under depolarizing, dephasing and amplitude-damping noise. Attenuation-aware correction improves DFE under measurement noise, while an L2-optimized expansion improves survival-based estimates in high-noise regimes and retains intrinsic SPAM robustness.
main_result: Both protocols estimate fidelity without full tomography, with tailored corrections improving accuracy under realistic noise.
application_angle: The software-oriented methods offer scalable diagnostics and benchmarking for noisy quantum devices.

title: Fast, parallel, three-dimensional rearrangement of atom arrays using superpositions of elementary holograms
abstract: Assembling defect-free arrays of neutral atoms requires real-time rearrangement of stochastically loaded optical tweezers. Conventional rearrangement methods shuttle atoms sequentially, whereas high-speed spatial light modulators (SLMs) can move all atoms in parallel, which scales more favorably as the array size grows. For fast parallel rearrangement, the sequence of holograms displayed on the SLM should be computed more rapidly than the SLM refresh rate, and there should be phase continuity between successive holograms to minimize transient intensity fluctuations. We calculate holograms analytically by adding together the complex fields needed to produce each individual trap, and we ramp the phase of each trap linearly as it moves to its target location. Trap positions enter as continuous variables, rather than tied to points on a grid, so the method provides high positioning accuracy. Using a single GPU, we compute each intermediate hologram in 0.284 ms, considerably faster than the SLM refresh time of 0.696 ms, so the rearrangement speed is hardware-limited. In each step, we use the free processing time to iteratively optimize the holograms for equal intensity across the traps, decreasing trap non-uniformity to 1.24% during rearrangement at no cost in total time. Starting from an array of 256 sites loaded stochastically with $^{87}$Rb atoms, we assemble a 100-atom array in under 20 ms with a rearrangement survival probability of 99.31(12)% per atom. This rearrangement increases the temperature of the atoms by 9(3) $μ$K, which is small compared to the trap depth of 480 $μ$K. Our method can also move individual atoms axially, enabling transport in different planes. We demonstrate this capability with a rearrangement protocol where one set of atoms leapfrogs over another.
one_liner: GPU-computed holograms rearrange neutral atoms in parallel across three dimensions, assembling 100 atoms in under 20 ms.
why_it_matters: Hardware-limited, high-survival rearrangement directly improves the preparation speed and scalability of neutral-atom quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The method analytically superposes elementary trap fields and uses continuous coordinates with linear phase ramps to preserve smooth motion. A GPU computes each hologram in 0.284 ms, faster than the SLM's 0.696 ms refresh time, while spare computation equalizes trap intensities to 1.24% nonuniformity. From 256 stochastically loaded sites, the experiment assembles 100 87Rb atoms in under 20 ms with 99.31(12)% per-atom survival and also demonstrates axial leapfrog transport.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates fast parallel 3D rearrangement of 100 atoms with high survival and low added heating.
application_angle: The technique accelerates defect-free register preparation for scalable neutral-atom computing and simulation.

title: Remote Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Entanglement Generation between Trapped Ions
abstract: Distributing entanglement directly between error-corrected logical qubits is an important capability for scalable quantum networks. We propose a heralded protocol for generating remote entanglement between Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill qubits encoded in the motional modes of spatially separated trapped ions, using the internal electronic states to interface the motional qubits with emitted photons. We derive the protocol for single-rail and polarization photonic encodings and evaluate the effects of finite GKP squeezing, photon loss, photon recoil, motional heating, and motional dephasing on the decoded logical state. Moreover, we numerically analysed the fidelity of distributed logical Bell-pair fidelity. We find that one can achieve more than 95% of fidelity in the realistic situation. The protocol combines motional-control and photonic-networking operations that have already been demonstrated in trapped-ion experiments.
one_liner: A heralded photonic protocol distributes logical GKP Bell pairs between motional modes of spatially separated trapped ions.
why_it_matters: It provides a route to network entanglement directly between error-corrected bosonic qubits using demonstrated ion-photon operations.
detailed_summary: The proposal encodes GKP qubits in ion motion and uses internal electronic states to couple those logical qubits to emitted photons. It derives heralded schemes for single-rail and polarization photonic encodings and models finite squeezing, photon loss, recoil, heating and motional dephasing. Numerical analysis indicates decoded logical Bell-pair fidelities above 95% under realistic conditions.
platform_or_system: Motional GKP qubits in trapped ions
main_result: The protocol is predicted to generate remote logical Bell pairs with greater than 95% fidelity under realistic imperfections.
application_angle: Directly networking error-corrected qubits could support modular trapped-ion computers and fault-tolerant quantum links.

title: Probing Deconfined Quantum Criticality Point on a Digital Quantum Computer
abstract: A deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP) is a continuous transition between ordered phases with unrelated broken symmetries, beyond the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm. In one dimension, such a transition between a $z$-polarized ferromagnet (zFM) and a valence-bond solid (VBS) is well established numerically in a frustrated spin-$1/2$ chain. Here we ask whether a superconducting quantum processor can resolve this transition and its signatures despite finite-size effects and device noise. The ground states are prepared by ancilla-projected quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE), whose exact target states are compressed by tensor-network optimization into shallow depth quantum circuits. The hardware data distinguish the phases through their order parameters, spin and dimer correlations, structure factors, correlation ratios, and snapshot distributions. The crossing of the order parameters locates the transition, and its finite-size extrapolation lies close to the thermodynamic-limit value obtained from large-scale numerics. A noise model based on the device calibration accounts quantitatively for the reduced amplitudes measured on hardware. Our findings demonstrate that a Landau-forbidden transition between competing orders can be resolved on current quantum processors.
one_liner: A superconducting processor resolves signatures of a one-dimensional deconfined quantum critical point despite finite size and noise.
why_it_matters: The experiment shows current digital quantum hardware can distinguish subtle competing phases and estimate a non-Landau critical transition.
detailed_summary: Ancilla-projected quantum imaginary-time evolution prepares target ground states compressed by tensor-network optimization into shallow circuits. Hardware measurements distinguish ferromagnetic and valence-bond-solid phases through order parameters, correlations, structure factors, correlation ratios and snapshot distributions. Finite-size extrapolation places the transition near large-scale numerical predictions, while a calibration-derived noise model explains the measured amplitude reduction.
main_result: Current hardware resolves a Landau-forbidden transition and locates its critical point close to the numerical thermodynamic-limit value.
application_angle: The workflow advances near-term quantum processors as tools for studying strongly correlated phases and critical phenomena.

title: Local finite rate semi device independent randomness expansion from quantum contextuality
abstract: Finite rate randomness expansion (RE) which is secure against quantum adversaries is a crucial information processing task which is well studied in the case of two non-communicating parties sharing Bell non-local correlations in a device independent manner. In this paper we show that contextual correlations with only a single localized party are sufficient for RE in a semi-device independent (SDI) manner. We propose a template SDI-RE protocol which is applicable for arbitrary $N$-cycle non-contextuality (NC) inequalities and derive its RE rate under finite statistics. As a special case, we also highlight the advantages of the situation when RE is constrained by Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequality but with characterized measurements implemented by only a single party. Our template protocol also incorporates non-ideal statistics which may not satisfy perfect commutativity and perfect repeatability, both of which are necessary in a loophole-free test of NC inequalities. As such, several recent experimental implementations of significantly loophole-free tests of NC inequalities can be modified for secure RE following our approach.
one_liner: Single-party contextuality enables finite-rate randomness expansion secure against quantum adversaries under semi-device-independent assumptions.
why_it_matters: The protocol removes the need for two separated noncommunicating devices and accommodates imperfections found in contextuality experiments.
detailed_summary: The authors give a semi-device-independent randomness-expansion template for arbitrary N-cycle noncontextuality inequalities and derive finite-statistics generation rates. A single-party CHSH-constrained variant uses characterized measurements without requiring spatially separated devices. The security treatment incorporates imperfect commutativity and repeatability, allowing recent contextuality experiments to be adapted rather than assuming ideal measurements.
main_result: Contextual correlations from one localized party are shown to support finite-rate randomness expansion secure against quantum adversaries.
application_angle: The scheme could simplify practical certified random-number generators by avoiding a two-device Bell-test architecture.

title: Watt-level single-cavity dual-comb laser at 2.1 $μ$m wavelength
abstract: Compact ultrafast laser combs around the 2 $μ$m atmospheric transmission window are of growing interest for direct spectroscopy and as drivers for nonlinear conversion to otherwise hard-to-reach spectral regions.
