Dual-comb systems in this region remain very scarce: existing implementations rely mostly on nonlinear conversion, resulting in complex systems with poor conversion efficiency and overall low average and peak power. In this paper, we report on a watt-level dual-comb laser directly emitting at 2.1 $μ$m. The system is based on a single-cavity, soft-aperture Kerr-lens mode-locked (KLM) laser using a broadband holmium (Ho)-doped CaAlGdO$_4$ (CALGO) gain crystal. The laser delivers a total output power exceeding 2 W (1 W per comb) with a sub-100-fs pulse duration (50 nm bandwidth) at a repetition rate of 96.5 MHz, corresponding to a pulse energy of 10 nJ and a peak power of 100 kW per comb. To assess the source's potential for future spectroscopic applications, we characterize the free-running dual comb in detail for frequency stability, phase noise, and relative intensity noise (RIN), and benchmark the achievable spectral resolution by measuring spectral modulations imposed by Fabry-Pérot etalons. Our system combines the compactness, high efficiency, and passive mutual coherence of a single-cavity oscillator with watt-level average power at 2.1 $μ$m, making it a promising source for environmental sensing in the atmospheric transmission window, or as a driver for nonlinear frequency conversion, for example, to the MIR and THz regions.
one_liner: A single-cavity Ho:CALGO laser directly generates two mutually coherent, watt-level frequency combs near 2.1 μm.
why_it_matters: The compact source combines high power and passive mutual coherence in an atmospheric window useful for spectroscopy, environmental sensing, and nonlinear conversion.
detailed_summary: The soft-aperture Kerr-lens mode-locked Ho:CALGO oscillator emits two combs from one cavity with more than 2 W total power and 1 W per comb. It produces sub-100-fs pulses at 96.5 MHz, with 10 nJ pulse energy and about 100 kW peak power per comb. Frequency stability, phase noise, relative intensity noise, and etalon-imposed spectral modulation measurements benchmark its free-running spectroscopic performance.
main_result: The system directly delivers two passively coherent 2.1 μm combs at watt-level power with sub-100-fs pulses.
application_angle: It offers a compact source for atmospheric-window spectroscopy, environmental sensing, and efficient pumping of mid-infrared or terahertz conversion stages.

title: Controlled-Memory Identification with Shared Generators: Dimension--Horizon Tradeoffs and Quantum--Classical Separation
abstract: We determine the finite-horizon identification limits of a \(d\)-dimensional memory when the control interface is restricted to four shared, time-homogeneous generators. A writer encodes a message by applying a prefix word to a common root state. The verifier then applies a candidate-dependent query word followed by a shared terminal binary test, with each word of length at most \(T\). For fixed error tolerances \(λ_2>0\) and \(λ_1+λ_2<1\), the optimal identification sizes satisfy \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d^2,T\})\) for arbitrary CPTP generators and \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d,T\})\) for stochastic maps. Four unitary letters and four permutation letters attain these respective bounds, showing that a four-letter reversible alphabet reaches the static code-size orders in optimal quadratic and linear word length. In the fully dimension-limited regime, this yields \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ(d^2)\) versus \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ(d)\), establishing a quadratic quantum--classical separation in logarithmic code size. Low-overlap Grassmann and agreement-code packings supply the orbit endpoints, while exact inverse query words match each encoded state to its designated test. At the sharp boundary \(λ_2=0\), \(0\leqλ_1<1\), all four model classes satisfy \(\ln N=Θ(\min\{\ln d,T\})\). Thus any fixed positive false-acceptance tolerance activates the metric-packing regime, whereas zero false acceptance imposes an exclusive-witness constraint and yields the logarithmic-dimension boundary.
one_liner: Four shared reversible generators give quantum memories a quadratic advantage over classical memories in dimension-limited identification capacity.
why_it_matters: The bounds identify how memory dimension and control horizon constrain compact quantum devices operated through a small, fixed instruction alphabet.
detailed_summary: The work derives finite-horizon identification bounds for a d-dimensional memory controlled by four shared, time-homogeneous generators and words of length at most T. With nonzero false-acceptance tolerance, quantum CPTP dynamics achieve ln N=Θ(min{d²,T}), whereas stochastic dynamics achieve Θ(min{d,T}); four unitaries and four permutations attain the respective orders. At zero false acceptance, all considered models instead obey Θ(min{ln d,T}).
main_result: A four-letter reversible control alphabet attains a quadratic quantum-classical separation in logarithmic identification size in the dimension-limited regime.
application_angle: The results provide design limits for memory identification and addressing under severely restricted, reusable control interfaces.

title: Three-axis Active Magnetic Compensation with Spatial Feedforward Matrix Decoupling and Hysteresis PI Regulation for Suppressing Zeeman Decoherence of Cold Atom Quantum Memories
abstract: Cold-atom quantum memories require a near-zero magnetic environment (residual field <1 microtesla) to mitigate Zeeman decoherence. Conventional three-axis active compensation suffers from inter-coil crosstalk and geomagnetic drift, which degrade the uniformity and long-term stability of the zero-field region. To address this, we propose a spatiotemporally cooperative feedback-controlled suppression architecture for magnetic interference. An integrally printed three-dimensional orthogonal coil frame mechanically suppresses inter-axis flux leakage. A spatial feedforward inverse matrix is introduced to algorithmically eliminate first-order cross-coupling. A dual-threshold hysteresis incremental-PI controller filters magnetometer quantization fluctuations and avoids frequent small jitter adjustments of coil driving currents. Hardware ablation experiments, long-duration stability tests and spatial magnetic-field mapping were conducted. Experimental results show that during a 714.4 s continuous steady-hold stage, the mean and maximum residual fields at the central point reach 0.112 microtesla and 0.224 microtesla, respectively. The overlapping Allan deviations of all three components remain below 5 nT for averaging times of 1.9-178.2 s. Based on differential-ferrofluid lattice-scan measurements combined with centre-constrained quadratic vector reconstruction and soft Maxwell regularization, a weak-field spatial distribution with an RMS variation of 5.65 microtesla is fitted within a spherical region of interest of radius 5 mm, where 67.5% of the model volume meets the sub-5 microtesla coverage criterion. For a prolate ellipsoidal region matching the atomic-cloud distribution with full axis lengths of 10, 5, and 5 mm, the upper field bound within 93.7% of the volume is 2.68 microtesla.
one_liner: A decoupled three-axis coil controller holds the central residual magnetic field near 0.1 μT for a cold-atom quantum-memory environment.
why_it_matters: Stable low fields suppress Zeeman decoherence, while the reported spatial maps expose how much of an extended atomic-cloud volume actually meets weak-field targets.
detailed_summary: The architecture combines a printed orthogonal coil frame, inverse-matrix feedforward decoupling, and dual-threshold hysteresis incremental-PI regulation. During a 714.4 s hold, the central field had a 0.112 μT mean and 0.224 μT maximum, while all three components showed overlapping Allan deviations below 5 nT for 1.9–178.2 s averaging. Regularized vector reconstruction also quantified residual-field coverage across spherical and atomic-cloud-shaped regions.
main_result: The controller maintained sub-microtesla central residual fields with nanotesla-scale Allan deviations over a broad averaging-time range.
application_angle: The approach supports longer-lived cold-atom memories and provides spatial qualification methods for other field-sensitive quantum sensors and atomic systems.

title: Superconducting circuits host two-level systems with lifetimes exceeding one second
abstract: Understanding the microscopic environment of superconducting qubits is a central challenge for quantum technologies. Parasitic two-level systems (TLSs) of various microscopic origins are ubiquitous and limit qubit performance through decoherence, frequency drifts, and leakage. Recently, long-lived TLSs with lifetimes exceeding those of state-of-the-art qubits have been shown to induce correlated qubit dynamics, with direct implications for quantum error correction. Here, we perform wide-band quantum-jump correlation spectroscopy on flux-tunable transmon qubits and identify microscopic degrees of freedom that outlive the qubit by orders of magnitude. Pump-probe measurements at varying detunings from these objects reveal intrinsic lifetimes exceeding one second. Their weak coupling to the qubit, in the kilohertz range, is consistent with positional defects described by the standard tunneling model, without excluding other microscopic origins such as magnetic spin impurities or trapped quasiparticles. More broadly, these results establish superconducting qubits as a sensitive probe of exceptionally long-lived microscopic degrees of freedom and open a route toward their controlled access and functionalization.
one_liner: Quantum-jump spectroscopy reveals weakly coupled defects in superconducting circuits with intrinsic lifetimes exceeding one second.
why_it_matters: Such defects outlive transmon qubits by orders of magnitude and may drive correlated errors, slow drifts, and leakage relevant to quantum error correction.
detailed_summary: Wide-band quantum-jump correlation spectroscopy on flux-tunable transmons identifies microscopic degrees of freedom far longer-lived than the qubits. Detuning-dependent pump-probe measurements indicate intrinsic lifetimes above one second and qubit coupling in the kilohertz range. The coupling is compatible with positional tunneling defects, although spin impurities and trapped quasiparticles are not excluded.
main_result: The experiments detect circuit-hosted microscopic two-level systems with intrinsic lifetimes beyond one second and kilohertz-scale qubit coupling.
application_angle: Characterizing these persistent defects can improve noise models, correlated-error mitigation, materials diagnostics, and potentially controlled defect-based memory functions.

title: Optical Coherent Combining in Multi-Aperture Free-Space Receivers through Atmospheric Turbulence via Optically Computed Alignment Gradients
abstract: Multi-aperture reception converts spatial diversity into a coherent-combining gain, but only if the relative phase and polarization of the collected field replicas are aligned before they are summed. In a satellite-to-ground downlink the atmosphere perturbs amplitude, phase and polarization, so the alignment must track a fluctuating channel rather than a fixed offset. This paper proposes a new optical-domain combining scheme in which the alignment information is computed by light itself: the ascent directions that maximize the combined output power are formed by optical interference and read out directly as differential photocurrents of balanced detection, so no estimate of the channel, no deliberate perturbation, and no per-branch digital processing is needed to obtain them. Every branch is aligned against one shared reference - a passive tap of the combined field itself - so no independent laser or optical frequency lock is required, and the update directions of all branches are available simultaneously in a single averaging window without frequency, code, or time multiplexing. The data path needs a single dual-polarization coherent receiver regardless of the aperture count, and the readout is built from elementary parts only - a 3 dB directional coupler, static phase shifters, a Faraday rotator, and balanced photodiodes - so no 90-degree optical hybrid, mixer, or polarization-diverse hybrid is required. The phase and polarization loops are fixed-gain and division-free, and each branch carries one phase modulator and one polarization controller with no amplitude actuator. A closed-form combining-gain and loss budget is derived, the assumptions and limitations of the scheme are stated explicitly, and experimental validation remains open.
one_liner: An optical circuit computes phase and polarization alignment gradients for coherent combining across turbulent multi-aperture free-space receivers.
why_it_matters: The scheme could scale receiver aperture count without per-branch channel estimation, dithering, independent local lasers, or duplicated coherent receivers.
detailed_summary: The proposed receiver derives ascent directions for phase and polarization alignment directly from interference and balanced differential photocurrents. Each branch is referenced to a passive tap of the combined field, allowing simultaneous gradient readout without channel estimation, deliberate perturbations, or multiplexed digital processing. A closed-form gain and loss budget is presented, but experimental validation remains outstanding.
main_result: The analysis shows how light can directly compute simultaneous branch-alignment gradients using simple passive optics and balanced photodetection.
application_angle: The architecture targets scalable, turbulence-tolerant satellite-to-ground optical and quantum communication receivers with a single dual-polarization coherent data path.

title: Looking Beyond Visibility: Resolving the Temporal Structure of Continuous-Wave Four-Photon Hong-Ou-Mandel Interference
abstract: Hong-Ou-Mandel interference underpins many photonic quantum information protocols and is commonly characterized by a single visibility parameter. This quantity is typically obtained by averaging over a fixed coincidence window, thereby discarding details of the underlying temporal structure that are critical in continuous-wave processes. Four-photon interference with continuous-wave sources furthermore requires photon pairs with long coherence times, which we generate in microring resonators and measure with ultrafast time-resolved detection. Here, we model and resolve their interference and temporal structure by recording all four photon arrival times and mapping their relative delays onto a three-dimensional coincidence histogram relative to a trigger detection. The resulting structure preserves relative arrival-time correlations that are usually discarded and enables post-processed optimization of coincidence windows to trade off visibility against count rate. This method provides a general benchmark for continuous-wave sources in interference-based quantum network protocols.
one_liner: Four-photon arrival-time recording resolves the full 3D temporal structure of continuous-wave Hong-Ou-Mandel interference from microrings.
why_it_matters: Temporal maps reveal correlations hidden by a single visibility value and allow coincidence windows to be optimized for visibility versus usable count rate.
detailed_summary: Long-coherence photon pairs generated in microring resonators undergo continuous-wave four-photon interference measured with ultrafast time-resolved detection. Recording all four arrival times enables a three-dimensional histogram of relative delays referenced to a trigger event. The resolved structure supports post-processing of coincidence windows and exposes correlations discarded by conventional window-averaged visibility.
main_result: The experiment reconstructs the three-dimensional timing structure of continuous-wave four-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel interference.
application_angle: The method provides a richer source and interference benchmark for entanglement swapping and other interference-based quantum-network protocols.

title: ZZ-Free bSWAP Gates under Strong Driving in Far-Detuned Fixed-Frequency Transmons
abstract: Far-detuned frequency allocations in fixed-frequency superconducting processors mitigate spectral crowding but constrain cross-resonance interactions at practical drive amplitudes. Here, we demonstrate that a single strong drive induces a large $XX-YY$ interaction in the far-detuned regime, while a weak second tone tunes the accompanying $ZZ$ phase. The interaction realizes a 150-ns $\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}$ gate, which can directly prepare a maximally entangled state from the ground state. For the implementations on the same qubit pair at matched drive strengths, cross resonance gives a shorter CNOT operation, while $\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}$ gives a 33% shorter SWAP operation with a higher IRB fidelity. The multilevel theory further predicts a regime where stronger driving can yield a speed advantage for CNOT as well, a possibility absent in the two-level model. As an application of the $XX-YY$ interaction, we also demonstrate two-spin squeezing beyond the standard quantum limit through two-axis countertwisting. The interaction realized here complements cross resonance and offers a route to efficient gate synthesis and quantum simulation of interacting spin systems.
one_liner: Strong two-tone driving enables a 150-ns ZZ-corrected √bSWAP gate between far-detuned fixed-frequency transmons.
why_it_matters: The interaction accelerates SWAP synthesis, improves interleaved-RB fidelity, and supports spin-squeezing experiments without tunable qubits.
detailed_summary: A strong drive induces an XX−YY interaction between far-detuned fixed-frequency transmons, while a weaker second tone controls the accompanying ZZ phase. The experiment realizes a 150-ns √bSWAP that directly creates a maximally entangled state and yields a 33% shorter SWAP with higher interleaved randomized-benchmarking fidelity than matched-drive cross resonance. The same interaction produces two-spin squeezing beyond the standard quantum limit via two-axis countertwisting.
main_result: A 150-ns ZZ-tunable √bSWAP gate was demonstrated with faster, higher-fidelity SWAP synthesis than matched-drive cross resonance.
application_angle: The gate offers efficient routing, entanglement generation, and analog simulation of interacting spin systems in fixed-frequency superconducting processors.

title: Thermal activation of photon catalysis in difference-intensity Mach-Zehnder interferometry with squeezed thermal light
abstract: Realistic non-Gaussian operations, which can be implemented by mixing a nonclassical Gaussian state with a Fock state at a beam splitter and then heralding on a photon-number-resolving detector, are known to improve phase estimation in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The existing studies have considered the single-mode squeezed vacuum for difference-intensity and parity detection, and the two-mode squeezed thermal state for parity detection alone as the initial Gaussian resources. However, a real squeezer in the lab actually produces single-mode squeezed thermal light, which has not been studied in a coherent-plus-resource interferometer. We take up this case and using the phase space Wigner picture, we obtain the heralded state produced by photon subtraction, addition and catalysis on a single-mode squeezed thermal resource, and evaluate the corresponding phase sensitivities. Single-photon catalysis, which is useless on squeezed vacuum, becomes a useful operation for any thermal occupation above $\nth\simeq0.2$, and since it heralds with a probability near one-half, it turns out to be the best success-weighted operation over the whole thermal range. In the vacuum limit our results reproduce the known hierarchy, where two-photon catalysis is the best operation. The quantum Fisher information computations confirms that thermal noise enhances the phase information encoded in the catalyzed state, demonstrating that difference-intensity detection closely approaches the ultimate precision bound across most operational regimes, and, together with a loss analysis, verifies the robustness of the effect.
one_liner: Thermal occupation activates efficient single-photon catalysis for phase sensing with squeezed thermal light.
why_it_matters: It turns unavoidable squeezer thermal noise into enhanced phase information while retaining high heralding probability and loss robustness.
detailed_summary: The authors derive photon-subtracted, photon-added, and photon-catalyzed squeezed thermal states in a Wigner-phase-space treatment of Mach–Zehnder difference-intensity sensing. Single-photon catalysis becomes beneficial above a thermal occupation of about 0.2 and, with heralding probability near one-half, is the best success-weighted operation across the studied thermal range. Quantum Fisher information and loss calculations show that thermal noise can increase encoded phase information and that difference-intensity detection approaches the ultimate bound in most regimes.
platform_or_system: Mach–Zehnder interferometer with squeezed thermal light
main_result: Single-photon catalysis becomes the optimal success-weighted operation for nonzero thermal occupation and remains effective under loss.
application_angle: The result provides a realistic route to non-Gaussian-enhanced optical metrology using imperfect laboratory squeezers.

title: Loss-independent time-delay estimation via Hong-Ou-Mandel photon bunching detection
abstract: In this work we study the application of two-photon correlated quantum states for high-precision time estimation. To achieve this, photon pairs were fed into a Hong-Ou-Mandel polarization interferometer to generate N00N entangled states with $N = 2$. Two- and four-detector schemes were considered, and the achievable time estimation precision of each was studied, with particular emphasis on the system's Fisher information in each case. Our results reveal that using a four-detector scheme, enabling the measurement of both coincidence and photon-bunching terms, achieves the maximum precision given by the quantum Fisher information, without the need of characterizing system losses. We also show that correlations between repetitions arise due to systematic errors, limiting the precision enhancement that can be obtained by increasing the number of repetitions. Taking these correlations into account, we show that the four-detector scheme outperforms the two-detector scheme in the precision of time-delay estimation. With the experimentally determined calibration uncertainties, the four-detector scheme improves the dispersion by a factor of 2 for the repetitions performed, reaching up to a factor of 4 as both schemes approach their systematic floors.
one_liner: Detecting both coincidences and photon bunching enables loss-independent, quantum-limited Hong–Ou–Mandel delay estimation.
why_it_matters: The four-detector readout removes the need to calibrate loss and improves timing precision despite repetition-correlated systematic errors.
detailed_summary: Photon pairs are injected into a polarization Hong–Ou–Mandel interferometer to form N=2 N00N states, with two- and four-detector readouts compared. Recording both coincidence and bunching outcomes lets the four-detector scheme attain the quantum Fisher information without prior loss characterization. After accounting for systematic correlations between repetitions, it reduces the measured dispersion by a factor of two and is projected to reach a factor of four near the systematic floors.
main_result: Joint coincidence-and-bunching detection achieved loss-independent delay estimation at the quantum Fisher-information limit.
application_angle: The method can improve robust optical timing, ranging, synchronization, and dispersion measurements in lossy systems.

title: Bubble-Sort Exchange Networks: Symmetry Selection Rules and Language-Model Distillation on Exchange-Only Spin Chains
abstract: On a chain of exchange-coupled quantum dots a Heisenberg exchange pulse of area pi is a SWAP, so the parallel bubble-sort SWAP network of superconducting chains is native to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits, and any other pulse area fuses routing with an entangling interaction. We build a variational "bubble-sort exchange network" (odd-even transposition, one parameter per pulse) and study it as a Born machine read out by Pauli spin blockade. Exchange conserves total spin, so the reachable readout distributions are fixed by the total-spin content of the initial product state. For the two-spin singlet-triplet encoding we derive a selection rule -- outcomes with k triplet pairs are bounded by the initial weight in sectors S <= k (S = 0 excluded for k = 1) -- and prove by a transportation argument that it is also sufficient: the reachable distributions form the polytope cut out by the rule, and its total-variation floor is attained. Products of singlets and T0's forbid whole outcome classes; the Neel state forbids none; the three-spin EO code has no floor. We then distil, in noise-free simulation, next-token distributions of GPT-2 over restricted vocabularies into the network, with matrix-product-state (MPS) Born machines as classical control. At six logical qubits the three-spin chain reaches KL = 0.011 nat at depth N and 0.004 at 2N, below the bond-dimension-4 MPS; the two-spin chain from the Neel state reaches 0.014 at 2N and 0.004 at 3N, against 0.28-1.5 from singlet/triplet products for the first teacher. Final states lie largely outside the code space: leakage is a resource, not an error. No arrangement of disjoint pulses meets every pair in fewer than N-1 rounds, and at depth 2N the chain distils as well as a 2D array or non-local couplings. Sector-restricted simulation extends this to 10-14 logical qubits (up to 30 dots).
one_liner: Native exchange-pulse networks combine routing and entanglement for variational Born machines on spin-qubit chains.
why_it_matters: The work establishes exact reachability limits and shows shallow nearest-neighbor spin chains can distill language-model distributions competitively.
detailed_summary: The paper maps an odd-even bubble-sort network onto Heisenberg exchange pulses in quantum-dot chains, allowing each pulse to combine state routing with entanglement. It derives necessary and sufficient total-spin selection rules for two-spin singlet-triplet encodings and identifies the resulting total-variation floor. Noise-free simulations distill restricted-vocabulary GPT-2 next-token distributions with KL divergence as low as 0.004 nat, while sector-restricted calculations extend to 10–14 logical qubits and up to 30 dots.
main_result: A depth-2N to 3N exchange network distilled language-model distributions to 0.004-nat KL divergence while obeying exact spin-sector reachability bounds.
application_angle: The architecture provides a hardware-native variational model for near-term exchange-only processors using nearest-neighbor control and spin-blockade readout.

title: Operational Limits of Gravity-Mediated Entanglement
abstract: Tests of gravity-mediated entanglement aim to determine whether two massive objects in spatial superposition can become entangled through their mutual gravitational interaction. In an ideal model, the two objects are often treated as pointlike branches, but real wave packets have a finite width and are also exposed to dephasing and residual non-gravitational forces. We study these effects in a two-branch gravitational cat-state model with Gaussian wave packets. The Newtonian interaction is averaged over the finite wave-packet width, and spatially correlated dephasing is included phenomenologically. We then ask a practical question: when does the generated state remain useful rather than merely entangled? To answer this, we examine Bell violation, teleportation fidelity, coherent information, Fisher information, and state distinguishability. We find finite parameter windows where the same state is Bell-nonlocal and teleportation-useful, but these windows shrink as the wave packets become broader or the dephasing becomes stronger. We also show that a residual electrostatic branch interaction can coherently cancel the gravitational nonlocal phase and strongly suppress the operational signal. The results identify finite-width and electrostatic tolerance boundaries that should be considered in future tests of gravity-mediated entanglement.
one_liner: Finite wave-packet width, correlated dephasing, and electrostatic forces sharply constrain useful gravity-mediated entanglement.
why_it_matters: The analysis converts idealized entanglement proposals into experimental tolerance windows for Bell tests, teleportation, and information transfer.
detailed_summary: The study averages the Newtonian interaction over finite-width Gaussian wave packets in a two-branch gravitational cat-state model and includes spatially correlated dephasing. It evaluates Bell violation, teleportation fidelity, coherent information, Fisher information, and distinguishability rather than entanglement alone. Useful Bell-nonlocal and teleportation-capable regions shrink with packet width and dephasing, while residual electrostatic coupling can cancel the gravitational phase and suppress the signal.
main_result: The model identifies finite experimental windows for operationally useful gravitational entanglement and quantitative tolerances on wave-packet width, dephasing, and electrostatics.
application_angle: These bounds guide the design and systematic-error control of laboratory tests probing whether gravity can mediate quantum information.

title: Patchwork: automated lattice surgery and space-time partitioning for real-time decoding
abstract: We introduce patchwork, a lattice-surgery compiler for arbitrary multi-qubit Pauli measurements on a prescribed narrow-corridor two-dimensional surface-code layout. Systematic geometric rules simplify stabilizer placement and gate scheduling, including for logical $Y$ measurements implemented using twist defects. We introduce measurement circuits and schedules that, together with protruding lobes of $Y$-extension patches, preserve the full effective code distance for all numerically tested code distances. To support parallel decoding, we develop a wavefront algorithm that partitions merged lattice-surgery patches into space-time commit, buffer, and cleanup regions. Simulations of three sequential multi-qubit Pauli measurements acting on ten logical qubits show that staged decoding achieves total failure probabilities close to those of monolithic decoding over the parameters tested. These methods provide an automated framework for fault-tolerant lattice surgery and a route toward scalable, real-time decoding.
one_liner: Patchwork automates distance-preserving lattice surgery and partitions decoding into real-time space-time regions.
why_it_matters: It addresses two scaling bottlenecks at once: compiling arbitrary Pauli measurements and decoding large merged surface-code patches in parallel.
detailed_summary: Patchwork compiles arbitrary multi-qubit Pauli measurements onto a narrow-corridor two-dimensional surface-code layout using systematic geometry and scheduling rules. Its Y-measurement circuits use twist defects and protruding extension lobes that preserve full effective distance for all tested code distances. A wavefront algorithm divides merged patches into commit, buffer, and cleanup regions, and simulations on ten logical qubits find staged-decoding failure rates close to monolithic decoding.
main_result: Automated lattice-surgery compilation and wavefront-partitioned decoding preserved code distance and closely matched monolithic-decoder failure rates in simulation.
application_angle: The framework supports scalable fault-tolerant control by enabling automated surgery layouts and parallel, low-latency decoding.

title: Frequency comb stability, bistability, and self-starting in normal dispersion microresonators
abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that it is possible to generate frequency combs in normal dispersion microresonators by taking advantage of fabricated mode coupling that induces a mode split. In particular, photonic crystal resonators periodically modulate the microresonator's width, which geometrically creates mode coupling. In contrast to frequency combs generated by microresonators in the anomalous dispersion regime, which are typically generated using bright solitons, the frequency combs generated by normal dispersion regime microresonators are dark pulses that are commonly referred to as dark solitons or platicons. In this work, we examine the linear stability of platicons in the pump-detuning and pump-power parameter space as the mode split strength and cavity dispersion is varied. Our work reveals a broad region of stability for platicons. Our work also reveals the existence of fingers at high power at whose boundaries a sharp transition occurs and inside of which platicon solutions are bistable. Finally, we investigate the overlap of the region where platicons are stable with the region where continuous waves are modulationally unstable, and it is possible for a platicon to self-start. Simulations show that platicons consistently self-start inside this region.
one_liner: Stability maps identify broad operating regions for self-starting dark-pulse frequency combs in normal-dispersion microresonators.
why_it_matters: The results give practical design and operating guidance for robust normal-dispersion microcombs without requiring deterministic external pulse initiation.
detailed_summary: The authors map platicon linear stability across pump detuning and power while varying engineered mode splitting and cavity dispersion. They find a broad stable region plus high-power fingers whose boundaries show sharp transitions and whose interiors support bistable platicon solutions. Simulations indicate consistent self-starting where platicon stability overlaps continuous-wave modulational instability.
main_result: The study identifies broad stable and bistable platicon regimes and a parameter region in which dark-pulse combs consistently self-start.
application_angle: The stability maps can guide the design and control of robust integrated frequency-comb sources for metrology, communications, and spectroscopy.

title: Connectivity Bounds for GHZ Graphs
abstract: Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states are multipartite entangled quantum states that play a central role in quantum information theory, with applications in quantum communication, cryptography, and distributed quantum computing. A major experimental goal is to create high-dimensional GHZ states using multiple entangled parties. Krenn, Gu and Zeilinger discovered a surprising bridge between these quantum-optical experiments and graph theory: certain photonic experiments can be represented by edge-coloured, edge-weighted graphs, and the dimension of the produced GHZ state equals the number of feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings. This led Krenn and Gu to conjecture that every GHZ graph with more than four vertices has dimension at most $2$. A counterexample would give a new high-dimensional multipartite GHZ construction, while a proof would clarify fundamental resource limitations in quantum optics. It is known that the conjecture holds for graphs of vertex connectivity at most $2$ [MFCS 2024], and that simple GHZ graphs with $n>4$ vertices have dimension less than $n/\sqrt{2}$ [Quantum 2024]. However, no general upper bound depending only on vertex connectivity was known. We prove that every simple connected GHZ graph $G$ with at least four vertices has dimension at most $2^{κ(G)-1}+\binom{κ(G)}{2}$, where $κ(G)$ is the vertex connectivity of $G$. We also prove new bounds in terms of edge connectivity and maximum degree.
one_liner: Graph-connectivity bounds constrain the dimensionality of photonic GHZ states obtainable from edge-coloured optical experiment graphs.
why_it_matters: The bounds clarify how optical-network connectivity limits high-dimensional multipartite entanglement for communication and distributed quantum processing.
detailed_summary: The work studies graph representations in which feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings determine the dimension of a photonic GHZ state. It proves that a simple connected GHZ graph with at least four vertices has dimension at most 2^(κ−1)+C(κ,2), where κ is vertex connectivity. Additional bounds are derived using edge connectivity and maximum degree.
main_result: A general upper bound links achievable GHZ dimension to graph vertex connectivity, supplemented by bounds involving edge connectivity and degree.
application_angle: These constraints help assess whether proposed optical networks can generate the high-dimensional GHZ resources required by quantum networking protocols.

title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation
abstract: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.
one_liner: A system-level energy model projects roughly 100 kW for a fault-tolerant silicon spin-qubit computer with one million physical qubits.
why_it_matters: It identifies instrumentation, decoding, cryogenic cooling, and control demultiplexing as decisive engineering levers for energy-efficient quantum scaling.
detailed_summary: The authors construct an energy budget for Loss–DiVincenzo spin-qubit hardware and compare quantum Fourier transforms with classical FFTs. After incorporating surface-code cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding, they find that instrumentation and decoding dominate at scale while cooling constrains scalability. Optimizing control-signal demultiplexing is projected to lower total energy by about two orders of magnitude.
main_result: The model estimates about 100 kW for one million physical qubits and predicts an energy crossover before the execution-time crossover for polynomial sampling workloads.
application_angle: The analysis provides quantitative targets for cryogenic systems, control multiplexing, and decoders in large fault-tolerant spin-qubit machines.

title: Classification of bipartite observables III: simplicity, mixtures and quantum error correction
abstract: The paradigm of a simple unstable theory in the sense of Shelah is the theory of the random graph, the Fraïssé limit of the finite graphs. Quantum error correction has a paradigm of its own, and we show that it is the counterpart of the random graph: the Pauli group on countably many qubits, taken modulo phases and with commutation as its relation, is the Fraïssé limit of the finite alternating spaces over the two-element field, and its form computes the syndromes of stabilizer codes. Seen through this correspondence, simplicity theory turns out to be a theory of error correction. Clifford encoding circuits implement the homogeneity of the Pauli group, forking recognizes the logical errors, and the independence theorem of Kim and Pillay is the gluing of syndromes. The two paradigms look alike as first-order structures, and they part company only when observables enter. Each defines a bipartite observable, and we prove that, once preparations are mixed, both acquire the tree property of the second kind in real-valued logic. They reach it by different roads, however, and we show that the probes decide which. The probes of the Pauli observable are the Pauli channels; for them the indicator of each syndrome sector is the difference of the responses of two uniform mixtures, and actual mixtures already witness the tree. The probes of the Rado observable see only marginals; conditions given by actual mixtures remain compatible on disjoint blocks, and the tree must be sought among idealized preparations.
one_liner: A model-theoretic correspondence recasts stabilizer error correction through Pauli commutation, syndromes, Clifford encoding, and logical errors.
why_it_matters: Although theoretical, the framework offers a new structural language for reasoning about stabilizer codes, Pauli noise, and syndrome composition.
detailed_summary: The paper identifies the countable Pauli group modulo phases, equipped with commutation, as the Fraïssé limit of finite alternating spaces over the binary field. Under this correspondence, the alternating form computes stabilizer syndromes, Clifford encoders realize homogeneity, and forking captures logical errors. It further shows that mixed preparations give both Pauli and Rado bipartite observables the tree property of the second kind, though their physical probes distinguish the mechanisms.
main_result: The authors establish a precise correspondence between simplicity-theoretic structures and stabilizer quantum error correction, including operational roles for syndromes and Pauli channels.
application_angle: The abstraction may support new ways to classify code behavior and compose syndrome constraints, but it does not present an experimental hardware demonstration.

title: Programmable all-to-all entangling gates for cavity-coupled atoms
abstract: Fault tolerant quantum computers greatly benefit from having both high fidelity entangling gates and a non-local qubit connectivity. However, most entangling gates for neutral atoms are local, requiring separated atoms to be moved using optical tweezers to yield entanglement between them. Here, we design a high fidelity Mølmer Sørensen-like entangling gate between neutral atoms coupled to a photonic cavity, enabling a programmable all-to-all connectivity through the shared cavity coupling. The gate is both robust to changes in cavity photon number, and enables selective entanglement between any subset of separated atoms through local laser addressing. This eliminates the need to physically move atoms to perform the gate, and therefore motional errors and erasure are suppressed. Using experimentally realistic parameters we demonstrate gate fidelities exceeding $F > 0.99$, with higher fidelities achievable through optimal control of the pump amplitudes.
one_liner: A cavity-mediated Mølmer–Sørensen-like gate enables programmable all-to-all entanglement among selectively addressed neutral atoms.
why_it_matters: The scheme could remove atom-shuttling overhead and associated motional errors while retaining nonlocal, subset-selective entangling operations.
detailed_summary: The proposal uses a shared photonic cavity to mediate a Mølmer–Sørensen-like interaction between spatially separated neutral atoms. Local laser addressing selects arbitrary atom subsets, while the gate is designed to tolerate variations in cavity photon number. Simulations with experimentally realistic parameters yield fidelities above 0.99, with further gains available from pump-amplitude optimal control.
main_result: The designed gate provides programmable all-to-all, subset-selective entanglement with simulated fidelities exceeding 0.99 under realistic parameters.
application_angle: Avoiding physical atom transport could improve circuit speed and suppress motional error and erasure in scalable neutral-atom processors.

title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.
one_liner: SynDebug adds encoded assertions to fault-tolerant quantum programs with 1.8% average depth overhead and no measured logical-error penalty.
why_it_matters: Practical systems-level debugging is essential for validating complex QEC control stacks and encoded workloads before large-scale FTQC deployment.
detailed_summary: SynDebug introduces assertion primitives that execute inside encoded fault-tolerant infrastructures without adding logical surface area. The framework is evaluated across multiple QEC code families, distances, and workloads covering state preparation, entanglement checks, and Shor-style programs. It reports 1.8% average added circuit depth, zero overhead in most cases, and no measurable increase in logical error rate.
main_result: SynDebug demonstrates low-overhead assertion-based debugging across several QEC codes and encoded applications without a measurable logical-error increase.
application_angle: The framework could accelerate bring-up, verification, and diagnosis of programs running on future fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

title: Classical Capacity of Single-Mode Bosonic Gaussian Channels
abstract: The classical capacity of a noisy optical channel is the maximum rate at which information can be transmitted reliably, given a constraint on the mean input energy. For the ubiquitous bosonic Gaussian channels, which include standard models of loss and noise in fibre and free-space optical links, determining this rate requires addressing whether entanglement between channel uses or non-Gaussian signals can outperform Gaussian encodings. More precisely, the question is whether the energy-constrained Holevo information is additive across arbitrarily many channel uses and coincides with its Gaussian counterpart. We answer these fundamental questions in the affirmative for every single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel at every input energy. Namely, we prove that independently prepared Gaussian states with Gaussian-distributed random displacements achieve the capacity, including in the low-energy regime where squeezing the signals competes with encoding information in their displacement. Our proof connects an entanglement inequality to a sharp, additive lower bound on output entropy. We then characterise communication above capacity: under a strict total photon-number cutoff, the probability of correct decoding decreases exponentially with the number of channel uses, and we derive explicit bounds on the decay exponent. When only the mean photon number is constrained, a simple energy-rescaling formula determines exactly the entire asymptotic rate--error trade-off: the capacity at mean photon number $N$ and allowed average decoding error $ε$ equals the vanishing-error capacity at mean photon number $N/(1-ε)$. Together, these results identify the ultimate limits of classical communication for some of the most fundamental models of optical communication.
one_liner: The classical capacity of every energy-constrained single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel is achieved by independent Gaussian encoding.
why_it_matters: The result settles the ultimate classical data rates and above-capacity error behavior of fundamental models for fiber and free-space optical links.
detailed_summary: The authors prove additivity of the energy-constrained Holevo information for every single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel and show that Gaussian-modulated, independently prepared Gaussian states achieve capacity at all energies. They also establish exponential decoding failure above capacity under a strict photon-number cutoff. With only a mean-energy constraint, they derive the exact asymptotic rate-error trade-off through an energy-rescaling relation.
main_result: Independent Gaussian encodings achieve the full classical capacity, with explicit characterizations of communication above capacity.
application_angle: The bounds provide definitive performance targets for classical communication over lossy and noisy fiber or free-space quantum-optical links.

title: Magna: simulating magic state factories as cheaply as Clifford circuits
abstract: Classical simulation of magic state factories, including distillation, cultivation, and code switching, is challenging because of their substantial non-Clifford content. We introduce $\texttt{magna}$ (magic-state-factory assessment via global network algebra), a classical simulator that simulates such protocols as cheaply as Clifford circuits. $\texttt{magna}$ expresses the figures of merit of a protocol, namely the acceptance rate and the fidelity of the accepted states, as tensor networks, which it reduces globally by exploiting a structural correspondence with transversal gates on quantum codes. $\texttt{magna}$ further supports feedforward conditioned on arbitrary functions of mid-circuit measurement outcomes, including decoder outputs. We simulate Bravyi--Haah distillation with up to 100 output magic states at a cost that does not grow exponentially in the number of outputs, and achieve state-of-the-art sampling times for distance-5 magic state cultivation on both color codes and RP$^2$ surface codes. Finally, we validate nonlinear feedforward on a logical-level distillation protocol with 15 rounds of decoder-dependent feedforward. $\texttt{magna}$ aims to contribute to the key infrastructure for the large-scale evaluation and optimization of magic state factories.
one_liner: Magna evaluates complex magic-state factories with simulation costs comparable to those of Clifford circuits.
why_it_matters: Efficiently predicting acceptance and output fidelity can accelerate the design of fault-tolerant quantum computers without prohibitive classical simulation.
detailed_summary: Magna represents magic-state-factory acceptance rates and accepted-state fidelities as tensor networks and reduces them globally using a correspondence with transversal code gates. It supports feedforward based on arbitrary functions of mid-circuit outcomes, including decoder outputs. Demonstrations include Bravyi–Haah distillation with up to 100 output states, distance-5 cultivation, and 15 rounds of nonlinear decoder-dependent feedforward.
main_result: The simulator handles large non-Clifford factory protocols without simulation cost growing exponentially with the number of output magic states.
application_angle: It enables scalable assessment and optimization of the factories that supply non-Clifford resources to fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Projected sensitivity of a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate comagnetometer to proton monopole-dipole interactions
abstract: Light spin-zero bosons with scalar and pseudoscalar couplings mediate a parity- and time-reversal-violating monopole-dipole interaction between unpolarized matter and polarized spins. For proton spins, the interaction has been probed directly only at ranges $λ\gtrsim$ 5 mm; below this range, laboratory limits are inferred from neutron-dominated nuclei through nuclear-spin models. We analyze a direct search with a single-domain $^{87}$Rb spinor Bose-Einstein condensate in close proximity to a source mass. The F=1 and F=2 manifolds act as two co-located magnetometers that precess in opposite directions in a magnetic field but in the same direction under the exotic interaction. They thus form a natural comagnetometer, in which the sum of their precession angles suppresses field noise by a measured 44 dB and a weighted sum cancels the field altogether. Taking as a starting point the demonstrated magnetometry [Palacios et al. Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. \textbf{119}, e2115339119 (2022)] and comagnetometry [Gomez et al. Phys. Ref. Lett. \textbf{124}, 170401 (2020)] performance of the $^{87}$Rb single-domain spinor condensate at ICFO [Palacios et al. New J. Phys. \textbf{20}, 053008 (2018)], we study the projected sensitivity as a function of source-mass geometry and in-progress improvements to atom loading methods, trap beam geometry, and magnetic environment. With an insulating bismuth germanate source mass with a spherical top, whose apex sits 50 $μ$m below the center of the condensate, one week of acquisition would reach $|g_s^N g_p^p|\approx 2\times10^{-22}$ with these upgrades and $3\times10^{-24}$ at the projection-noise limit ($λ=100\, μ$m, 95\% C.L.). This is more than three and five orders of magnitude below existing laboratory limits. The improvement covers boson masses of 0.3-50 meV/c$^2$ after the upgrades and 0.09-70 meV/c$^2$ at the projection-noise limit.
one_liner: A dual-manifold spinor-BEC comagnetometer could directly probe proton monopole-dipole forces at previously inaccessible ranges.
why_it_matters: The projected search improves direct laboratory limits by three to five orders of magnitude for short-range, symmetry-violating interactions.
detailed_summary: The proposal uses the F=1 and F=2 manifolds of a single-domain 87Rb spinor condensate as co-located magnetometers with opposite magnetic-field response but common exotic-force response. Their summed precession suppresses magnetic noise by a demonstrated 44 dB, while a weighted sum can cancel it. With a bismuth-germanate source 50 μm from the condensate, one week of data is projected to reach |g_s^N g_p^p| near 2×10^-22 after upgrades and 3×10^-24 at the projection-noise limit for λ=100 μm.
main_result: The projected experiment offers direct proton-coupling sensitivity three to five orders of magnitude beyond existing laboratory bounds.
application_angle: The sensor would directly test new parity- and time-reversal-violating forces mediated by light spin-zero bosons.

title: Stability of Quantum LDPC States under Local Pauli Noise
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have a canonical mixed state---the normalized projector onto the code space---that lies at the intersection of quantum error correction and quantum many-body physics, yet the stability of its information-theoretic structure under local noise remains poorly understood. Recent progress on mixed-state phases of matter has identified the spatial decay of conditional mutual information (CMI) $I(A:C|B)$ as a key diagnostic of such stability, analogous to the role of the spectral gap for quantum ground states. We prove that, for the normalized code-projector state of a $\mathbb{Z}_d$ qLDPC stabilizer code under local Pauli noise, the CMI across a buffer $B$ separating $A$ from $C$ decays exponentially with the width of $B$ in two complementary noise regimes independent of system size. At weak noise, this holds for full-system tripartitions, where correlations between the two sides require an error cluster to cross the buffer, an exponentially unlikely event. At strong noise, exponential decay holds whenever the buffer supports no logical operator, since correlations can persist only along rare chains of buffer qudits that remain informative. Under an additional space-uniformity assumption, we establish the robustness of Levin--Wen topological entropy. On finite-dimensional lattices of size $n$, the weak-noise bound further implies a constant-layer quasi-local Petz recovery channel of range $O(\poly(\log n)/\varepsilon)$ that recovers the noiseless state within trace-distance error $\varepsilon$. Both CMI bounds apply to general qLDPC interaction graphs, including geometries where such constant-depth quasi-local recovery need not exist. Thus, the exponential decay of the noise-induced CMI provides a general criterion for mixed-state phase stability.
one_liner: Quantum-LDPC code-projector states retain exponentially localized information correlations under both weak and strong local Pauli noise.
why_it_matters: The bounds connect error-correcting-code structure to mixed-state phase stability and identify conditions for efficient quasi-local recovery.
detailed_summary: For Z_d qLDPC stabilizer codes, the authors prove that conditional mutual information across a separating buffer decays exponentially with buffer width in complementary weak- and strong-noise regimes. The strong-noise result requires that the buffer support no logical operator, while an added uniformity assumption preserves Levin–Wen topological entropy. On finite-dimensional lattices, the weak-noise bound yields a constant-layer quasi-local Petz recovery channel with polylogarithmic range dependence.
main_result: System-size-independent exponential CMI decay is established under local Pauli noise, together with quasi-local recovery guarantees on finite-dimensional lattices.
application_angle: These criteria can guide the design and validation of quantum memories whose encoded information and topological structure remain stable under local noise.

title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
abstract: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.
one_liner: Evaluator-guided LLM evolution discovers reversible quantum circuits that improve resource counts across diverse computational primitives.
why_it_matters: Lower Toffoli and qubit requirements could materially reduce the hardware overhead of useful fault-tolerant quantum algorithms.
detailed_summary: The framework lets large language models propose circuit designs while an independent evaluator verifies correctness and scores quantum resources. It reduces both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to prior best designs in seven of eight tasks spanning chemistry, simulation, optimization, numerical methods, and number theory. For the remaining task, it discovers a reversible prime-field modular-inversion architecture that makes the classical divsteps method practical in a quantum circuit.
main_result: The search improves state-of-the-art Toffoli and qubit counts in seven tasks and finds a new modular-inversion architecture in the eighth.
application_angle: Automated circuit co-design can reduce logical-resource demands before algorithms are mapped onto costly fault-tolerant hardware.

title: Exploring Quantum Phase Transitions Beyond Landau Theory on a Quantum Processor
abstract: Direct continuous quantum phase transitions between phases that break distinct symmetries challenge the conventional Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm and provide a framework for deconfined quantum criticality. Here, we investigate a Landau-forbidden ferromagnetic-to-valence-bond-solid (FM-VBS) transition in a frustrated one-dimensional spin chain using superconducting quantum processors. Combining matrix-product-state-assisted circuit preparation with quantum-hardware measurements, we resolve the suppression of long-range ferromagnetic correlations and the redistribution of competing-order fluctuations across the transition. Distance-resolved correlations and finite-size analyses reveal signatures consistent with critical behavior. We further extend our investigation to nonequilibrium dynamics, directly preparing dimerized states and tracking the evolution of VBS order and joint FM-VBS fluctuations under local unitary interactions. Our results establish a versatile quantum-hardware framework for probing competing orders, critical correlations, and many-body dynamics beyond conventional Landau theory.
one_liner: Superconducting processors probe a Landau-forbidden ferromagnetic-to-valence-bond-solid transition and its nonequilibrium dynamics.
why_it_matters: The experiment expands quantum processors from computation platforms into controllable probes of unconventional criticality and competing many-body orders.
detailed_summary: The experiment studies a frustrated one-dimensional spin chain using matrix-product-state-assisted circuit preparation and measurements on superconducting quantum hardware. Distance-resolved correlations and finite-size analyses track the loss of ferromagnetic order and redistribution of valence-bond-solid fluctuations near the transition. The team also prepares dimerized states and follows VBS order and joint FM–VBS fluctuations during local-unitary dynamics.
main_result: The processor resolves signatures consistent with a direct FM–VBS critical transition and tracks competing-order dynamics out of equilibrium.
application_angle: The approach provides a hardware-based route to studying unconventional quantum materials and benchmarking analog-digital many-body simulation.

title: Resonant pair production and flat band melting in a driven Rydberg chain
abstract: We study a Rydberg chain subjected to a two-tone periodic drive of the detuning $Δ(t)$ and Rabi frequency $Ω(t)$ at frequencies $ω_1$ and $ω_2=νω_1$ respectively with $ν\in \mathbf{Z}$. In the strong Rydberg blockade limit, such a system reduces to the PXP model and exhibits exact Floquet flat band. Here we determine, using a time-dependent Schrieffer-Wolff transformation, the domain of validity of such PXP dynamics once the blockade-violating processes are taken into account. We study the melting of such flat bands in the presence of strong, but finite, blockade strength. Using Floquet perturbation theory (FPT), we identify two mechanisms for such melting; the first occurs due to the presence of many-body resonances involving resonant production of nearest-neighbor Rydberg excitation pairs while the second involves virtual processes that access intermediate states with such pairs. Our analytical FPT results match with those obtained using exact diagonalization on a finite chain. We study the dynamics for $|{\rm vac}\rangle$ (Fock state with no Rydberg excitation), $|{\mathbb {Z}}_2\rangle$, and $|{\mathbb {Z}}_3\rangle$ (Fock states with Rydberg excitations on alternate and every third site respectively) initial states. We find that $|{\rm vac}\rangle$ shows exceptional stability against resonant pair formation while $|{\mathbb {Z}}_3\rangle$ exhibits flat band melting via virtual processes away from the direct resonances. We find oscillatory dynamics with large time period for the $|{\mathbb {Z}}_2\rangle$ initial state and the presence of Floquet scars that have large overlap with $|{\mathbb {Z}}_3\rangle$ state; these phenomena occur due to processes that are absent in the PXP limit. We propose measurement of nearest neighbor pair correlation functions using Rydberg atom quantum simulator platforms as an accessible experimental probe for these effects.
one_liner: Finite-blockade processes create resonant Rydberg pairs, melt Floquet flat bands, and generate scarred dynamics beyond the ideal PXP model.
why_it_matters: The work identifies experimentally measurable limits and signatures of constrained Floquet dynamics in programmable Rydberg-atom quantum simulators.
detailed_summary: A time-dependent Schrieffer-Wolff treatment and Floquet perturbation theory quantify when a strongly blockaded, two-tone-driven Rydberg chain departs from the PXP limit. Flat bands melt through direct resonant production of adjacent Rydberg pairs and through virtual pair-containing states, with analytical predictions matching finite-chain exact diagonalization. Vacuum, Z2, and Z3 product states show markedly different stability, long-period oscillations, and scar overlaps.
main_result: The study identifies direct and virtual blockade-violating mechanisms that melt Floquet flat bands and predicts state-dependent dynamical signatures.
application_angle: Nearest-neighbor pair-correlation measurements provide an accessible way to diagnose nonideal blockade physics in Rydberg quantum simulators.

title: Two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg transition for quantum sensing in ytterbium
abstract: Here we report atomic structure calculations and experimental observations of the two-photon $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ transition in Yb. The unique level structure of Yb places the $6s6p\;^1P_1$ state's energy at $\approx\!49.7\%$ of the ionization energy, which facilitates two-photon Doppler-free excitation of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg state from the $6s^2\;^1S_0$ ground state at a relatively low optical intensity. This $J= 0 \rightarrow J=0$ transition is immune to first-order Zeeman and electric quadrupole shifts, has reduced sensitivity to higher-order Zeeman shifts, and is further predicted to have relatively low sensitivity to density shifts. Using configuration interaction theory, we compute relevant properties of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg state for sensing, including the $C_6$ coefficient, dc polarizability, blackbody radiation (BBR) shift, and BBR depopulation rate. As a first experimental step, we demonstrate two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ transition. From our experimental spectra, we estimate the natural linewidth (lifetime) of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ state to be 90 kHz (1.8 $μ$s). We believe this transition, or other $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6sns\;^1S_0$ transitions in Yb with $n\approx23$, may find use in a variety of sensing applications, potentially including a two-photon clock, electrometer, or BBR thermometer.
one_liner: Doppler-free two-photon spectroscopy accesses a field-insensitive ytterbium Rydberg transition with an estimated 90 kHz natural linewidth.
why_it_matters: The J=0 to J=0 transition combines modest excitation intensity with low field sensitivity, supporting compact clocks, electrometers, and BBR sensors.
detailed_summary: The authors calculate the C6 coefficient, dc polarizability, blackbody-radiation shift, and BBR depopulation rate of the Yb 6s23s singlet Rydberg state using configuration interaction theory. They then experimentally demonstrate Doppler-free two-photon excitation from the 6s2 ground state. Spectra yield an estimated natural linewidth of 90 kHz, corresponding to a 1.8 microsecond lifetime.
main_result: A Doppler-free, low-intensity two-photon route to a magnetically insensitive Yb Rydberg state is experimentally demonstrated.
application_angle: The transition is a candidate reference for two-photon clocks, electric-field sensing, and blackbody-radiation thermometry.

title: Ultra-stable laser with sub-Hz intrinsic linewidth using a silicon photonic chip
abstract: Here, we demonstrate a novel optical self-injection-locking scheme integrated with a modulation-free laser frequency stabilization technique co-integrated with a compact vacuum-gap micro-Fabry-Perot cavity (uFP), with Q-factor of 3.46E9, to realize an ultra-stable laser with sub-Hz fundamental linewidth using a silicon photonic chip. The demonstrated electro-optic self-injection locking (EOSIL) chip suppresses a commercial DFB diode laser's frequency noise power spectral density by more than 110 dB at 1 Hz offset, approaching the theoretical thermal noise limit of the uFP cavity, and enables a laser fundamental linewidth of 58 mHz with a fractional frequency instability of 8.68E-13 at 1 sec averaging time. The chip is fabricated using the Advanced Micro Foundry standard silicon photonic process and occupies a footprint of 10 mm^2.
one_liner: A 10 mm² silicon-photonic stabilization chip narrows a commercial DFB laser to a reported 58 mHz fundamental linewidth.
why_it_matters: Foundry-compatible integration of extreme laser stability could shrink precision optical references for sensing, clocks, coherent links, and quantum systems.
detailed_summary: The system combines electro-optic self-injection locking with modulation-free frequency stabilization and a vacuum-gap micro-Fabry-Perot cavity having a reported Q factor of 3.46 billion. It suppresses the frequency-noise power spectral density of a commercial DFB diode by more than 110 dB at 1 Hz offset. The reported fundamental linewidth is 58 mHz, with fractional frequency instability of 8.68×10^-13 at one-second averaging.
main_result: The integrated system achieves a reported 58 mHz intrinsic linewidth and approaches the microcavity thermal-noise limit.
application_angle: The compact, standard-foundry implementation supports deployable precision lasers for metrology, coherent communications, and quantum instrumentation.

title: Area Theorems for Quantum Error Correction
abstract: The extrinsic information transfer (EXIT) and generalized EXIT (GEXIT) area theorems provide fundamental conservation laws that connect the rate of classical codes to the performance of maximum-a-posteriori decoding on binary memoryless channels. In this work, we generalize these area theorems to quantum error correction. We first develop a coset-entropy formalism for nested linear codes, where the message specifies a coset and encoder randomization selects a codeword within that coset. The area under the resulting coset (G)EXIT function equals the normalized dimension of the quotient. For stabilizer codes, the measured syndrome restricts the Pauli error but does not always determine its logical effect, and the remaining uncertainty is an entropy over logical correction classes. We show that this entropy equals a classical coset entropy associated with the stabilizer group and the Pauli operators that commute with it. The resulting quantum GEXIT function has area equal to the number of encoded qubits per channel use for any stabilizer code, and this applies to the depolarizing channel through its joint four-valued Pauli-error distribution. For CSS codes on the quantum erasure channel and under independent bit- and phase-flip noise, the logical correction problem separates into two binary coset-decoding problems. On the quantum erasure channel, the duality between the stabilizer group and the Pauli operators that commute with it gives a folding identity at complementary erasure probabilities. Using this and the area theorem, we derive an upper bound on the rate of code families with vanishing logical error probability that matches the capacity of the quantum erasure channel. For the depolarizing channel, we also derive a rate-dependent converse, using a connection between correction-class entropy and coherent information to establish an inequality involving the complementary channel.
one_liner: Quantum GEXIT area theorems connect stabilizer-code rate to logical-correction uncertainty and yield channel converse bounds.
why_it_matters: The framework supplies analytical limits for quantum-code design and decoding, including a capacity-matching bound for the erasure channel.
detailed_summary: The paper maps residual uncertainty over logical Pauli correction classes to a classical coset entropy for stabilizer codes. The resulting quantum GEXIT curve has area equal to the number of encoded qubits per channel use, including for joint four-valued Pauli errors on the depolarizing channel. For CSS codes, the framework separates bit and phase decoding and produces a capacity-matching rate upper bound on the quantum erasure channel.
main_result: A quantum area theorem is derived that relates integrated logical-correction uncertainty to code rate and establishes rate-dependent converse bounds.
application_angle: These bounds can guide code-family and decoder evaluation for fault-tolerant processors and quantum communication links.

title: Metric and Dispersive Dynamics of Phase Perturbations in Bohmian Quantum Mechanics
abstract: By linearizing the hydrodynamic equations associated with the Madelung transformation in the context of Bohmian dynamics, we derive an effective metric for the phase perturbation around a background state. We show that the metric previously obtained previously by the same authors arises naturally as a particular case of a more general structure, in which the complete functional variation of the quantum potential is retained and external classical potentials can be incorporated. This generalization preserves the dependence of the quantum potential on the density and its spatial derivatives, generating additional terms that introduce dispersive corrections and act as sources in the effective Klein-Gordon equation. To organize these contributions, we introduce differential operators that separate the local sector responsible for the effective geometry from the corrections associated with the complete functional structure of the quantum potential. We identify the conditions under which these additional terms become negligible, recovering homogeneous propagation and the effective geometry for the Gaussian wave packet of a free particle.
one_liner: Linearized Bohmian hydrodynamics yields an effective metric plus dispersive and source corrections from the full quantum potential.
why_it_matters: The theory clarifies when phase perturbations admit an effective geometric description, but it does not demonstrate a photonic device or experiment.
detailed_summary: The authors retain the complete functional variation of the Bohmian quantum potential while linearizing Madelung hydrodynamics around a background state. They separate the local terms defining an effective metric from derivative-dependent corrections that introduce dispersion and sources into an effective Klein-Gordon equation. Conditions are identified under which these corrections vanish, recovering homogeneous propagation for a freely evolving Gaussian wave packet.
main_result: The work generalizes the effective-metric description of phase perturbations by explicitly deriving quantum-potential-induced dispersion and source terms.
application_angle: The formalism may support analogue-gravity modeling, although no direct quantum-photonic hardware or sensing application is established.

title: Programmable Preparation of Topological Entangled States
abstract: Programmable preparation of entangled quantum states is a central requirement for scalable quantum information processing, quantum networking and photonic quantum computing. Topological photonic platforms offer an attractive route towards robust quantum-state generation by encoding information in symmetry- protected optical modes, yet the generated entangled states are typically dictated by the lattice geometry and therefore lack programmability. Here we demonstrate programmable preparation of topological entangled states by inverse engineering the nonlinear optical pump profile of an integrated photonic lattice. Our approach enables deterministic control over both the dimensionality and modal structure of the generated entangled state while preserving its topological character. We experimentally realize silicon photonic topological superlattices in which the nonlinear generation pathway itself becomes programmable via tailored excitations. The superlattices host a multiband manifold of co localized topological interface modes, while coherently controlled inputs synthesize pump superpositions within this protected basis. We showcase this principle by selectively addressing topological biphoton eigenstates, steering correlations to produce a desired target state in a high-dimensional Hilbert space, and inverse-designing pump states that generate targeted Schmidt dimensionalities. Site-resolved two-photon correlation measurements remain reproducible across nominally identical fabricated devices, demonstrating robustness to realistic nanofabrication-induced disorder. Programmable preparation of topological entangled states establishes a pathway towards exploiting topological photonic modes as application-specific quantum resources, enabling tailored input states for high-dimensional quantum communication, quantum networking and photonic quantum computing.
one_liner: Inverse-designed pump profiles program high-dimensional topological biphoton states in silicon photonic superlattices.
why_it_matters: The experiment combines programmable entanglement dimensionality with disorder-robust topological modes for scalable photonic quantum technologies.
detailed_summary: Silicon photonic superlattices provide co-localized multiband topological interface modes, while coherent pump superpositions control nonlinear photon-pair generation within that protected basis. The experiment selectively addresses biphoton eigenstates, steers spatial correlations toward target states, and inverse-designs pumps for chosen Schmidt dimensionalities. Site-resolved correlation measurements are reproducible across nominally identical devices despite fabrication disorder.
main_result: Programmable pump synthesis deterministically controls the modal structure and Schmidt dimensionality of topological biphoton states.
application_angle: The approach enables tailored, robust high-dimensional entangled resources for quantum networking, communication, and photonic computing.

title: Development of a fabrication-to-benchtop process for SiN-based quantum devices
abstract: Silicon nitride has emerged as a key material for the advancement of future quantum communication and computational devices.
