However, challenges persist in establishing a comprehensive development process, spanning from fabrication to optical characterization, essential for advancing these devices to their next stage of potential. Maintaining control over the entire process, from start to finish, alongside device modeling, enables more efficient and timely iteration and optimization. Here we introduce a fabrication-to-benchtop process. We employ an in-house stoichiometric recipe for device fabrication and conduct comprehensive characterization of optical losses and material properties. Understanding and controlling the refractive index of the device are vital for predicting device geometries and group indices. Implementing the refractive indices of our fabricated devices, we simulate microring resonators and demonstrate their application in generating optical solitons.
one_liner: An end-to-end SiN workflow links in-house fabrication and optical characterization to microring design and soliton generation.
why_it_matters: Closing the loop between measured material properties, device simulation, and benchtop testing can accelerate reproducible quantum-photonic device development.
detailed_summary: The authors establish a fabrication-to-benchtop workflow for stoichiometric silicon-nitride photonic devices. They characterize optical losses and refractive-index properties, then incorporate the measured indices into microring-resonator simulations. The resulting devices are used to demonstrate optical-soliton generation.
main_result: The work demonstrates an internally controlled process from SiN fabrication and material characterization through predictive microring modeling and optical-soliton generation.
application_angle: The workflow supports faster iteration of integrated sources and resonators for quantum communication and photonic information processing.

title: Chirality-resolved imaging of spin waves with a quantum spin
abstract: Spin waves carry their propagation direction in the handedness of their circularly polarized stray field, a property inaccessible to scalar magnetometers. In the Damon-Eshbach surface wave of an in-plane magnetized film, the dipolar field above the film rotates with a handedness fixed by the direction of travel. The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre in diamond is an intrinsic polarization analyser: a right-handed field about the NV axis drives one spin transition, and a left-handed field drives the other, in both the ground and the excited state. Here, we exploit the two excited-state transitions, which lie inside the spin-wave band of yttrium iron garnet (YIG), as a pair of chirality channels and image Damon-Eshbach waves in both directions. Because reflection from an etched boundary reverses the handedness, the incident and reflected waves appear as two lines in one spectrum and are imaged separately. In the ground state, the same rule applies, and the selected field drives Rabi oscillations, a route to chirality-selective control of the NV spin by magnons. Reading the two channels gives the direction of a spin wave at one point, without a phase reference. This advances chirality-resolved quantum sensing and provides insight into chiral spin-wave dynamics.
one_liner: An NV center resolves the handedness and propagation direction of YIG spin waves through polarization-selective spin transitions.
why_it_matters: It enables local, phase-reference-free identification of magnon direction and opens a route to chirality-selective quantum-spin control.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses the two excited-state transitions of a diamond NV center as separate detectors for right- and left-handed microwave magnetic fields within the YIG spin-wave band. Damon-Eshbach waves traveling in opposite directions, including incident and boundary-reflected components, are spectrally distinguished and imaged separately. Ground-state measurements further show chirality-selected driving of NV Rabi oscillations.
platform_or_system: Diamond NV center coupled to a YIG film
main_result: The authors image counterpropagating spin waves by chirality and determine their local direction without an external phase reference.
application_angle: The method could support directional magnon imaging, characterization of chiral spin-wave circuits, and magnon-mediated control of quantum spins.

title: Encodings and Node Architecture: Lessons from the Fault-Tolerant Distributed Transversal Fanout
abstract: An encoding choice specifies the quantum error-correcting code used to encode logical qubits at a given node. Different encoding choices may differ in the number of physical qubits, the number of encoded logical qubits, the code distance, and the available fault-tolerant operations. We study different encodings for a distributed transversal fanout operation and look at its implications on node architecture. Our experiments suggest that an encoding with higher distance, even if requiring more ebits, can yield a lower logical error rate for distributed operations, and that ``upgrading'' an encoding prior to distributed operations and having a cache, as part of node architecture, for qubits can be useful for distributed operations.
one_liner: Distributed-fanout studies show that higher-distance encodings can reduce logical errors despite consuming more entanglement.
why_it_matters: The results connect code selection with practical network-node features, including temporary code upgrades and cached qubit capacity.
detailed_summary: The study compares quantum-error-correcting encodings for a fault-tolerant distributed transversal fanout operation. Its experiments indicate that a higher-distance code can achieve a lower logical error rate even when it requires more shared ebits. The authors also examine node-level support for upgrading encodings before distributed operations and caching the required qubits.
main_result: Higher-distance encodings, pre-operation code upgrades, and qubit caches are found to improve the reliability or practicality of distributed fanout.
application_angle: The findings inform hardware provisioning and code-management policies for modular quantum processors and quantum-network nodes.

title: Thermalization-induced self-polarization of temporally incoherent light: A nonequilibrium wave turbulence kinetic approach
abstract: Conservative nonlinear waves generally undergo an irreversible process of thermalization toward the Rayleigh--Jeans (RJ) equilibrium state. Light thermalization has recently been experimentally investigated in the two-dimensional transverse spatial dynamics of multimode waveguides. Here, we consider the one-dimensional temporal dynamics of incoherent light propagating in a weakly birefringent single-mode fiber. We show that light thermalization is responsible for a self-polarization of the incoherent wave during its propagation. Within the framework of wave turbulence theory, we show that this phenomenon originates from a nonequilibrium process of adiabatic cooling: polarization fluctuations are continuously transferred toward the high-frequency tails of a local RJ equilibrium state, whose effective temperature decreases during propagation, thereby increasing the degree of light polarization. Moreover, in the absence of a high-frequency cut-off that would regularize the ultraviolet catastrophe in the temporal domain, the optical wave exhibits an ever-increasing degree of polarization, ultimately approaching unity. These results show that it is thermodynamically advantageous for the optical field to evolve toward a polarized state, which provides new insight into spontaneous self-organization phenomena in conservative Hamiltonian systems operating far from thermodynamic equilibrium.
one_liner: Wave-turbulence theory predicts that incoherent light in a weakly birefringent fiber spontaneously approaches full polarization.
why_it_matters: The mechanism reveals a new form of nonequilibrium optical self-organization that may shape polarization dynamics in nonlinear fiber systems.
detailed_summary: The authors develop a wave-turbulence kinetic description of temporally incoherent light propagating through a weakly birefringent single-mode fiber. Adiabatic cooling transfers polarization fluctuations toward the high-frequency tails of a local Rayleigh-Jeans distribution, increasing the net degree of polarization. Without a high-frequency cutoff, the theory predicts that polarization continues to rise toward unity.
main_result: The theory identifies thermalization-driven adiabatic cooling as a mechanism for spontaneous self-polarization of incoherent light.
application_angle: Understanding this effect may aid polarization control and stability analysis in nonlinear fiber links and broadband photonic systems.

title: Concrete Functions in Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages and Structural Limitations
abstract: Private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM) provide a minimal model of noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation, yet their communication complexity for concrete functions remains poorly understood. We show that familiar total functions already exhibit both genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations. For three-party equality on $n$-bit inputs, which determines whether the players' $n$-bit strings are identical, we construct an entanglement-assisted protocol with asymptotic communication $(1.633\ldots)n$ qubits, whereas every perfectly correct protocol without prior entanglement requires at least $3n$ qubits. For three-bit majority, one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player suffice for perfect correctness and perfect privacy, reducing the communication from the optimal classical cost of six bits to three qubits. Three-bit AND behaves differently. No perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when the players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitary encodings, and transmit one qubit each. However, increasing the local dimension overcomes this obstruction: one shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yield a one-shot protocol with total communication $3\log_2 3$. Together with the six-bit classical lower bound, this gives a strict quantum communication advantage. More generally, for every $k\geq 3$, we construct a perfectly correct and perfectly private one-shot protocol for $k$-bit AND using one qudit of dimension at most $k$ per player, and hence at most $k\log_2 k$ qubits in total.
one_liner: Entanglement-assisted private quantum messaging yields concrete communication savings for equality, majority, and AND.
why_it_matters: The work identifies both deployable quantum advantages and dimension-dependent limits in noninteractive secure multiparty computation.
detailed_summary: For three-party equality, the authors construct an entanglement-assisted protocol using asymptotically 1.633n qubits, compared with a 3n-qubit lower bound without prior entanglement. Three-bit majority is computed privately and exactly using one GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player. Three-bit AND is impossible within the studied one-qubit local-unitary model, but a three-qutrit GHZ protocol succeeds; the construction extends to k-bit AND with local dimension at most k.
main_result: Concrete total functions exhibit strict private quantum communication advantages, while AND requires higher local dimension under the examined protocol constraints.
application_angle: These protocols and lower bounds guide the design of bandwidth-efficient, noninteractive secure computation over future quantum networks.

title: From quantum emitters to technological platforms: a perspective on semiconductor quantum dots
abstract: Photonic quantum technologies are based on controlled photon states. To generate these, quantum dots have emerged as excellent sources of single and entangled photons. In this Perspective, we briefly review the chronological development of quantum dots as photon sources, from their beginnings as quantum emitters in the early 2000s to the advanced photonic devices being developed today. We highlight the interplay between fundamental research and industrial aspects before discussing the photonic quantum technologies we expect to emerge in the near future.
one_liner: A perspective traces semiconductor quantum dots from early emitters to engineered sources for emerging photonic technologies.
why_it_matters: It connects source-performance advances with manufacturability and industrial requirements for scalable single- and entangled-photon platforms.
detailed_summary: This Perspective reviews the development of semiconductor quantum dots as controlled sources of single and entangled photons. It follows progress from early quantum-emitter demonstrations to advanced photonic devices and discusses the interplay between fundamental research and industrial constraints. The authors also outline photonic quantum technologies they expect to emerge in the near term.
main_result: The article synthesizes the technical evolution and commercialization outlook of quantum dots as photonic quantum-technology platforms.
application_angle: The perspective highlights pathways toward practical photon sources for quantum communication, photonic computing, and related integrated systems.

title: Multiscale Quantum-Classical Simulation of Protein Autoproteolysis in a Million-Atom Membrane Environment
abstract: Predicting chemical reactions in biomolecules is challenging because reactive centers are embedded within complex environments that strongly influence their energetics and mechanisms. Here, we present a hybrid quantum-classical workflow that combines molecular dynamics, density functional theory, and correlated wavefunction methods, tightly integrating CPUs, GPUs, and quantum processing units (QPUs) to enable simulations across multiple length and accuracy scales. We apply this approach to ADGRG1 autoproteolysis, a maturation reaction in an adhesion G protein-coupled receptor that has not previously been studied using correlated electronic-structure methods. Our simulations treat a biologically realistic system containing more than one million atoms, including the full-length uncleaved receptor embedded in an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane, while incorporating a 54-qubit IQM quantum processor and up to 1,200 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. These results demonstrate how quantum computers can serve as accelerators within scalable scientific workflows, extending correlated electronic-structure methods to biologically relevant systems.
one_liner: A hybrid CPU–GPU–QPU workflow models protein autoproteolysis inside a biologically realistic million-atom membrane system.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates how a 54-qubit processor can participate as an accelerator in a scalable, multiscale electronic-structure workflow.
detailed_summary: The workflow combines molecular dynamics, density functional theory, and correlated wavefunction methods across CPUs, GPUs, and a QPU. It studies ADGRG1 autoproteolysis in a full-length receptor embedded in an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane containing over one million atoms. The computation incorporates a 54-qubit IQM processor and as many as 1,200 NVIDIA H100 GPUs.
main_result: The authors extend correlated electronic-structure calculations to a million-atom biomolecular environment using an integrated 54-qubit quantum accelerator.
application_angle: The architecture offers a route to embedding quantum processors within large-scale drug-discovery and biomolecular-reaction simulations.

title: Exponential-SWAP gate between bosonic motional modes of trapped ions
abstract: The exponential-SWAP (eSWAP) gate generates a coherent superposition of identity and SWAP operations, with continuously tunable amplitudes. We experimentally implement this gate between two bosonic motional modes of trapped ions using spin-independent and spin-dependent beam splitter interactions. Measurements of selected slices of the joint characteristic function for distinct input states test the gate and demonstrate continuous control of the identity-SWAP superposition. This implementation provides a tunable interaction for hybrid qubit-bosonic quantum information processing.
one_liner: A trapped-ion experiment realizes a continuously tunable exponential-SWAP gate between two bosonic motional modes.
why_it_matters: The gate supplies a controllable identity–SWAP interaction for hybrid architectures that process information in both spins and oscillator modes.
detailed_summary: The experiment implements an exponential-SWAP gate between two trapped-ion motional modes using spin-independent and spin-dependent beam-splitter interactions. Selected slices of the joint characteristic function are measured for several input states. The results verify continuous control over the coherent superposition of identity and SWAP operations.
main_result: A tunable eSWAP gate was experimentally demonstrated between two ion-motion modes and tested through joint characteristic-function measurements.
application_angle: The interaction can support state manipulation and information exchange in hybrid qubit–bosonic processors.

title: Anticommuting Displacement Operators, Exact Pauli Algebras,and the Singlet State from the Oscillator Vacuum
abstract: We give an explicit construction of a pair of anticommuting Weyl displacement operators for a harmonic oscillator and use bounded functional calculus to obtain exact dichotomic representatives of the Pauli algebra. Two independent oscillators provide commuting Pauli algebras for Alice and Bob. The standard singlet-sector projector, written entirely in terms of these bounded oscillator observables, is then applied to the two-oscillator vacuum. We show explicitly that the projected vacuum has nonzero norm, so its normalization is well defined, has the exact singlet correlations, and reaches the Tsirelson value $2\sqrt2$ for the usual Bell--CHSH settings. We also clarify that the construction generally realizes a singlet sector with multiplicity, rather than selecting a unique vector in the full oscillator Hilbert space, and we compare the construction with the older pseudospin approach to continuous-variable Bell tests.
one_liner: Exact Pauli observables built from oscillator displacements generate a singlet sector from vacuum and attain maximal CHSH violation.
why_it_matters: The construction gives a mathematically exact bridge between continuous-variable oscillator hardware and qubit-like Bell correlations.
detailed_summary: The authors construct anticommuting Weyl displacement operators for one harmonic oscillator and use bounded functional calculus to obtain exact dichotomic Pauli representatives. Two oscillators then provide commuting local Pauli algebras for Alice and Bob. Applying the resulting singlet-sector projector to the two-oscillator vacuum yields nonzero norm, exact singlet correlations, and the CHSH value 2√2, although the singlet sector can have multiplicity.
main_result: The projected oscillator vacuum realizes exact singlet correlations and reaches the Tsirelson bound using bounded displacement-derived observables.
application_angle: The framework may inform continuous-variable photonic Bell tests and oscillator-based encodings of qubit observables.

title: Resonance crossings and diabolical points for DC electric field quantum sensors
abstract: Since the 1990s, experiments on double-well heterostructures have highlighted a key phenomenon: applying an external DC electric field induces pronounced wave packet oscillations at specific field strengths. \ To gain a deeper insight into this effect, a comprehensive quantitative analysis of the properties of quantum resonances near a crossing point is required. \ This approach lays the theoretical foundation for devising a quantum sensor capable of rapidly and efficiently determining whether the strength of an external DC electric field lies within a narrow target range.
one_liner: A resonance-crossing analysis links field-specific wave-packet oscillations in double wells to narrow-range DC electric-field detection.
why_it_matters: Sharp behavior near resonance crossings could provide a fast threshold-like method for determining whether a DC field lies in a target interval.
detailed_summary: The study quantitatively examines quantum resonances near crossing points in double-well heterostructures under a DC electric field. At particular field strengths, the system exhibits pronounced wave-packet oscillations associated with resonance structure. The analysis is presented as a theoretical foundation for detecting whether an applied field falls within a narrow prescribed range.
main_result: The work characterizes resonance crossings that produce field-selective wave-packet oscillations suitable for narrow-window DC-field discrimination.
application_angle: The proposed sensing principle targets rapid detection of whether an external DC electric field is inside a specified range.

title: Quantum Sensitivity of $N$-Component Cat States
abstract: We extend our previous study of squeezed two-component Schrödinger cat states to a phase-referenced single-mode family with an arbitrary number $N$ of coherent components and general relative phases. Within the established circular-state construction, we derive a closed complex overlap kernel for the ordered action of displacement, phase rotation, and squeezing, retaining exact finite-amplitude normalization. We distinguish finite-displacement orthogonality from local phase-estimation sensitivity quantified by quantum Fisher information (QFI). For equal-phase states, we compare $N=2,\ldots,9$ at a common mean photon number and include coherent-state and squeezed-vacuum benchmarks. A bound on the higher photon-number sectors establishes the fixed-energy asymptote $F_{Q,N}=4\bar n(N-\bar n)+o(1)$. Its leading term agrees with the known QFI of a vacuum--$N$-photon superposition. The resulting decrease of the ideal local quantum Cramér--Rao bound does not establish unlimited attainable precision: prior phase information, sample size, phase-reference resources, optical loss, state preparation, and measurement choice remain relevant.
one_liner: Exact finite-energy analysis quantifies phase sensitivity in single-mode cat states containing up to nine coherent components.
why_it_matters: It separates formal QFI gains from experimentally attainable precision and identifies the practical resources that constrain cat-state sensing.
detailed_summary: The authors derive a closed overlap kernel for displacement, phase rotation, and squeezing of phase-referenced, N-component single-mode cat states with exact finite-amplitude normalization. Equal-phase states with N=2 through 9 are compared at fixed mean photon number against coherent-state and squeezed-vacuum benchmarks. They obtain the fixed-energy asymptote F_Q,N=4n̄(N−n̄)+o(1), while emphasizing that loss, preparation, measurement, phase references, and prior information limit realizable precision.
main_result: The paper derives exact finite-amplitude QFI expressions and a fixed-energy asymptotic scaling for N-component cat-state phase sensing.
application_angle: The results guide the design and realistic assessment of nonclassical optical probes for precision phase measurements.

title: ConQUESTA: Topology-Aware Post-Training Structural Pruning of Quantum Neural Networks
abstract: Deploying quantum neural networks (QNNs) on sparse hardware requires preserving task accuracy while reducing compiler-induced two-qubit gates, SWAPs, and depth. We present ConQUESTA (\underline{C}onstrained \underline{Qu}antum \underline{E}ntangler \underline{S}election with \underline{T}opology \underline{A}wareness), a post training pruning framework that combines task saliency with compiler cost, screens candidate entanglers, and searches complete pruning masks under an explicit accuracy constraint. Unlike one-shot ranking, each mask is transpiled as a whole across multiple coupling topologies. Across 4-, 6-, and 8-qubit QNNs and eight model seeds at 55% pruning, ConQUESTA achieves mean resource reductions of 61.6% on Breast Cancer, 72.0% on Digits01, and 82.2% on Iris, exceeding the strongest matched simple baseline by 3.5, 1.7, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Fixed-mask recovery raises feasibility from 16/24 to 22/24 runs. In a fixed-k=4 scaling study on a scaling probe of 4 to 12-qubits, the raw mask space grew from 495 to 12.1M while the evaluated masks increase only from 189 to 305. Resource-weight changes alter depth/routing priorities with at most a 0.44-point mean validation shift.
one_liner: ConQUESTA prunes trained quantum neural networks using task saliency and hardware topology to reduce compiled circuit resources.
why_it_matters: Topology-aware pruning can make trained QNNs substantially cheaper to execute on sparse-connectivity processors without major accuracy loss.
detailed_summary: ConQUESTA selects entanglers after training by combining task saliency with compiler cost, then evaluates complete pruning masks after transpilation across multiple coupling graphs. At 55% pruning on 4-, 6-, and 8-qubit QNNs, mean resource reductions range from 61.6% to 82.2% across three datasets. Fixed-mask recovery improves feasibility from 16 of 24 to 22 of 24 runs, while the scaling probe evaluates only 305 masks from a 12.1-million-mask space at 12 qubits.
platform_or_system: Sparse-connectivity QNN hardware and compiler stack
main_result: Topology-aware post-training pruning reduces compiled QNN resources by 61.6–82.2% while enforcing an explicit accuracy constraint.
application_angle: The method can lower routing, two-qubit-gate, and depth overhead when deploying trained QNNs on connectivity-limited quantum processors.

title: A Fibre-Integrated SPDC Heralded Single-Photon Source Using Zn-Indiffused PPLN Ridge Waveguides at Telecom Wavelengths
abstract: We demonstrate a fully fibre-integrated source of broadband polarisation-entangled photon pairs at telecom wavelengths based on a commercially available Zn-indiffused MgO:PPLN ridge waveguide incorporated within a Sagnac interferometer. Operating across the full degenerate SPDC spectrum using pump-suppression filtering only, the source exhibits a measured bandwidth of approximately 67 nm. Strong non-classical correlations are observed, with an average two-photon interference visibility of 96.9 +/- 0.2 %, a fidelity to the Phi + Bell state of 78.1 %, and a CHSH Bell parameter of S = 2.501 +/- 0.005. We further explore the effect of increasing source brightness on Bell-state performance, revealing the limitations of accidental-corrected metrics in high-flux operating regimes.
one_liner: A fibre-integrated PPLN Sagnac source generates broadband polarization-entangled photon pairs across a 67 nm telecom band.
why_it_matters: The commercial-waveguide design combines fibre integration, broad bandwidth, high interference visibility, and Bell violation for practical quantum photonic links.
detailed_summary: A commercially available Zn-indiffused MgO:PPLN ridge waveguide is incorporated into a Sagnac interferometer to generate polarization-entangled photon pairs at telecom wavelengths. With pump-suppression filtering only, the source spans about 67 nm and achieves 96.9 ± 0.2% average two-photon interference visibility, 78.1% fidelity to the Phi+ Bell state, and CHSH S = 2.501 ± 0.005. Brightness-dependent measurements also expose limitations of accidental-corrected metrics at high photon flux.
main_result: The source demonstrates broadband telecom entanglement with 96.9% interference visibility and a clear CHSH Bell violation.
application_angle: Its fibre-ready architecture and broad spectrum support deployable entangled-photon links, multiplexing, and quantum-network sources.

title: Temperature dependence of a warm ensemble based memory on quantum communication rates
abstract: The success of long-distance quantum communication will hinge on quantum repeater nodes equipped with robust and scalable quantum memories. Such memories must possess specific operating characteristics to make these nodes practical. An attractive option for these memory devices is an atomic warm vapor system operating under the conditions of electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT). These systems are easy to implement and require relatively low equipment overhead. A key metric in atomic-based quantum memory performance is optical depth, as it is closely tied to the strength of light-matter coupling. Here, we simulate and measure the optical depth-based performance of an EIT quantum memory using a warm atomic vapor cell. We then translate the simulated and measured optical depth and efficiency metrics into expected entanglement distribution rates. Our analysis evaluates the feasibility of these memories in optical quantum repeater nodes, which are essential for robust long-distance quantum communication.
one_liner: Measured and simulated warm-vapor EIT memory performance is mapped onto expected entanglement-distribution rates for quantum repeaters.
why_it_matters: Connecting temperature-dependent optical depth and memory efficiency to network rates clarifies whether low-overhead warm-vapor memories can serve repeater nodes.
detailed_summary: The study simulates and measures the optical depth and efficiency of an electromagnetically induced transparency memory based on a warm atomic vapor cell. It examines how temperature-dependent operating conditions affect light–matter coupling and memory performance. These measured and simulated metrics are then translated into expected entanglement-distribution rates for optical quantum-repeater nodes.
main_result: The work quantitatively links temperature, optical depth, and memory efficiency to projected quantum-repeater entanglement rates.
application_angle: The analysis provides operating guidance for scalable, comparatively low-overhead memory nodes in long-distance quantum networks.

title: Action-Quantized Scar Multiplets and Dissipative Cat States from Fractal Period-Locking in the Open Quantum Baker Map
abstract: We open the quantum baker map with a position window of width $w$ and center $q_c$. Classical pruning tiles the $(q_c,w)$ plane into diamonds where the $T$ leading resonances form root-of-unity multiplets. At $w=1/2$ one periodic orbit survives for almost every $q_c$, and the multiplets are quantized without free parameters: their modulus $2^{-1/2}$ saturates the pressure bound and their phase is the orbit action. They form cycling multicomponent cat states, and the opening becomes one mid-circuit measurement, enabling spectroscopy with $\sim10^2$ shots on quantum processors.
one_liner: An opened quantum baker map yields action-quantized resonance multiplets and cycling cat states accessible through a single mid-circuit measurement.
why_it_matters: The parameter-free spectral structure offers a shot-efficient route to studying open-system resonances and dissipative cat states on quantum processors.
detailed_summary: Opening the quantum baker map with a movable position window produces classical pruning regions where the leading resonances form root-of-unity multiplets. At window width 1/2, a surviving periodic orbit fixes the multiplet modulus at 2^-1/2 and its phase through the orbit action, without free fitting parameters. The resulting resonances form cycling multicomponent cat states, while the opening can be implemented as one mid-circuit measurement.
platform_or_system: Gate-based quantum processor simulating an open baker map
main_result: The proposal enables spectroscopy of action-quantized scar multiplets and dissipative cat states with roughly 100 measurement shots.
application_angle: It supplies a hardware-light protocol for probing non-Hermitian dynamics, quantum chaos, and measurement-induced states on current processors.

title: Noise suppression of quantum frequency conversion in thin-film lithium niobate waveguides via adapted poling
abstract: Quantum frequency conversion (QFC) enables optical interfaces between dissimilar quantum systems, but suppressing noise while maintaining high conversion efficiency remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate that adapted poling in thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) waveguides reduces the pump-power requirement while shifting the dominant noise mechanism and its power scaling. In 2-cm-long waveguides, adapted poling enables maximum conversion efficiency at an on-chip pump power of $19\pm0.8$~mW, reducing the required pump power by 8~dB and the total conversion noise by 14~dB relative to conventional periodic poling at their respective maximum-conversion operating points. Controlled measurements with different pump conditions and device configurations reveal a transition from predominantly quadratic noise scaling in periodically poled devices to predominantly linear scaling in adapted-poling devices. This transition accompanies a shift from noise dominated by cascaded second-harmonic generation and Stokes spontaneous Raman scattering to direct anti-Stokes spontaneous Raman scattering. These results establish adapted poling as an effective approach to suppressing nonlinear noise, enabling low-noise integrated frequency converters for quantum networks.
one_liner: Adapted poling cuts pump demand by 8 dB and conversion noise by 14 dB in thin-film lithium-niobate quantum frequency converters.
why_it_matters: Lower pump power and noise directly improve integrated interfaces that translate photons between otherwise incompatible quantum systems and network bands.
detailed_summary: In 2 cm thin-film lithium-niobate waveguides, adapted poling reaches maximum conversion efficiency with 19 ± 0.8 mW of on-chip pump power. Relative to conventional periodic poling at maximum conversion, it reduces required pump power by 8 dB and total conversion noise by 14 dB. Measurements identify a shift from quadratic noise dominated by cascaded second-harmonic generation and Stokes Raman scattering to primarily linear direct anti-Stokes Raman noise.
main_result: Adapted poling achieves maximum conversion at 19 mW while reducing conversion noise by 14 dB versus periodic poling.
application_angle: The method enables quieter, lower-power integrated wavelength interfaces for heterogeneous quantum networks.

title: Broadband chiroptical sensing with two-mode subwavelength grating waveguides
abstract: Engineering local optical chirality in planar photonic structures offers a route to selective and enhanced light-matter interactions with chiral media. Here, we introduce periodic dielectric waveguides that support chiral evanescent fields through the interaction of two nearly degenerate waveguide modes. We develop a perturbation theory for such a waveguide covered by a chiral layer, relating chirality-induced modal coupling and propagation-constant corrections to measurable intermodal power conversion and differential transmission. Whereas modal detuning confines the chiral response of a symmetric waveguide to a narrow spectral range, mode hybridization in an asymmetric waveguide creates individual eigenmodes that carry nonzero local chirality over a broad spectral range. We show that modal dichroism in realistic lossy waveguides can produce a significant background differential transmission signal. Such a background, however, can be suppressed by comparing transmission through two asymmetric waveguides with opposite structural asymmetries, allowing the chiral response to be reliably extracted. Together, these findings provide a basis for developing integrated photonic components with locally chiral fields, including waveguides, metasurfaces, and resonators.
one_liner: Two nearly degenerate modes create broadband chiral evanescent fields in subwavelength-grating waveguides for integrated chiroptical sensing.
why_it_matters: The design broadens planar chiral sensing while providing a differential strategy to reject loss-induced backgrounds that can mimic molecular chirality.
detailed_summary: The authors develop perturbation theory linking chirality-induced modal coupling and propagation-constant shifts to intermodal conversion and differential transmission. In symmetric waveguides, modal detuning confines the response spectrally, whereas asymmetry hybridizes the modes and gives individual eigenmodes broadband local chirality. Comparing devices with opposite structural asymmetries suppresses differential-transmission backgrounds caused by modal dichroism in lossy waveguides.
main_result: Asymmetric mode hybridization produces broadband local optical chirality with a paired-device method for isolating the true chiral response.
application_angle: The approach supports compact on-chip enantiomer sensing and chiral light–matter interfaces in waveguides, metasurfaces, and resonators.

title: Delta-sigma noise shaping for low-resolution quantization in Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum key distribution
abstract: Low-resolution digital-to-analog conversion can simplify continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD) transmitters, but coarse quantization increases excess noise and can generate data-correlated spectral replicas. We demonstrate digital delta--sigma modulation (DSM) for low-resolution waveform generation in Gaussian-modulated CVQKD. In a 500-MBaud CVQKD system over 20~km of fiber, 3-bit second-order DSM achieves an estimated asymptotic secret key rate of 46.38~Mbps at an oversampling ratio of 12, whereas uniform quantization yields no positive rate. With 4-bit second-order DSM, the rate reaches 50.11~Mbps, approximately 97\% of the 12-bit reference. A noise model combining the DSM noise-transfer function with matched filtering guides the sampling-rate and signal-band design for effective noise suppression. We also identify a phase-conjugate spectral replica arising from third-order intermodulation between the pilot tone and quantum signal, and evaluate its key-rate penalty using a linear-replica security model. At 3-bit resolution and an oversampling ratio of 24, first-order DSM reduces the experimentally estimated leakage-mode strength by approximately four orders of magnitude. Together, our findings establish the security boundaries and operating conditions of DSM, providing design guidance for low-resolution CVQKD transmitters.
one_liner: Delta–sigma modulation enables 3–4-bit waveform generation for 500 MBaud CVQKD over 20 km with secret rates approaching a 12-bit reference.
why_it_matters: Noise-shaped low-resolution conversion could reduce transmitter complexity and cost while retaining secure high-rate CVQKD performance.
detailed_summary: A 500 MBaud Gaussian-modulated CVQKD experiment over 20 km uses digital delta–sigma modulation to move coarse-quantization noise outside the matched signal band. Second-order 3-bit modulation yields an estimated asymptotic secret key rate of 46.38 Mbps at oversampling ratio 12, while uniform quantization gives no positive rate; the 4-bit result reaches 50.11 Mbps, about 97% of the 12-bit reference. The study also models a phase-conjugate replica from pilot–signal intermodulation and reports an approximately four-order reduction in leakage-mode strength under a 3-bit first-order configuration at oversampling ratio 24.
main_result: Low-resolution delta–sigma modulation preserves positive key generation, reaching 50.11 Mbps with 4 bits over 20 km.
application_angle: The technique offers concrete sampling, filtering, and security-design guidance for simpler low-resolution CVQKD transmitters.

title: Experimental Demonstration of a Balanced Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifier
abstract: Superconducting travelling-wave parametric amplifiers (TWPAs) provide broadband gain, low added noise, and high dynamic range, making them attractive for applications requiring wide instantaneous bandwidth. This is crucial for amplifying multiplexed narrow band signals spread over a wide frequency range, such as qubit resonator arrays, or amplifying inherently wide band signals, such as in spectrometers or radiometers. In many cases, however, the useful bandwidth of a TWPA is limited by the production of the idler tone at an image frequency. For three-wave-mixing (3WM) TWPAs, for example, an input signal at $f_s$ is indistinguishable from one at $f_p - f_s$, which can produce spectral ambiguity when the input spectrum is broadband or not known in advance. We experimentally demonstrate a balanced architecture that doubles the instantaneous image-rejected bandwidth available to a 3WM TWPA by spatially separating the amplified signal from the output pump and generated idler, which resolves the sideband degeneracy. The architecture consists of two amplifiers connected between a pair of 180$^{\circ}$ hybrid couplers, with the signal and pump injected and output through the sum and difference ports, respectively. Using two kinetic-inductance TWPAs, we demonstrate approximately 20 dB of signal gain across nearly an octave of bandwidth, together with pump rejection below --20 dB and an average image rejection of approximately --15 dB over the operating band. These results establish balanced TWPAs as a practical approach to broadband parametric amplification, enabling improved contamination free bandwidth and eliminating the need for complex filtering.
one_liner: A balanced pair of kinetic-inductance TWPAs delivers image-rejected, near-octave microwave amplification with about 20 dB gain.
why_it_matters: The architecture expands contamination-free bandwidth for multiplexed qubit readout and broadband cryogenic sensing without complex image-rejection filters.
detailed_summary: Two kinetic-inductance three-wave-mixing TWPAs are connected through 180° hybrid couplers, with signal and pump routed through the sum and difference ports. This balanced arrangement spatially separates the amplified signal from the pump and generated idler, resolving sideband ambiguity. The experiment reports approximately 20 dB gain across nearly an octave, pump rejection below −20 dB, and about −15 dB average image rejection.
main_result: The balanced amplifier doubles the instantaneous image-rejected bandwidth while maintaining approximately 20 dB gain across nearly an octave.
application_angle: It supports cleaner broadband amplification for multiplexed superconducting-qubit resonators, spectrometers, and radiometers at cryogenic temperatures.

title: Quality-of-Transmission Estimation in Quantum Networks: Compute, Simulate, or Learn?
abstract: Future quantum networks will rely on control-plane decisions such as routing, scheduling, entanglement provisioning, purification, and memory allocation. Each decision depends on a timely and reliable estimate of the quality of the entanglement that a candidate path can deliver, with end-to-end fidelity as a central metric. Inspired by the optical-networking experience with quality-of-transmission (QoT) estimation, this article asks when a quantum controller should compute fidelity analytically, simulate it, or learn a surrogate model. The optical analogy is useful but incomplete: optical QoT estimation often predicts a scalar transmission margin, whereas quantum QoT estimation must account for probabilistic entanglement generation, random memory waiting times, decoherence, state consumption, and measurement constraints that can make fidelity a stochastic target. We propose a compute/simulate/learn framework for quantum QoT estimation and illustrate it with a simulation-based proof of concept. Our study shows that analytical composition can be sufficient in simple regimes, that simulation becomes necessary when stochastic memory effects shape the delivered fidelity distribution, and that lightweight learned surrogates can approximate simulator labels at much lower runtime cost for online control. We close with open challenges for deployment, including stochastic targets, sim-to-real transfer, data-generation cost, physics-informed learning, and generalization beyond individual paths to full network topologies.
one_liner: A compute–simulate–learn framework selects practical methods for estimating end-to-end entanglement fidelity in quantum networks.
why_it_matters: Fast, reliable fidelity estimates are essential for online routing, scheduling, purification, entanglement provisioning, and quantum-memory allocation.
detailed_summary: The work frames quantum quality-of-transmission estimation as a choice among analytical composition, stochastic simulation, and learned surrogate models. A simulation-based proof of concept shows that analytical methods can suffice in simple regimes, while random memory waiting times and decoherence require distribution-aware simulation. Lightweight surrogates reproduce simulator-generated labels with lower runtime cost, although deployment challenges such as sim-to-real transfer and topology generalization remain open.
main_result: The study demonstrates that learned surrogates can approximate simulation-based fidelity estimates at substantially lower runtime cost for online network control.
application_angle: The framework can guide controller design for real-time path selection and resource management in future quantum communication networks.

title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor
abstract: Quantum error correction can suppress logical errors exponentially with code distance when physical noise is below threshold. Realizing this on hardware requires tight coordination among quantum gates, mid-circuit measurements, and qubit coherence. Device variation, noise asymmetry, and correlations across space and time complicate the translation of these capabilities into logical error suppression. Here, we study rotated surface-code memory on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor. Performance varies across tested processor placements, which we attribute to differences in qubit quality. We optimize the code by combining short readout, fused measurement and reset, and an XX echo on data qubits during ancilla readout. Compared with standard readout without reset or echo, the optimized syndrome extraction circuit reduces the median per-round logical error rate by factors of 3.8 in the X basis and 1.4 in the Z basis. In memory experiments of up to 150 rounds, the distance advantage weakens, alongside long-lived correlations that may reflect a persistent error component. Under our optimization recipe, increasing the protected distance from 3 to 6 while holding the other distance fixed reduces the per-round logical error rate from 0.53% to 0.24% in Z memory and from 0.52% to 0.22% in X memory. The corresponding error-suppression factors under maximum-likelihood decoding are 1.68 and 1.85. These results connect circuit compilation and optimization to surface-code memory performance and limitations, and motivate QPU and QEC circuit codesign for fault-tolerant quantum computing primitives on current cloud hardware.
one_liner: A cloud-accessible IBM processor shows lower logical error rates with increasing surface-code distance after syndrome-circuit optimization.
why_it_matters: The experiment links practical compilation choices to logical error suppression while exposing persistent correlations that limit long-duration QEC performance.
detailed_summary: Rotated surface-code memories were implemented on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor using short readout, fused measurement and reset, and an XX echo during ancilla readout. These changes reduced median per-round logical error rates by factors of 3.8 in the X basis and 1.4 in the Z basis relative to standard circuits. Increasing one protected distance from 3 to 6 lowered logical error rates from 0.53% to 0.24% for Z memory and from 0.52% to 0.22% for X memory, though long-lived correlations weakened the advantage over 150 rounds.
main_result: Optimized surface-code memories achieved error-suppression factors of 1.68 and 1.85 under maximum-likelihood decoding as protected distance increased from 3 to 6.
application_angle: The results provide actionable QPU–QEC circuit codesign guidance for improving fault-tolerant memory primitives on current cloud quantum hardware.

title: Quantum simultaneous decoding via pretty-good measurements of tilted states
abstract: A multiple-access channel transmits messages from several senders to one receiver. For quantum outputs, the receiver must distinguish states depending on all messages, while tests for different decoding errors may not commute. In this paper, we give a self-contained account of simultaneous decoding, in which one joint measurement recovers the messages at the established achievable rates using independent codebooks. The proof combines Sen's tilted-subspace method with Cheng's analysis of the pretty-good measurement, a standard measurement for distinguishing quantum states. Auxiliary labels close to a common reference state separate the geometric directions associated with different errors. A Gram-matrix bound then allows separately chosen binary tests to certify the performance of one measurement. The labels are removed from the completed decoder, leading to a deterministic packing theorem that applies to finite state ensembles, including unequal priors. We develop the two-sender case first, with worked examples and figures, before treating any fixed number of senders. Sharper finite-error guarantees for the same decoder are developed separately, with sharp bounds for two specified steps of the analysis rather than a claim of globally optimal decoding. Applications recover known achievable rates for unassisted and entanglement-assisted classical communication, distributed classical compression with quantum side information, and coherent-state communication through a beamsplitter or passive multiport device. The common proof makes the geometric mechanism and its quantitative consequences available without repeating the construction for each application.
one_liner: A joint pretty-good measurement decodes quantum multiple-access messages at established achievable rates using independent codebooks.
why_it_matters: The unified packing theorem covers unequal priors and several classical-communication and compression settings.

title: Adaptive Entanglement Witnessing for Two-Qubit Systems
abstract: Entanglement witnesses are a key instrument in determining the entanglement of unknown bipartite qubit systems without requiring a full tomography. Riccardi et al. (2020) proposed a set of two-qubit witnesses, denoted $\{W^3\}$, which require a set of local measurements in three bases. In this work we propose an additional set of witnesses, denoted $\{W^5\}$, that build on $\{W^3\}$ and require measurements in two additional bases. We present an adaptive two-step method that uses the measurement results obtained for $\{W^3\}$ to select which $W^5$ to evaluate. We computationally demonstrate that our adaptive two-step protocol can identify 72% of entangled states generated according to the methods of Roik et al. (2021) while requiring measurements in only five of the nine bases needed for full quantum tomography. Additionally, we experimentally verify the behavior of both sets of witnesses using polarization-entangled photon pairs.
one_liner: An adaptive two-step witness protocol detects 72% of sampled entangled two-qubit states using five measurement bases.
why_it_matters: It reduces measurement demands relative to nine-basis tomography and is validated with polarization-entangled photons.

title: Sequential optimization for orbital-optimized variational quantum eigensolvers
abstract: Orbital optimization within the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) framework is useful for improving active-space quality and accurately capturing electron correlation with shallow quantum circuits. The orbital-optimized unitary coupled cluster (OO-UCC) method [W. Mizukami et al., Phys. Rev. Res. 2, 033421 (2020)], in its original formulation, employs the orbital gradient and Hessian in a Newton--Laphson procedure. In this study, we propose sequential orbital-optimized unitary coupled cluster doubles (SOO-UCCD), extending the gradient-free sequential minimal optimization approach [K. M. Nakanishi et al., Phys. Rev. Res. 2, 043158 (2020)] to orbital rotation parameters. Based on the frequency structure implied by the algebraic properties of the orbital rotation generators, our method determines each orbital rotation angle from a nine-point energy profile. The energy landscape is evaluated by classically transforming the Hamiltonian integrals and contracting them with the reduced density matrices already measured for the VQE energy evaluation. This allows for orbital optimization without evaluating the orbital gradient or Hessian. By building on the core benefits of the OO-UCC framework, our method provides a gradient-free and hyperparameter-free orbital-optimization procedure. State-vector simulations for LiH in the STO-3G basis show that SOO-UCCD reproduces UCCSD-level accuracy along the bond-stretching curve and exhibits macro-iteration convergence comparable to that of L-BFGS-based orbital optimization.
one_liner: SOO-UCCD optimizes molecular orbitals from nine-point energy profiles without orbital gradients, Hessians, or tuned hyperparameters.
why_it_matters: LiH simulations attain UCCSD-level accuracy with convergence comparable to L-BFGS orbital optimization.

title: Measuring higher-order bulk topology in a programmable quantum simulator
abstract: Topological insulators lie outside the standard Landau paradigm: Instead of being characterized by local order parameters and spontaneous symmetry breaking, their defining properties are encoded in the global structure of their quantum states and manifested as robust boundary states. Crystalline higher-order topological insulators can extend this principle by hosting localized corner modes in two and higher dimensions. Although these boundary modes can be detected spectroscopically through the local density of states, determining the underlying bulk topology, for example through nested Wilson loops, remains an outstanding experimental challenge. Here we use up to 728 qubits in a superconducting analogue-digital quantum simulator to realize and probe a hierarchy of one-, two-, and three-dimensional topological insulators governed by effective tight-binding Hamiltonians. By reconstructing complex propagators from real-space measurements, we obtain complementary boundary and bulk characterizations: local densities of states reveal localized boundary modes, whereas experimentally reconstructed band projectors yield bulk topological invariants, culminating in a three-dimensional octupole moment extracted through third nested Wilson loops. These results establish a route to realizing, characterizing, and manipulating topologically protected states in programmable three-dimensional quantum matter.
one_liner: A 728-qubit simulator reconstructs bulk invariants of 1D–3D topological insulators, including a 3D octupole moment.
why_it_matters: It experimentally connects boundary modes with nested-Wilson-loop bulk topology in programmable quantum matter.

title: Multipolar Nanophotonics with Quantum Computers
abstract: Small particles respond to light through electric and magnetic patterns called multipoles. Their interference determines the direction of scattered light and affects the decay of nearby emitters. Larger nanoantenna arrays, metasurfaces, and other nanophotonic systems demand increasingly costly simulations to meet strict performance and reliability requirements. We show how to represent these responses with quantum bits (qubits) and use quantum circuits to calculate scattering and the Purcell effect, the change in an emitter's decay rate caused by its surroundings. The circuits can encode known multipoles or estimate unknown ones from Maxwell's equations at the particle surface. We test the method against classical theory using an ideal quantum simulator and real IBM and IonQ quantum computers. For a silicon nanoparticle of radius 78 nm illuminated at 679 nm, IonQ gives a forward directivity of 2.984, close to the ideal dipolar value 3, quantifying the concentration of scattered light in the forward direction. For an emitter 10 nm from a gold nanoparticle and emitting at 510 nm, IBM measurements yield a calculated total decay rate 20.48 times its vacuum value versus 20.47 from theory, with correction for errors in reading the qubit states. We also establish how the number of multipoles and the required accuracy set the demands on qubits and measurements. These results motivate quantum-assisted design studies of directional radiation and emitter decay in nanophotonic systems.
one_liner: Quantum circuits calculate multipolar light scattering and emitter Purcell enhancement on simulators and IBM and IonQ hardware.
why_it_matters: The method offers a quantum-assisted route to designing directional nanoantennas and controlling emitter decay.

title: Permanent Thermodynamic Mpemba Inversion from Quantum-Jump Feedback
abstract: We show that a common quantum-jump feedback protocol can permanently reverse the nonequilibrium free-energy ordering of two prescribed initial states while preserving their Gibbs equilibrium. The construction exploits collective compensation between monitored channels: their feedback corrections cancel at equilibrium but remain active during relaxation. This balance preserves free-energy monotonicity while allowing the relaxation modes to be reshaped. We prove that eliminating the complete slow-sector contribution of the initially higher-free-energy state, while retaining it for the comparison state, produces distinct asymptotic decay exponents. Their free-energy ratio then vanishes at long times, guaranteeing a permanent thermodynamic quantum Mpemba inversion under the same controlled dynamics. A thermal qutrit realizes the mechanism through coherence interference and exhibits distinct detection thresholds for spectral selection and exact slow-sector cancellation under feedback retuning.
one_liner: Quantum-jump feedback can permanently reverse the free-energy ordering of two relaxing states while preserving Gibbs equilibrium.
why_it_matters: The construction turns Mpemba inversion into an asymptotically guaranteed effect through controlled relaxation modes.

title: From isolated singular wells to exact Bloch bands: the trigonometric Pöschl-Teller lattice
abstract: An exactly solvable lattice with periodic inverse-square singularities exhibits two physically distinct mechanisms of spectral-gap closure. The model arises from the generalized trigonometric Pöschl-Teller potential in the coupling range where both local solutions at each singularity are square-integrable. A transmitting, current-preserving self-adjoint matching condition connects neighboring cells and generates a nontrivial Bloch spectrum. For a generic lattice with two inequivalent singular sublattices, the spectrum contains two alternating families of gaps, and the band edges reproduce the scale-invariant spectra of the associated finite singular system. One gap family closes when the two sublattices become equivalent. In this symmetric limit, however, the primitive period halves, so the apparent band crossing results from Brillouin-zone folding. A different family closes at a critical but genuinely asymmetric configuration. Because the primitive period is preserved, adjacent bands then meet at the center of the original Brillouin zone in a genuine massless Dirac-like cone. Near either critical limit, a small finite gap acts as an effective Dirac mass: the dispersion remains quadratic near a band edge but crosses over to a massive Dirac-like form beyond that narrow region. The band curvatures define effective electron and hole masses. Exact Bloch eigenfunctions further reveal that isospectral lattices can display different single-particle probability densities. This model therefore provides an analytically controlled one-dimensional setting in which conventional quadratic carriers, massive Dirac-like band dispersions, and a tunable massless contact coexist within the same singular lattice.
one_liner: An exact singular Pöschl–Teller lattice exhibits quadratic bands, massive Dirac dispersion, and a tunable massless cone.
why_it_matters: It analytically separates genuine gap closure from Brillouin-zone folding and exposes distinct isospectral densities.

title: Quantum tomography of bright squeezed vacuum via strong-field ionization
abstract: Strong-field physics uses intense optical fields to probe and control electron motion on ultrafast timescales. Recent advances in bright squeezed vacuum have brought macroscopic quantum states of light into the ultrafast strong-field regime, opening prospects for high-harmonic generation and photoionization. Yet linking its phase-space structure to subcycle electron dynamics remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate strong-field tunneling ionization of xenon using a phase-referenced combination of coherent and squeezed fields, with the coherent field defining the ionization clock and quadrature fluctuations of the zero-mean squeezed field providing control. The squeezed field selectively modulates atomic tunneling barriers and electron wave packets, imprinting signatures on photoelectron momentum distributions, number statistics, and energy spectra. Using coincidence measurements of photon number and phase-sensitive photoelectron momentum distributions, we perform quantum state tomography of the driving field by reconstructing its Wigner function. These results establish a bidirectional interface between quantum optics and nonperturbative strong-field electron dynamics, in which the driving quantum field shapes subcycle electron motion while photoionization provides a phase-sensitive probe of the field's quantum state. This work opens new routes toward controlling electron dynamics with quantum light and phase-sensitive quantum state metrology through ultrafast strong-field electron dynamics.
one_liner: Phase-sensitive xenon ionization reconstructs the Wigner function of bright squeezed vacuum from correlated electron and photon data.
why_it_matters: It links quantum-light tomography with subcycle control and probing of nonperturbative electron dynamics.

title: Noise-resistant off-resonance π-rotation realized in an NMR system
abstract: Precise manipulation of qubits (spins) requires strong suppression of noise arising from couplings between qubits and their environment, as well as from driving field fluctuations. We propose a double-pulse sequence and an eighteen-pulse sequence to realize a single spin pi-rotation under off-resonance conditions (instead of conventional on-resonance or near-resonance conditions). It is proved that the latter sequence performs much better than the former in simultaneously suppressing both dephasing and driving field noise. As a proof of principle, we experimentally demonstrate, by implementing both sequences in an NMR spin system with a polarized initial spin state, that the off-resonance pi-rotation fidelity reaches as high as 0.9992 +/- 0.0008 for the double-pulse sequence and 0.9997 +/- 0.0006 for the eighteen-pulse sequence. In addition, the noise-tolerance range of the eighteen-pulse sequence is about 20 percent of the driving field strength, approximately three times wider than that of the double-pulse sequence. Besides its potential application in the NMR community, our proposal provides an alternative practical way to accurately control qubits by suppressing the coexisting transversal and longitudinal noises.
one_liner: An 18-pulse off-resonance NMR sequence achieves 0.9997 spin-flip fidelity while suppressing dephasing and drive noise.
why_it_matters: Its noise-tolerance range is about three times wider than that of the proposed double-pulse sequence.

title: Few-Magnon Universality beyond Contact Interactions in Long-Range Spin Chains
abstract: Quantum few-body systems exhibit a rich variety of phenomena that provide fundamental insights into universality. A paradigmatic example is the Efimov effect, in which an infinite tower of three-body bound states emerges with binding energies forming a geometric sequence. Motivated by advances in trapped-ion systems, recent theoretical work has predicted that the Efimov effect can arise in certain long-range quantum spin chains, where magnons exhibit a general dispersion $ε_k=u|k|^z$ with $z\in(0.52,0.88)$ and interact through a contact potential. Nevertheless, whether Efimov universality persists in the presence of experimentally relevant long-range interactions between magnons remains unexplored. In this work, we address this issue by investigating the two- and three-magnon problems with a model interaction potential $V(x)=V_0/(1+|x|^β)$. Our results demonstrate that few-body universality persists for any $β>1$: In the two-magnon sector, the low-energy expansion of the scattering matrix near a two-body resonance agrees with the universal form predicted by contact-interaction theory. The three-magnon bound-state spectrum exhibits Efimov scaling, with a scaling factor consistent with the theory. We further highlight the experimental relevance of our model, which can be readily realized in trapped-ion systems. Our results pave the way for quantum simulations of universal few-body physics beyond the traditional paradigm of nonrelativistic particles.
one_liner: Two- and three-magnon universality, including Efimov scaling, persists for power-law interactions decaying faster than 1/|x|.
why_it_matters: The result extends contact-interaction universality to long-range spin-chain models accessible with trapped ions.

title: Perfect discrimination of an orthogonal $2\otimes2$ basis may require collective separable measurements on two copies
abstract: We consider an orthogonal basis of $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$ with three entangled states and one product state. This basis is not perfectly distinguishable by LOCC or even by separable measurements when a single copy of the unknown state is available. We show that with two copies no adaptive separable protocol, which measures the copies one at a time, distinguishes the basis perfectly. We then show that a collective separable measurement on the two copies does. Whether two copies suffice for LOCC remains open.
one_liner: A two-qubit product-entangled basis needs a collective separable measurement on two copies for perfect discrimination.
why_it_matters: It separates collective separable measurements from all copy-by-copy adaptive separable protocols; the LOCC case remains open.

title: Architectural Robustness to Label Noise Using Variational Quantum Circuits for Medical Image Classification
abstract: Label noise is prevalent in medical image datasets, arising from observer disagreement and ambiguous cases and deep networks memorize the mislabeled examples at the cost of generalization. Current solutions such as loss correction and sample selection add training complexity and generally assume the noise rate is known or estimable. This paper investigates whether robustness can be obtained architecturally, by routing a frozen backbone's features through a low-dimensional bounded bottleneck and classifying them with a head whose function class is intrinsically smooth. Variational quantum circuits with angle encoding and a linear cost function realise exactly such a class. Their use in medical imaging, however, has been limited by the small number of qubits available on noisy intermediate-scale devices, which typically restricts inputs to low-resolution grayscale images. We therefore couple a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 backbone to a trainable linear bottleneck and an eight-qubit variational quantum circuit, allowing 224x224 RGB inputs to be processed. Under clean labels the model leads five of six MedMNISTv2 benchmarks against published hybrid quantum-classical models, with margins of 17.4 and 15.7 percentages on BloodMNIST and PathMNIST. The advantage emerges under corrupted labels. At symmetric noise rates of 30% and 50% the model outperforms many published quantum and noise-robust classical baselines on all six datasets without any explicit noise-handling component. Against a control that shares the backbone, bottleneck, parameter count and optimizer and replaces only the circuit with a ReLU layer, it retains 89.75% accuracy on PathMNIST at 50% noise where the control falls to 78.96%. Direct measurement of training dynamics shows that this advantage is not an inability to fit corrupted labels, which the circuit retains, but greater stability under prolonged training on them.
one_liner: An eight-qubit classifier coupled to a frozen vision transformer remains accurate on medical images with heavily corrupted labels.
why_it_matters: It suggests variational-circuit architecture alone can improve label-noise robustness without estimating the noise rate.

title: Bootstrapping Classical and Quantum Query Lower Bounds for Finding Tarski Fixed Points
abstract: The Tarski fixed-point problem asks for a fixed point of a monotone map on a $k$-dimensional grid lattice of width $n$ and has applications in game theory, economics, and verification. Substantial gaps remain between the known upper and lower bounds on its quantum query complexity. We prove two hardness bootstrapping theorems for quantum query lower bounds. Starting from a hard instance family whose instances have pair-wise incomparable unique fixed points, and a lower bound established by the nonnegative adversary method, we bootstrap this lower bound by (i) a factor of $Ω(t)$ when the dimension is multiplied by $t$ and the width remains unchanged, and (ii) a factor of $Ω(\log m)$ when the width is multiplied by $m$ and the dimension is doubled. Applying these theorems, we obtain three consequences: (i) an $Ω(k\log^2 n)$ lower bound for $k\geq 4$, improving previously best-known classical and quantum lower bounds; (ii) for every fixed constant $α>0$, there exists a constant $δ(α)>0$ such that $Q_ε(\text{Tarski}(n,k))=Ω(kn^{δ(α)})$ whenever $k>n^α$, and in particular, an $Ω(kn^{0.0072})$ lower bound for $k>n^{2/203}$, the first lower bound with simultaneous linear dependence on the dimension and polynomial dependence on the width; and (iii) a superpolynomial lower bound of $(k/\log k)^{Ω(\log k)}$ for exponentially wide grids, where $n=2^{Θ(k)}$. The last result rules out a route to polynomial-time algorithms for simple stochastic games and ARRIVAL through generic polynomial-query black-box Tarski solvers.
one_liner: Hardness bootstrapping yields stronger classical and quantum query lower bounds for finding Tarski fixed points.
why_it_matters: The results constrain black-box approaches to Tarski-based algorithms in games, economics, and verification.

title: Minimal Subsystems for Characterizing Genuine Multipartite Entanglement
abstract: Genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) is a valuable resource for quantum technologies, but quantifying it in many-body systems can be demanding since measures defined through optimizations over bipartitions are often assumed to require large joint measurements and many measurement settings. We introduce the concepts of GME evaluation length and GME evaluation number, which capture, respectively, the largest subsystem that must be jointly measured and the number of distinct subsystems that need to be measured to evaluate multipartite entanglement measures defined via bipartition optimizations. Taking the genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC) as a canonical example, we show that, for $N$-qubit Haar-random pure states, the GMC can be evaluated using only $N$ single-qubit purity measurements. Thus, for typical many-body states, evaluating the GMC requires considering only the $N$ single-site bipartitions, rather than the exponentially many distinct bipartitions. We further corroborate this behavior numerically for physically accessible states generated by local random quantum circuits. Our results show that the practical cost of quantifying GME can be dramatically lower than suggested by its formal definition, establishing measurement complexity as a complementary operational lens for multipartite entanglement.
one_liner: Typical many-qubit pure states need only single-qubit purity measurements to evaluate genuine multipartite concurrence.
why_it_matters: It reduces an apparently exponential entanglement-characterization task to measurements of N single-qubit subsystems.

title: Programmable spatiotemporal shaping for partially coherent structured wave packets
abstract: Providing more coherent light with space-time coupling offers unprecedented opportunities across diverse scientific disciplines and areas of technology. However, in many applications, tailored laser beams with partial coherence in space and time are desired. Here, we demonstrate a programmable approach for simultaneously shaping the intensity and coherence distributions of spatiotemporally coupled partially coherent wave packets. By jointly engineering the fractal speckle of a dynamic scatterer and applying tailored modulation of the illumination function, we experimentally generate partially coherent laser beams with arbitrarily designed intensity and nontrivial coherence distributions. The proposed approach is compatible with ultrafast laser pulses, enabling the on-demand generation of partially coherent space-time wave packets. The resulting spatiotemporally partially coherent wave packets exhibit non-separable space-time intensity profiles together with engineered spatiotemporal correlation distributions. This work provides a versatile framework for tailoring partially coherent light in space and time, with varied applications in relativistic laser-matter interaction, passive imaging and optical manipulation.
one_liner: A programmable optical method independently engineers intensity and coherence in partially coherent space-time wave packets.
why_it_matters: It enables tailored illumination for laser–matter interactions, passive imaging, and optical manipulation.

title: Classical and Quantum Information Measures Characterizing Convertibility: An Axiomatic Approach
abstract: In this PhD thesis, we take an axiomatic approach to studying multivariate divergences, which are measures of the information content of a tuple of classical or quantum states. These divergences are studied in the context of large-sample and catalytic convertibility of tuples of states. This type of convertibility is characterized by the ordering of an axiomatically defined family of divergences. In this thesis, we identify this family of divergences explicitly for two scenarios, one classical and one quantum. In the classical setting, we show that the relevant divergences are certain generalizations of the bivariate Rényi divergences. Unlike previous studies, we do not require the distributions to have the same support, yielding interesting new divergences. In the quantum setting, we consider pairs of classical-quantum states with pure component states, and find that majorization is characterized by all $α$-$z$ relative entropies for $α<1$. This demonstrates the first operational interpretation of these relative entropies.
one_liner: An axiomatic framework identifies divergences that characterize large-sample and catalytic convertibility of classical and quantum states.
why_it_matters: It gives α-z relative entropies an operational meaning and extends classical Rényi-type divergences to unequal supports.

title: Quantitative upper bounds for certain quantum channel divergences
abstract: We show that completely positive maps can be decomposed into sums of submaps which are close in completely bounded trace norm but as far apart as possible in terms of geometric channel fidelity. We then show that this kind of behavior extends to a large class of quantum channel divergences. We construct quantitative norm estimates for quantum channel divergences in terms of the Arveson-Radon-Nikodym theorem.
one_liner: Quantitative norm bounds are developed for a broad class of quantum-channel divergences using Arveson–Radon–Nikodym theory.
why_it_matters: The work clarifies how operationally close channel components can remain maximally separated by fidelity-based measures.

title: Nested polynomial algebras and the exact spectrum of a three-dimensional two-spin oscillator
abstract: We construct representations of the symmetry algebra and derive the exact spectrum of a three-dimensional oscillator with two spin-$\tfrac12$ degrees of freedom. The Hamiltonian and its first-order scalar and pseudo-scalar integrals were obtained in earlier classifications. Here we determine their action on the complete spectral basis. At fixed total angular momentum, a quadratic algebra acts on the three triplet orbital channels and admits a three-dimensional deformed-oscillator representation, while an overlapping two-state exchange algebra joins the middle triplet to the singlet. These finite modules determine angular--spin multiplicities but do not quantize the radial energy. A separate positive-discrete-series $su(1,1)$ representation of the common radial Hamiltonian generates the energy sequence. We give the finite matrices, Casimir and structure functions, normalized eigenfunctions, radial ladder actions, the exceptional $j=0$ sector, complete energy-shell multiplicities, and the effect of particle interchange.
one_liner: Nested polynomial and su(1,1) algebras yield the exact spectrum and eigenstates of a three-dimensional two-spin oscillator.
why_it_matters: It provides a complete algebraic solution, including multiplicities, radial ladders, exchange symmetry, and the exceptional sector.

title: Finite-time quantum equilibration from local correlations
abstract: An isolated quantum system evolves reversibly, yet a small subsystem can lose nearly all information about its initial state. Conserved quantities may retain some of this information, depending on how strongly they overlap with local observables. Here we consider a subsystem in an arbitrary initial state coupled to a maximally mixed bath. We show that the worst-input mean-square equilibration error, maximised over window origins, is bounded from above and below by the mean square of a complete local autocorrelation, with the stationary part subtracted. A correlation record over a finite interval therefore controls the equilibration error in every interval of the same length. The result allows arbitrary degeneracies of energies and gaps. We apply it to two static Hamiltonian families. For fixed spin subsystems in the one-particle sector of a bounded-range periodic clock, fixed-accuracy thermalisation is guaranteed on windows that grow only slightly faster than linearly with system size, despite exponentially small positive energies. A random commuting model with logarithmic interaction range retains an extensive set of conserved observables. Its expected mean-square error is bounded by a finite-size term and an inverse-time term. The inverse-time dependence is unavoidable because of the initial transient. These examples show how local relaxation can coexist with exact conservation laws and a finely spaced spectrum.
one_liner: Finite-time subsystem equilibration is bounded above and below by a stationary-subtracted local autocorrelation record.
why_it_matters: It connects measurable local correlations to rigorous relaxation guarantees despite degeneracies and conservation laws.

title: High Sensitivity Transient Holographic Full-Polarization Microscopy
abstract: The polarization state of light provides direct access to ultrafast electronic, magnetic, and structural dynamics in materials.
